translations.text: To Louis, king of the eastern realms, be eternal salvation.
Louis the bold, full of wisdom, rules all the eastern realm, as a king of the Franks should;
Over the land of the Franks extends all his power; all his power governs it, as I tell you.
To him be ever health and blessedness together; may the Lord increase his good fortune and ever gladden his heart;
May He raise his spirits always, at all times, well; may he rejoice at every hour! For this let everyone always pray!
If I choose to recount his praise, and spend my hours on writing his deeds:
That whole undertaking is beyond my powers; lofty, as I tell you, are all his affairs,
For he is a noble Frank, of wise thoughts, of wise speech; he does everything with fairness.
In his own breast is a very steadfast heart and manifold goodness; therefore he is gracious to his people.
Of keen thoughts is this same Frank, and so is this same nobleman; he is called Louis.
Often he was truly in distress; he escaped it at once by God's protection, quickly and very splendidly.
Whenever it came to the need to fight, he was always superior in the matter by God's powers.
God often counselled him in distress, in heavy toils; if he came into danger anywhere, the Lord at once helped him
in perilous deeds; for this he shall thank God; for this let his retinue thank Him too, and our poor lowliness!
He granted us His mercy, in that He preserved such a king for us; may He now spare him in life for us all, ever to our joy!
Now we enjoy the benefits and peaceful times through his own deeds; for this we ought to thank God;
For this let everyone now gladly ask His grace, that he may have protection from God and be long in health!
May he live always, at all times, well and in good spirits, and ever escape danger, the ambush of enemies!
Long, my dear Lord, let his days be; make all his life sweet for him, as one should for a good man!
In him I strongly call to mind the deeds of David himself: he too once suffered distress and many hardships,
For he wished to be a man (that later became very plain), to be truly a warrior in many perils.
He suffered many sorrows until God permitted it; afterwards he overcame them, as befits a warrior of God.
The good Lord Himself always counselled him graciously; this I tell you in all truth; you can read it there yourself.
We have the same goodness, a like heroism, in this man's own spirit, to our great benefit.
Certainly, I will not hide it from you, this man likewise suffered hardships enough; he likewise endured them with patience;
For all that, he did not let hatred into his heart; with patience, as he had begun, he overcame all his enemies.
If anyone ever set out to strive against him, the Lord always lovingly protected him;
He always counselled him in troubles and in heavy hardships, and lightened for him all his years, which had seemed very heavy to him,
Until He led him on and widened his kingdom for him. Therefore this one may be counted as of David's lineage.
In the same way he too came to the kingship. That one was very much God's beloved; so this one has become too, as is fitting.
That one ruled God's people well in the Lord's service; so does this one too, year after year, as befits God, that is true;
Constantly for good, always with a sound heart, from year to year; this I tell you truly.
Through hardship David held to what the Lord commanded him, and he made his affairs secure, and the kingdom itself too, all around.
In this one it is also plain that, as far as his strength allows him, he is always earnestly serving God;
He governs his whole kingdom well, as he should, and he is of good courage and of a very lively spirit.
Indeed, among others these kingdoms and their splendour inevitably waver;
Yet this one, of necessity and as the Lord Himself commanded, has nailed this firmly shut, so that the enemy does not come against us;
It is always barred, so that the adversary does not hinder us; of that we can be sure. Long may he enjoy life!
Through all the times that are his, may Christ comfort his heart; may he escape all pain too; may God gladden his soul!
Long may his days be, until eternal life; may he also escape the fall of hostile attacks, so that we may be safe above all!
For this has been found: as long as we keep him in good health, we live, as I mean it, with joy and with well-being,
Always contented, and we have good times. May he also enjoy gladness, and may it never fail him in eternity!
May all his children have power along with love; and may the queen herself also have love toward God!
May they forever enjoy eternal loving fellowship, as I said, truly there in heaven with Louis!
For him I compose this book. If he cares for it, or if he comes to know of it, may he at once order it to be read:
Here in these words he may hear the gospels, and what Christ commanded in them to the people of the Franks.
The rule of this book shows us the kingdom of heaven. May Louis forever enjoy God's eternal years there!
May his heart forever enjoy the eternal good; and there too, my Lord, let me be with him forever!
May he live there contentedly for all time; may the eternal sun ever shine joy upon him there!
Otfrid to Bishop Salomo.
May pleasant blessings come to Salomo the good, who is now bishop of the noble see of Constance;
may he who called him to that office double upon his head all the good that the bishops who were there before him had!
I send you a reading of this book into the kingdom of the Swabians, so that you may examine it thoroughly and decide whether it ought to be of use;
if you find anything here that is worth reading, may your mind, full of wisdom, ponder it.
Your learning, your wisdom, was often very useful to me in the past; for that I give great praise.
I often call to mind the many good things that you taught me earnestly with your own words.
Not that my abilities could ever have earned it, or have won such favor in those matters;
it was done by your noble kindness, your own goodness, your provision, and not at all by my deeds.
Now above all I shall continually ask the Lord to repay you for it with a reward, and with his own word;
may he give you the rest of Paradise to delight you. He who held fast to God's law has never gone unrewarded.
In the beauty of the kingdom of heaven may it be your reward, with an abundance of recompense, that you gave me instruction.
If there is anything in this book that any man might care for, of words or of good things, anything that pleases your mind:
in your mind, turn that to your own credit on account of your instruction, and count it, without wavering, wholly to your merit.
It often happens that when a man's disciple does good, the good teacher profits greatly by it.
May Peter the mighty reward you gladly for it, he for whom the Lord dug a grave at Rome and gave house and court;
may Christ the good himself always send you pleasant blessings in joy from heaven above!
If I dare to make so bold, I shall not leave it at all of that, but shall always gladly ask his grace for you,
that he may raise up your dignity with his own favor and fix his manifold goodness firmly in your heart;
may he grant you his kingdom, the high kingdom of heaven, because the good man here always wept and continually called upon God;
may he guide you both there early, and join me to it, so that we may rejoice there in God's eternal year,
may he gladden us in heaven so that we escape punishment; and may he show us that kindness through his goodness!
May he do it for our good, with a glad heart! Born in good fortune was he who ever found that blessedness there,
for he will never again fail (believe me in this) to rejoice in his heart there forever in good things.
May Christ the good himself kindly grant us here that we may ever be glad at heart in the eternal good!
HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE GOSPELS, WRITTEN IN GERMAN BY THE GRACE OF THE LORD. Here begin the chapters.
I. Why the writer composed this book in German.
II. The writer's invocation to God.
III. The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David.
IV. There was in the days of King Herod a priest named Zechariah.
V. The angel Gabriel was sent to the Virgin Mary.
VI. And Mary arose and went into the hill country.
VII. On the song of Saint Mary.
VIII. When Mary, the mother of Jesus, was betrothed.
IX. Now Elizabeth's time to give birth was fulfilled.
X. The song of Zechariah.
XI. A decree went out from Caesar Augustus, and so on.
XII. There were shepherds in the same region.
XIII. The shepherds said to one another.
XIV. On the circumcision of the child and the purification of Saint Mary.
XV. On the meeting with Simeon and his blessing.
XVI. On Anna the prophetess.
XVII. On the star and the coming of the Magi.
XVIII. Spiritually [interpreted] [?]: on the return of the Magi to their homeland.
XIX. On the flight of Joseph with the mother and the child into Egypt.
XX. On the slaughter of the infants.
XXI. On the death of Herod and the return of Joseph with the mother and the child.
XXII. When Jesus was twelve years old.
XXIII. On the preaching of John and his baptism.
XXIV. The crowds asked John: What shall we do?
XXV. Jesus came from Galilee to John, to be baptized by him.
Let that be sweet to you: then the feet measure it, the time and the rule; then it is God's own preaching.
If you want to consider this well, if you want to pay attention to metre, to win fame in your own tongue and to make beautiful verses:
Strive always to fulfil God's will at all times; then God's servants write the rule in Frankish;
Let your feet walk in the sweetness of God's command, and do not let the time slip away from you in it: then beautiful verse is made at once;
Always compose, as you must, these six ages, so that you prepare yourself in this way to rest in the seventh.
What Christ's words told us and what his beloved disciples recounted to us, I set all of that first, as I rightly must;
For they sang it most excellently in noble languages, they arranged it all with God and also adorned it with deeds.
That is sweet and also useful, and it teaches us wisdom, a thing fitting for heaven; beside it, anything else is a different matter.
Why, as I said, should the Franks alone be unfit for this, when the peoples we listed above did not hold back from it at all?
They are just as bold as the Romans themselves; and no one needs to claim that the Greeks rival them in this.
For their use they have wisdom just the same; in field and in forest they are equally brave;
They have wealth enough and are also very bold; all the warriors are quick to take up weapons.
They live well provided for (and have always been used to this) in a good land; for that reason they are without shame.
It is very fertile (this is well known), with many kinds of goods; and that is not because of our own merit.
For use, ore and copper are also dug there, and indeed ironstones as well;
Add to this silver in plenty; and in that land they also gather gold in their sand.
They are steadfast in many good things and for many uses; they do this through their wisdom.
They are very ready to defend themselves against enemies; their enemies do not dare to start anything, because the Franks have overcome them.
No people that borders their land escapes them; because of the Franks' strength, those peoples must always serve them;
And all people, unless the sea lies between them (I know God made it so), live in fear of them.
There is no people that undertakes to fight against them; the Franks have made that plain to them and shown it with weapons.
They taught it to them with swords, not with words at all, and with very sharp spears; for that reason they still fear them so much.
Let no people think of fighting with them, even if they are Medes or Persians, unless it is to go worse for them.
I once read for you, truly, in a certain book (I know where) that in kinship and lineage they are of Alexander's race,
who so threatened the world that he laid it all low with the sword under his hands, in very hard bonds;
I also found in the account that this people was, by birth, separated off from Macedonia.
Among them there is none who would tolerate a king ruling them, none in the world, unless it be one whom they raised at home;
or that anyone else on earth, from any other people, should undertake to command over them.
From this they always gain in boldness and in wisdom; they fear no one, so long as they have him safe.
He is ready for anything, as a noble warrior always should be, wise and bold; of such men they always have plenty.
He clearly rules over many peoples, and he governs them justly, just as he governs his own at home.
Nor are there any who can harm him, since the Franks defend him; their bold men are ready [?] to ride around him.
For all that they think of, they do it all with God; in time of need they do nothing without His counsel.
They are very eager for God's words, so that they learn what the books tell them;
so that they set about singing it out, and also carry it out with great will. — Established
is it now in the account that they are good warriors, all of them also serving God and full of wisdom.
Now I will write of our salvation, a part of the Gospels, in the Frankish tongue, as we have begun here;
so that they alone should not be deprived of this, with no one singing Christ's praise in their tongue;
and so that He who drew them to Himself and called them to His faith may also be greatly praised in their words.
If there is anyone in their land who does not understand it any other way, and cannot understand it in another tongue,
let him hear here, for his good, what God commands him, which we have sung to him here in the Frankish tongue.
Now let everyone rejoice in this who means well, and whoever is kindly disposed in mind toward the Frankish people,
that we have sung to Christ in our own tongue, and that we have also lived to see ourselves praise Him in Frankish!
II. The writer's invocation to God.
O my Lord, truly I am your servant; my poor mother is your own handmaid, she is yours!
Lay your finger on my mouth, and stretch your hand into my tongue too,
so that your praise may sound forth, the birth of your Son, my Lord;
and so that I may begin to tell how He began to preach, and may pay close attention to His words;
and to the miracles that He did then, which make us so glad now, and how that same salvation is now shared by all the world;
and so that I may also write here, to guide us to right living, how He found us lost when He Himself dared to face death;
and also how he then went up above all the heavens, above the light of the sun and all the peoples of this world;
that I, Lord, may not stumble in this story, nor get the words wrong in this fine work;
that I do not write for fame, but to praise you, so that it never turns into punishment for me.
If it still comes to that through my foolishness, then, Lord, mercifully blot out my sin.
For (I tell you my hope) it is not done out of malice; and I do not leave anything out out of any spite.
I tell you this hope because you know the heart far better; though it dwells within me, it is much better known to you.
Therefore, Lord, grant me grace fully; be mindful of me with the power of your creation!
Be mindful here of my words, so that you keep them firmly; may your grace grant them success, so that they prosper.
And may your adversary not come into my mind, so that he does not harm me here or hinder me in any way!
Let his wickedness withdraw and your grace come near; let his evil be driven far away. You, Lord, direct my words!
All languages, that is: you alone, Lord, are the Lord of them all; you rule this people and all the peoples of the world.
By your power you made them all able to speak, and by blessing the words in their tongues prospered for them,
so that they would always think of you and praise you forever into eternity, and know you and do you service.
From this multitude you soon set apart your followers; so let me, my Lord, be forever with your beloved ones!
And may it serve you here and now beautifully in my tongue (and in every language, as far as I know it),
so that in the kingdom of heaven I may please you forever, Lord, and rejoice forever, rightly, in your sight
with your angels; this is not by my works, but truly and rightly by your grace.
You always help with the power of your creation; show your favour to me, so that I may then praise you forever,
so that I also make it my practice now (so that it may always go better for me) to fulfil your service and never want anything else at all;
and that nothing at all may ever cling to me here in life, Lord, unless it is your will; you are always gracious.
I beg you with all my heart that an abundance of every good may come to me in eternity, and that you join me to your beloved ones,
so that I may be forever, my Lord, with that comfort, and with that good thing rejoice there all my days and all my years;
from year to year may I rejoice there forever, from eternity to eternity, with the blessed souls!
III. The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David.
These are holy books: they show very beautifully and tell us beyond dispute the ancestors of Christ.
They tell us a great deal here about how he himself came here into the world, and of the great joy that is his noble lineage.
Adam was the first of men, a famous forefather, made by the Lord.
In the earlier ages of the world he begot people; he kept spreading the lineage until Christ showed himself to us.
Noah, I tell you this, was not the least among them. From him the peoples were afterwards restored [?], and that was needed.
He built the ark for his children on the waters. He guided them through the flood and also rescued them from the danger.
Abraham did good and made himself pleasing to the Lord, for he was obedient. That is why he is now so greatly honoured.
The books teach us that he is an ancestor of Christ, and they also give us the famous account that his son was his father.
That was David, one of these men, who rose to be king. He reached such goodness through his valour as a warrior.
His kindness taught him to become such a man that he plainly became king of the people.
There is no man who could count the whole line, even if he wanted to. Yet these are, of necessity, the foremost in excellence.
Without doubt it is divided into three parts, this nobility growing out of them by birth:
The great patriarchs reach down to the kings, and the third line from there were noble lords.
They were the roots of the blessed flower, the mother of the glorious one, God's beloved maiden.
Pay attention to what we have told you. Do not be dull-minded. Take in this teaching, and I will tell you more about it:
I mean Saint Mary, the mighty queen. The host of angels honours her in heaven.
Likewise, whoever on earth seeks blessing should show great humility to her goodness.
Count the generations from the beginning of the world up to her time: they come to eleven times seven.
Her days were foretold by the ancient prophets: that she would bear for us the one who would heal us.
Hallowed for ever, he has shown mercy to us souls and to the whole world, as everyone can now see.
See, lordship is humility to him as far as the world reaches, for he is the Lord.
He is exceedingly mighty, and he came here into the world to us, here among human beings, with wondrous deeds.
I want to tell this here to all his faithful ones, as we now begin here in Frankish words.
But first I will write here, as it is in the gospels, how John, his servant, was born before him.
John prepared the way for him ahead of time in the face of what the world had done wrong. He made the ways straight for him everywhere, as one should for a lord.
IV. THERE WAS IN THE DAYS OF KING HEROD A PRIEST NAMED ZACHARIAS.
For us the days of bearing children are long past; heavy old age makes it hopeless for us.
Much of our youth has passed over us; old age does not give us what youth should have given.
How then can I know that a child will come to us? For in old age it has been taken from us, right up to the end."
Then the messenger of God spoke, though not in anger; he told him the same message again:
"I am one of the seven, of God's beloved messengers, who stand always in his sight,
whom he sends here into the world when he works mighty deeds, and they make known very weighty works.
He sent me from heaven to tell you this very thing, from the height of the heavenly kingdom, so that I might make it known to you.
Now, since you scorn the message so strongly, you shall at once become mute, until you see it truly come to pass;
because you are contrary to God's message, and you also deny what God himself is giving.
It will be fulfilled nonetheless, at the time God has set; until then you will sorely lack your words."
The people were standing outside, and they wondered greatly why the priest was taking so long;
why he did not tell them that God had accepted the prayer, and did not bless them with his hand.
Then he came out late, badly frightened; he had been struck dumb, because he did not believe.
Then he made signs, without speaking, that the crowd of people should go home.
They left in sorrow and also pondering, because he told them nothing of the wonder he had seen there.
When the days of the offering came to an end, he too went straight away to his home.
Grieving for his speech, he rejoiced in the hope; he believed very late, and so he had to wait so painfully.
The woman was carrying a son and was very ashamed that in her old age she would have to go about with a child in hand.
5. THE ANGEL GABRIEL WAS SENT.
After this there passed, as it might be, half a year: by count of months, three times two.
Then came a messenger from God, an angel from heaven; he brought this world a precious message.
He flew the sun's path, the road of the stars, the ways of the clouds, to the holy lady;
to the noble lady, Saint Mary herself, whose forebears had all been kings, generation after generation.
He went into the palace and found her sorrowful, with the psalter in her hand, which she was singing through to the end;
she was weaving fine cloths from precious yarn, which she always did gladly.
Then he spoke with full honour, as one should to a lady, as a good messenger always should, to the mother of the Lord:
"Hail, glorious maiden, maiden so beautiful, of all women the most pleasing to God!
Do not trouble your heart, and do not let the colour of your face change; you are full of God's grace!
The prophets sang of you, blessed one; through all the ages they were pointing to you.
White gem, shining maiden, you alone shall be the precious mother.
You shall bear one who rules over all: over earth and heaven and every living thing,
the Creator of the world (that is my message), born of the Father and coeternal with him.
God will give him consecration and very high honour (do not doubt it at all): the seat of King David.
He will reign openly as king of this people (that lies in God's hand) without any end.
He gives life to the whole world, so that he will also unlock the kingdom of heaven for humankind."
The maiden spoke very fittingly to the Lord's messenger; she gave him an answer with sweet graciousness:
"How can it be, my lord, that I am worthy of this, that I should nurse the Lord's son?
How can it ever come true that I become pregnant? No man has ever touched me, not even in my thoughts.
I have resolved, and it is fixed firmly in my heart, that I would live my life alone."
Then that same beloved servant of the Lord spoke to her aloud a swift and very excellent message:
"I shall tell you, maiden, a very secret matter: blessedness is with your soul forever.
I tell you one thing: this child of yours shall rightly be called the holy Son of God.
His throne is established in heaven; there is no king in the world who will not serve him,
nor any emperor among men who will not bring him gifts, falling at his feet and honouring him.
He shall greatly protect his beloved ones; he will capture the old Satan.
There is no place on earth where Satan can ever escape him, nor any corner under heaven where he can save himself.
If he flees into the sea, he will harm him there; he will shut him out from the high kingdom of heaven.
He has already passed judgement on him and resolved for himself that he will crush him in the pit of hell with a chain.
There is a kinswoman of yours, barren in her womb, who has already lived out many days, for a long time now;
now she is pregnant with so precious a child that there is no woman in the world bearing a child who is more distinguished."
Then many noblemen stood around there, and they were reaching agreement among themselves on what the child should be named.
Out of love, they all spoke with one voice, saying that he should take after his father, now in his old age.
They said it would be fitting for him to take his father's name, so that the old man would always be remembered in the naming.
Then the mother spoke aloud (the son was dear to her): "This is my dear child; John shall be his name.
Truly, I refuse you the father's name at once. You must say what I say; this is how the name shall always be."
They spoke very cheerfully to the blessed woman and said that it was not fitting. They did not accept the name.
"In your family, count them all man by man, no one is remembered who ever had that name."
Then they stood looking at the mute father and made signs to him, asking what he wanted the name to be.
At once he removed the doubt entirely. He wrote it down, so that the people saw it, just as the mother had said.
The crowd in turn marvelled at this: his tongue was mute, yet they were of one voice.
Then his mouth at once began to speak, and the bond on his tongue was loosened.
He praised the Lord who had done this, the like of which no one had ever seen in the world before.
Then the people were afraid at the wondrous deeds, and they made the beautiful marvel known.
All the hill country, all the towns and the plains of the valley: all of it was praising it.
And I will tell you what all those who heard it did: they at once fixed the good thing very firmly in their minds.
They spoke very boldly: "What do you think he will become?" The child grew in the hand of the Lord.
X. The Canticle of Zacharias.
Then the old father was filled with God's holy spirit, and he spoke what the old prophets have told us.
"Blessed be the Lord God of this people, who has redeemed us and has himself visited us.
He has raised up for us a horn of salvation, not of fighting, in the lineage of a king, his beloved servant,
just as he had always promised to this wretched world through all his prophets.
He has also raised up for us a saviour, so that our enemies avoid us, along with all the people who persecute us.
Now he wills to show mercy to our forefathers. He remembers that he left here [?] what he often promised them,
as he long ago promised to his beloved man that he would give us the sight of himself in the flesh,
so that we, comforted in this way and redeemed from our enemies, may serve him without fear,
Then she gladly offered her maidenly breasts; she did not hold back but showed them, and she suckled the Son of God.
Blessed were the breasts that Christ ever kissed, and the mother who spoke to him and constantly kept him covered;
Blessed was she who nursed [?] him and set him in her lap, who gently lulled him to sleep and laid him beside her!
Blessed was she who clothed him and cared for him, and who lies in bed with such a child;
Blessed was she who protected him when the frost hurt him, her arms and hands embracing him!
There is no one on earth who could sing her praise to the end, nor any man ever so zealous that he could recount all her goodness;
There is no one the day touches or the sun shines on who could ever finish it, even if he began it!
For her good son graciously glorifies her; her praise and renown are such that you cannot count them.
She is a glorious mother, and yet truly a virgin; she bore for us the most perfect heavenly Lord.
Mystically. The Lord chose to come at the time when the whole world was being counted, so that all of us alike would be enrolled in the kingdom of heaven.
They laid him in a manger, where the cattle were fed, because he wishes to provide for us and lead us to the eternal feast.
If that birth had not happened, the world would have been lost; Satan would have taken it if he had not come then.
We were in bonds, in hostile hands; you, Lord, gave us help in our utmost need!
XII. And there were shepherds in the same region.
There were shepherds in that land, keeping watch over the livestock to guard them against enemies.
A beautiful messenger came to them, a shining angel, and they were lit up by heavenly light.
They were suddenly afraid when they saw him, and the words of God's messenger startled them greatly.
God's messenger spoke at once: "I am going to tell you something wonderful: salvation will come to you from God, and you have nothing to fear.
I am going to give you a message that the God of heaven commanded, and no one has ever heard so lordly a message.
Because of it his world will be joyful forever, and so will all creation in the world that walks on this earth.
This land has had the heavenly Savior newly born to it, that is the good Lord Christ, from a young mother,
In Bethlehem. The kings all came from there, and from them his mother was born too, the fair maiden.
Good men, I will tell you how you will find him, and a sign is fitting too, because of the wonder of it.
Go from here to the town. As I told you, you will find a newborn child lying in a manger."
Then, while he was speaking to them, a host of angels came, a heavenly multitude, all singing like this:
In the height of the kingdom of heaven, glory be to God, and on earth peace also to all who are full of good will!
Mystically. They announced the good news to us early, and also taught a song with it. Consider within your heart what this verse sings:
Do not let the desire for evil will into your breast, so that it does not take away from you the peace in the kingdom of heaven.
We should practise that song; it is a beautiful way of receiving God, because the angels brought it to us from heaven as an example.
A bishop who keeps watch over Christian people is also worthy of the beautiful sight of angels.
The angels flew back to heaven, singing, into the sight of the Lord; that was fitting for them.
XIII. THE SHEPHERDS SPOKE TO ONE ANOTHER.
Then the shepherds, those same keepers of the herds, spoke (they were considering the message, those same words of the angel):
"Let us all hurry now to the town, so that we too, with the country people [?], may see that word of God
that the Lord wished to bring about and sent here into the world; indeed, the gracious God showed us the message first."
Then they went quickly and in great haste; they set out very early, and their minds were firmly set on it.
When they came there, they saw the mother; she had set the best of children in her lap;
and also the man who had brought her there, who watched over the two of them; it had to be so, that he served them.
They saw the word there and recognized it at once, which the angels had shown them where they were tending the cattle.
All who heard it were greatly amazed, and they also felt more fear when the shepherds told this.
The mother kept the words firmly in her breast, pondering this carefully in her heart and mind:
how the words that the prophets had spoken before were coming to pass here, and how all this had also come about so fittingly.
Then the shepherds went straight back home on their way; they rejoiced greatly at the true words.
They had found it all there just as the angels had told them; for this each of them praised the Lord gloriously.
XIV. ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE CHILD AND ON THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY.
When the eighth day came during which she had nursed the child, they had to fulfil the law willingly,
the custom that the old forefathers had always kept. They also knew how things stood with the name; they called him Savior,
as the angel had told them and shown it to them before she was with child.
The name is well meant, because he heals the people. The angel had announced it before, and the meaning of the name is explained there.
The law commanded the people very strictly (and we too should now fulfil it willingly and constantly),
Any woman who gave birth to a male child would be unclean from the birth for forty days;
she was to keep herself apart during that time and not pray in God's house; after that she was at once to present the child there.
This applied if the child had been born of a man's begetting; so the virgin and her son had no need of it.
Yet she came, as she was obliged to, as the law prescribed, once the days we have just spoken of no longer kept her from the journey.
They went out of the town to the Lord's house. They remembered the commandment and brought the child there too,
for it was a male child, the woman's first child (I shall tell you a wonder): it belonged especially to God;
so that they would also offer to God there on the child's behalf a pair of doves, as the law commanded to be done.
XV. On the meeting and blessing of Simeon.
There was an old man there, counted among the blessed; he had served God there for very many years.
He was God-fearing and lived rightly in all things; he waited there in sweet hope for the Lord's promises.
The Spirit of God that was upon him had promised him that he would carry Christ in his hands before the end of his days;
he would never taste death before he had that comfort. The holiness of God's Spirit granted him what was promised.
Then the blessed man came (he was far on in his days) into the house I have just spoken of, where he prayed continually.
The good mother also brought the child there; there the good Simeon met them gladly.
He bowed very low to him and lifted him into his arms; then his old servant also spoke very joyfully:
"Now, Lord, you let your servant be in peace, full of days and abundance, as your word always promised me;
for my eyes have now seen the salvation that you prepared for us before you made the world:
a light that shines and touches all the world, and the glory of this people."
Then the mother marvelled greatly at the words that were spoken at all those times,
and he who was thought to be the child's father pondered each of them with great awe.
Then the old man, already named above, blessed them, and the good prophet spoke to the mother:
"Take my word now into your heart, maiden, and remember it firmly above all things, virgin, what I shall tell you.
This child is set among men for the fall of many, and for the rising of those who are sure of life,
as a very weighty sign; yet people will speak against it." The benefit is shown here, to anyone who does not believe it:
he is the good Lord, and his mother is also a virgin; he turns himself toward death and rises on the third day;
Then he will also go over all the heavens, over the light of the sun and over all the people of this world.
He will come in power, as soon as the end of the world arrives, very high in the clouds, and we shall see him in his beauty.
With him are his followers and a host of angels; there, I tell you, he will hold a very weighty court.
There he will make plain what we hide here now; whether it is evil or anything else, it will not stay hidden there.
The unbelievers, who all scorn it, will always fiercely deny the wondrous deeds.
"And a very sharp weapon will wound your life, a bitter pain will pierce your very soul.
You will see your dear son dragged away to be tortured; then your heart will weep with great pain.
Then many people will speak out what they had long kept hidden; the hatred hidden in a person will all show itself then."
XVI. Of Anna the Prophetess.
There was a woman there named Anna; she had served there for many years and was already very far on in years.
She was a good prophetess and turned her mind to God; she kept her widowhood worthily and went on in goodness.
When she came to be without her beloved husband, she thought about where she should look for comfort.
She went at once to the house of God and spent her days there; there she made her sorrow known and cared no more about a husband.
Then she turned her thoughts to the service of God without wavering, and there she served God faithfully at all times.
She prayed at all hours and also fasted a great deal; she kept God's will and carried out his service.
Day and night she strove there for what is right; she became a widow in her youth and grew old in this way of life.
Then she came, at the same hour I told of concerning the old man, so that she saw the little child there and also spoke praise of the Lord.
She made known there how things stood: that blessing had come to them in this, salvation for life, for men and women alike.
"Old and young: whoever puts their hope in it will enjoy life and eternal joy."
When they had done everything there that the books laid down for them, they hurried at once on the road to their home.
The child grew among people like a lily among thorns; like a flower among the plants, he grew beautifully toward goodness.
Wisdom grew in him right away, which was truly fitting; he was filled with wisdom, as the Son of God should be.
The Spirit of God was on him; you need not wonder at that, for it was in his own hand, under his power.
XVII. Of the Star and the Coming of the Magi.
There is no one in the world who could tell all at once how many wonders happened at the birth of the Lord.
Because I put it off and did not tell it earlier, I shall now gladly recount some of it here.
When the Lord Christ was born (I need say no more about that now), so that the world became glad at the blessed birth,
And it was also brought about that the world would not be lost forever (that fate was close at hand for it when the Lord put an end to it):
Then there came into the land from the east men who knew the course of the sun and the order of the stars; that was their skill.
Throughout their journey they kept asking about the child, and they also spread the news that he was the king.
They asked where he had been born, and they begged urgently to be shown.
They told of strange things and very beautiful signs, a very great wonder, for no one had ever heard
That a man had been born of a virgin; and they also told of his beautiful sign shining so brightly in the sky.
They said that they had suddenly seen a star, and they declared loudly that it was his.
"We have seen his star, though we are not sure of the city, and we have come to worship him and receive his grace.
Far away in the east the star shone on us like this. Is there anyone here in this land who understands anything about it?
We have always counted the stars, and we never saw this one before. So we now agree that it can only point to a king.
That is what men wrote for us in our land in ancient times. Now tell us also what your books sing about it."
When these words suddenly reached the king, he was badly alarmed by them,
And everyone's mind there was troubled by it. They did not want to hear what we now gladly enjoy.
He also gathered the scribes there at once and asked them where Christ was to be born.
He spoke to the priests in these very words, and poor and rich alike gave him an answer.
They named the city at once, and they confirmed it truly with the words that the old prophets had spoken long before.
When he had found out for certain where the Lord Christ was born, he at once planned great wickedness in his heart.
He also summoned to himself the wise men I spoke of, and he held council with them in great secrecy.
He asked them the time when the star had first appeared to them. He also asked them to take care to seek out that child.
"Do this for me with care," he said, "by following the course of the star. Go, and ask about the child there at once!
Ask about him everywhere and very carefully, and then let me know quickly.
I want to go and worship him (many men have advised me to), so that I may commit myself to him and also bring him gifts."
The wretched man lied. He was full of deceit there. He wanted to destroy him and wipe out our salvation.
When they had heard the message and hurried on their way, the wondrous star at once appeared to them from afar.
They quickly rejoiced at it as soon as they saw it, and all together they watched it very joyfully.
Then it led them well to where the holy child was; by its course it was showing them the place.
Then they saw the house and at once went into it; there was the good son with his mother.
Then they fell forward, eager for that good; there they worshipped the child and sought his favor.
Then and there they at once opened their treasure; they were mindful of what was right, so they brought him gifts:
myrrh and frankincense, and shining gold as well, very glorious gifts; they sought his protection.
Mystically. I tell you this in truth: they could have brought more; but this was so fitting that it was spiritual.
Through these wondrous gifts they then proclaimed to us the true faith, so that we may all understand it:
that he was our renowned priest, also a king by birth, and that he died for our sake.
While they slept, they were warned by angels; in a dream the angels told them the way they should go,
so that they should not think of going near the king, nor tell that man what had happened.
Then the companions travelled by another road, hurrying hard to their own land.
XVIII. Mystically.
This journey warns us to pay attention to it, so that we too may take care of ourselves and seek our own land.
You do not know it, but I do: that land is called paradise. I can praise it greatly, and I do not run short of words.
Yet even if every limb of mine could speak every word, I still could not reach the end of its praise in words.
You will never believe it unless you see it yourself; and even then you could not describe it to anyone.
There is life without death, light without darkness, the company of angels, and eternal bliss.
We have left it behind; we may always lament that, and always weep without end for our homeland.
We went out of it under compulsion, because of pride; our own self-will lured us away so quietly.
We did not want to be obedient, and we clearly bear the signs of it; now we weep as exiles in a foreign land.
Now our noble inheritance lies useless to us, and we do not enjoy its goodness; this is what pride does to us!
Alas, we now lack a great many dear things, and here we suffer the hardship of bitter times.
Now we mourn here in this land with pain, in many kinds of wounds, because of our sins;
"There is no need for you to stay," he said, "their enemy is dead; so always hurry on the journey to your home."
He set out homeward at once and heard the words gladly; so the good son travelled together with his mother.
Then he heard news that there was another king, and he was greatly alarmed at those words.
Then he turned away into the distance, to a fine town; there he raised the child well and escaped the enemies.
The child grew very fair and very quickly in understanding, always thriving in wisdom before God and before people.
XXII. When Jesus was twelve years old.
When he was older, twice six years old, they made a point of hurrying to the high feasts.
Those days are so holy that no one can fully tell of them; we regard them with awe and call them Easter.
They went to the holy feast as they were used to doing, mindful of the law, and they took the child with them.
When they had prayed there and the festival was over, they hurried home at once and did not linger there.
The child held back from the journey. They did not notice it, and they left their only son unwatched.
Joseph, the wise man, thought the boy was with his mother; she thought, in all truth, that he was with Joseph.
Do not be surprised at this: the women travelled separately, and the men went in the group behind.
The children followed whichever group they wanted, running along quietly as they pleased.
So they were misled by this mistake, and in earnest they fell into very great anguish.
When they got home, they looked around them at once on that journey, and then they found the child missing.
They searched among acquaintances and among relatives. They found him nowhere there and could not bring him back at once.
Then the mother was alarmed (the son is so good!), and many anxieties stirred her breast.
She struck her breast with her hands and began to grieve bitterly, lamenting her grief sorely, for he was her only son.
They were deeply distressed, in great anguish the whole time; their haste was heavy.
The mother needed this badly, so they hurried back at once; the pain touched her deep in her heart.
They went back very quickly to the city where they had been, and there, on the third day, they found the child.
He was there. He had gone in with the teachers, and he eagerly joined the gathering.
He listened to their words and paid close attention. He sat alone in the middle of them and questioned them closely.
They were greatly amazed at the young child's words and listened with delight to his answers.
If there is anything there so sharp, or anything so proud [?], it will be made straight, into fair smoothness.
Make straight all the ways that lead to your hearts; with truly righteous works hasten to make them smooth,
so that if it ever happens that he walks on them, he does not stumble there because of you, to your ruin.
No one was ever born a man who will not at some time see, and indeed the whole world across the land will see, the Lord's salvation!"
He went about with this preaching, with great discourse, and rebuked them all alike very powerfully.
He spoke to those who cared about it, who sought his baptism, to very many people, and with very weighty words:
"Who showed you," he said, "you utterly lost ones, born of vipers, that you could escape God's judgment safely?
No one should even try, once He begins to grow angry, to hide himself anywhere from His wrath.
Begin to give thanks to God, so that you may escape this terrible misery, you brood of vipers!
You must always repent faithfully before God, so that it may grow for you in His sight.
Do not trust in this: that each of you is of noble birth, or that the virtue of your forefathers will shield these deeds.
God can bring these pebbles, and all these rocks, and all these stones to life as men,
so that they too are counted as your lineage, and are surely better than your goodness.
The axe is already sharpened and set to the root, and it is very keen for whatever it touches.
There is no tree in the world that does not bear fruit which it will not destroy and set fire to.
Therefore repent quickly, and let every man feel remorse, and take great care that you are not those trees."
Remember these words (there is great need of them!), so that each one takes care that the axe does not cut him;
and let every man take care that it does not hew him down, so that you, out of the whole forest, do not fall forever;
so that the fire never burns you, and your deeds do not torment you in eternity.
All this is said in this way (I am telling you about the axe; do not think that I am mocking you): it is the Lord himself.
XXIV. The crowds asked him: What shall we do?
Then the people asked him to counsel them on God's behalf about how they all might escape that terrible fall.
"Pay close attention," he said, "to the words that I now tell you, and let each of you fulfil them!
Let no man who has two garments be so doomed that he does not give away one of them as a fair share;
and whoever has food, let him give to the one who has none; let him do it with love, and give drink as well!
"Also do with it what the law teaches you, so that nothing the prophet wrote is left undone;
By this you act toward God so that he is merciful to you; and if you begin it, you will win his favor!"
We must heed these words, strive hard toward them as well, and fulfill them with great willingness.
What he teaches them here is now directed to us; we cannot turn aside from it, we must take it to heart!
Whoever among men repents and regrets his sins, and then truly does so, heaps up much good for himself;
And if he then faithfully fulfills what God above commanded here, he is (I tell you openly) the Lord's own beloved.
XXV. Jesus comes from Galilee to John.
Christ came from his homeland to the gathering, so that John might meet him there and wash him with baptism.
Then the dear prophet quickly drew back; he spoke out plainly and strongly resisted it.
"Lord," he said, "how can it be (for I am your lowly servant!) that my hands should touch you to baptize you?
It is rather you who should touch me and baptize your servant; how can I presume, then, that this office should be mine over you?"
Then the Son of God himself spoke gently to him and told him that he wished it, and that it had to be so.
"Let it be done this way, as we have now said; it is fitting for us to fulfill willingly everything that is good."
He quickly carried it out, as the Lord Christ wished; then he baptized him, as was required and as he himself had commanded him.
Then heaven was opened; he heard the Father speak, and there he gladly told of the goodness of that same Son.
"This is my dear Son, and in my heart dearer still; in him I am fully pleased, that I begot him such.
Adam once rejected me and also brought himself to ruin; I believe that this one fulfills everything I will.
He behaved as he should not have, and did what I did not wish; but this one wills everything, as my only Son should."
He saw the Spirit of God coming from the kingdom of heaven, as you know; it settled upon Christ as soon as he had washed him.
It was like a dove; that was most fitting, because of the dove's goodness and gentleness.
There is no gall in it at all, and nothing bitter; it does not fight with its beak, nor does it claw with its feet.
So is the Holy Spirit: in him is all beauty in the highest degree, sweetness and goodness and kindly gentleness.
XXVI. Moral interpretation (Moraliter).
Baptism benefits us all; the water is consecrated, since the Lord Christ came home to us and purified it with his body.
Since he bathed in it, he purified the spring; since then, salvation has awakened in the waves for all people.
Whoever hastens to holy baptism may learn here in full how he ought to believe.
You read here in truth: there they baptized the Son; there the Father spoke, as you know; the dove was the Spirit of God.
In the baptism in which the gracious God cleanses us, all this power is thus in the holy water.
This we must believe, and it must please us greatly, that baptism in God's consecration may always bring us blessing,
so that we come out of that bath whole and pure, and that faith also rightly directs us into His service.
27. As the crowds wondered whether John might perhaps be the Christ, and how the leaders sent to him.
The people spread it about that John was Christ, and they thought that it might well be so.
They considered his goodness and his excellence, and they marvelled all the more at his powerful teaching.
For no one was so mighty that John spared him any the more on that account, and no one was so excellent in wisdom that he could oppose him.
All of them, the highest and the lowest, poor and rich, went to him alike.
Then at that time the powerful rulers of the land sent men to him, the princes themselves and the wisest men
(perhaps they were afraid of it and did it for that reason, for the man was very famous), to ask who he was.
They got their errand ready and hurried on their journey. Then they spoke in turn with these words:
"Are you the good Christ? Tell us so kindly, so that we do not stay here long or drag out our errand."
And he told them how it was. He did not argue about it, nor did he deny it or quarrel over such a question:
"I am not Christ," he said to them, "nor am I worthy of it. No man at all would bring me to proclaim myself so high."
Perhaps they were not well satisfied, and they also came closer. They asked again because they had to, as they had been ordered at home:
"If, then, you are Elijah, who is to come to us, tell us that now at once, so that we may report it back there."
He recognized the name when they named him, and he answered that he was not that same man.
"The man you spoke of and called by name, I am not he. I tell you one thing: in years to come he will come home to you."
"Yet tell us now," they said, "whether you are a prophet. They have often told us of excellent and many strange things."
He wished them well, as he well knew how. Therefore he kindly gave them a gentle answer:
"I am not one of those men you are now asking about so eagerly, and in truth I do not readily claim that name for myself."
Then they spoke again quickly and very grimly (with hasty words), and they pressed him hard with questions.
"Then tell us this now: who among men are you? Then we can tell it to those who sent us here."
He readily gave them an answer in return; he did this to each one very boldly.
"I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: make straight his path for God, as the prophet said!"
They did not understand the teaching, and so they asked further; they did not tire of words, and they were sorely troubled [?] by it.
"Why do you go about and baptize, since you are not the Savior, nor yet one of those men whose office this is?"
He answered each of them manfully and at once made it plain to them that it was his office.
"Whoever among men wishes it, I gladly baptize him, and I consecrate each one; I do not refuse anyone the waters.
Yet you have no need on that account [?]; the man is now among you whose words declare what these works signify.
You know nothing of him; but this is my errand, that I should tell you what he intends here.
He comes after me, and yet he was before me for all time; whoever is foremost in the land, he is that one's lord.
So high is his majesty that I do not think I could be worthy to touch his shoe-straps to untie them;
or to kneel humbly before his feet so that I might loosen the straps that bind them.
He will baptize you, though you do not know it, through the Holy Spirit, and will soon cleanse you in shining fire.
He holds his winnowing fan in his hands so that he may cleanse his grain very thoroughly;
sweep his threshing floor and cast away the chaff, so that the grain shines and no refuse [?] touches it;
so that he may gather it all into his barns and then burn the chaff in fire."
I know that once the messengers had done their errand, they decided to set out and go home.
XXVIII. SPIRITUALLY.
With all our strength let us now pray to the Lord that he will not, to our sorrow, separate us from the good;
that we may not be parted in sorrow from the joyful, and may never have to see ourselves among those in grief;
that the winnowing fan may be a help to us at the Judgment and not blow us away forcibly forever;
and that afterward we may never burn there in fire like chaff, but by his grace escape that woe;
that his shepherds may watch over us and always keep us, and not winnow us out from among God's grain;
so that we, rich in good works, may be gathered with God's beloved servants into the high kingdom of heaven,
into high glory, which is the kingdom of heaven; and may escape this misery for the sake of eternal bliss,
and with the beloved may enjoy the kingdom of heaven, and enjoy in blessedness that ever-sweet granary,
the holy granary, so that we never go out of it again; with his own may we rejoice steadfastly in that rest;
and may we be there among them, happy before God, from eternity to eternity, with the holy souls! Amen. Here ends the first book of the Gospels, written in German.

How can there be a greater wonder than in her who bore him, that she is at once both a mother and a virgin?
No woman was ever born who was ever such as she, on earth or in heaven, who could ever equal her.
You can read how it happened at the Lord's birth, that an angel joyfully announced it at once to the shepherds;
and that it was not very long before the heavenly host sang with him; how the multitude of angels came there all toward them.
The shepherds set out at once, and they found the child there; they did not delay going to see him, as the angel had told them.
The Magi came in haste and saw the little child; in their hands they brought him treasures from their lands.
They came from very far; the star showed it to them. How can it be denied, what heaven shows to the world?
It made known to us completely what others do not show us, so that people took notice of it; that is why it was extraordinary.
Simeon the good and Anna came gladly; they went chastely out there to meet him at the house of God.
There they announced to the people, though the people paid no heed to it then, that the only Son of God had come here.
The Gospel also tells how the little children were slain, how short the span of their life was, when they died for Christ.
You can also read here earlier how he began to speak with wise words with the priests.
Those words became famous, though he was then a child; he also told his mother then that it was all his Father's.
The people were greatly startled by John's own words; all the people of the land fell silent when he spoke of him.
They were all moved and troubled in mind, because he made it known that the Lord had come.
So that they would also go to him and not mistake him, he at once pointed with his finger and said: "This is he, that is true;
this is your salvation and the common blessedness of all; be always watchful, very early, and hold fast to it!"
Never across the circle of the world was there a surer thing for us, that anything was ever so renowned on earth.
Even if all these wonders had been passed over in silence, so that the writer had left them out and not had them written down,
what the Father showed when the Son was baptized would alone be of use to us, if we had the wisdom.
In that, everything would be enough for us, if sloth did not deceive us about it and our pride did not carry it away from our hearts.
His own voice told us that he was his only Son; we have his teaching. What more do we ask for?
The same Holy Spirit showed it most of all after him; he came upon him so that it was seen, when the Father spoke to him.
Now the Lord Christ is baptized, and the sin in us is drowned; what always burned us, he drove it all out there;
Now let us all prepare ourselves for the fight; this is how we must guard ourselves against the adversaries.
This is shown to us here as an example and explained in Christ: if you have been bathed in it [baptized], he will always fight against you.
He went into the wilderness, though nothing forced him to do it; there that same adversary soon tempted him harshly.
He did this so that you would know it and arm yourself against it, because here in your life he always pursues you with hatred.
Therefore let us always hurry to the Lord's mercy, so that he may turn our ways away from the enemy,
so that the enemy does not drown us after baptism, and so that he may turn each one aside so that the enemy does not sink him.
May the grace of the one who himself overcame him protect us, and may we also move him to pity, as you shall now read here.
IV. JESUS WAS LED INTO THE DESERT.
Then the Lord Christ was led by the Spirit of God to a place where there is a wilderness, a very desolate place.
There he fasted with hardship for nine hundred hours, and sixty more besides, in truth. Then hunger came upon him.
Then the one who lies in wait, the devil himself, crept up to find out who he was and to test it thoroughly.
He thought, perhaps, that he was the doorkeeper, and that he himself had barred the entrance to this world;
that he had left no stile there unbarred either, and that no one would touch that entrance except his own,
those whom he had won in the first man with his lies, whom he had forced with his deceptions and led astray forever.
How had any such man come in this way, by wisdom? He wanted to find that gap and eagerly capture him!
He wanted, in all earnest, that this man should also be his. But not even the sand [?] became his, and he found nothing of his own there.
He would gladly have found out how it could ever happen that so fitting a man should ever come into this world;
how he could manage, among those who were his, to live so purely all alone,
or to conduct himself so beautifully and without blame (whatever he said or did, all of it was excellent);
from what birth such a man could ever have come, and where the world had ever gained such noble lineage.
Though he was not good, he did find out about the mother; but nowhere did he hear any report of who the father was.
Because he greatly feared him, he tested him in every way; so he may have thought or reasoned like this:
"If this is the son of the one who led the people here through the wilderness in great distress,
who protected them there with clothing, and also fed them from heaven, and supplied them there for many years:
now let him make bread for himself here, since hunger presses him to it; now, in need, let him show an example of his father's goodness!"
Amid these considerations and many thoughts, I do not think his heart was free of great anxiety.
Though he was so bold in evil (which always turned out to his harm), yet I think he timidly approached that great goodness.
Then he spoke to him in this way: "If you are God's son," he said, "then let all these stones become bread!"
Pay attention to what he wanted, what such a request was meant for, and what Christ would need the bread for; he had no need of it!
His torments trouble us enough, year after year; yet he urged him, as if out of need, to turn the stones into bread.
The fast caused him to desire it, but on this occasion he wanted to find out who he was.
Then Christ said: "It is written that bread is not enough, nor is there sufficiency in it for the nourishment of man;
The Lord's teaching does him more good, the words that he receives from the mouth of God."
From there he led him into a fine city, and from those places out to the Lord's house.
He set him on the walls at the very top, and there he called to him at once, very loudly from a distance:
"If you are God's son," he said, "let yourself down here through the air very gracefully, as the Lord's son ought to.
It is written of you that angels travel with you; they protect you entirely and do not let you fall;
They watch over you carefully and hold you firmly, so that your foot never strikes against a stone."
He twisted the scripture he read, true to his nature, and turned all of it deceitfully toward Christ.
Here it means God's beloved (in the verse this is plain), whom the angels always gladly protect;
So that nothing harms him or hinders him on his way, and nothing at all delays the one who wishes to travel that way.
Christ, who is our Lord, governs what is in the world; his journey does not need the guidance of angels.
Now pay close attention to Satan's words, and what senseless speech he spoke to him up there.
If he had spoken at all as one ought to speak to God's son, he would have spoken in this way, which would have been fitting:
"If you are God's son, then go homeward from here, up beyond all the heavens; then people will recognize you."
Then Christ said to him at once: "It is truly written that everyone should take care not to tempt the Lord himself.
I can easily do without it, and I can come down here; why then should I ever tempt God
By stretching myself out here and leaping down, and going through the air over to you? I have no need of anything like that!"
Then, out of anxiety, he went with him up high mountains; there he showed him in an image all the kingdoms of the world,
The honour and the realms and much splendour, so that it would seem fitting to him and come into his mind.
"All this I hand over," he said, "into your hands, into your power, if you will fall down and worship me."
He lures all of us toward a great fall, in words and in deeds; may we escape it.
Those who are willing to worship him lose salvation, and suffer the many kinds of woe forever.
Then he gave him an answer, though he was not worthy of one, and here, as often, he did so with great restraint:
"Go away, adversary, I do not care for these words. It is decided in the books, and declared elsewhere as well.
There it is strictly commanded by God's own word that every person should serve him with fear;
and also that one should keep in mind not to worship any other, no one in the world, except the Lord alone."
The devil went away at once. Then angels were there, and they never failed to serve him.
The devil would not have tempted him if he had not taken him for a man. The angels came because he was their Lord.
All these speeches that we have written above here, that the adversary addressed him with these words: it did not
truly come into his mind (that could not happen at all), nor did it touch in any way the goodness of his heart within.
He could not touch him or lead him anywhere. These journeys would not have happened at all if he had not willed it.
V. Spiritually (Spiritaliter).
We should now take this to heart for our own good: how the devil once deceived the first man in this way.
We should reflect on this so that we guard ourselves better, and always carefully avoid it.
He deceived the old Adam with these words; the young and good one readily avenged it on him.
He kept urging the former hard toward pride, toward greed and toward glory, toward oppressive power.
He saw him enjoying what was already his own; then he begrudged him the path to the beautiful homeland.
Then, since he had won over the first, he set about the other man in the same way. He found that it came to nothing; none of it succeeded for him.
He meant to lay the same kind of trap for him without fail. As the former fell, here he himself was put to great shame.
He made it sweet to the old one to eat the fruit; he enticed him to abandon what the Lord had commanded him to do.
He said they would be like gods if they did not refrain from it. He said they would know good and evil, yet would not lose any of the good.
He also pressed this one hard, though he did not listen to him in it (he did not do it for any good purpose!), to turn the stones into bread;
and to let himself down from the height of the house. He said he would fill him with lordship if he would worship him.
With these same words he had once won over the first man. So here he was condemned by this one (that was necessary!),
so that by this same course he would be driven away from us, the one who first deceived us and crept into our hearts;
so that in that bath he too, who once tripped us up and turned us away from the kingdom of heaven, should fall and lose his blessedness.
VI. AGAIN ON THE SAME.
Earlier I did not tell in full, as I wanted to, of our many kinds of suffering; so now I will tell you more of it here.
When the Lord watched over the man I mentioned above, he strictly forbade him the fruit I spoke of before:
He told him very firmly to guard himself against it all the better, and with threats, since it was necessary, he forbade it very sharply.
He said that if he ate it, it would go badly for him, and if he swallowed it, he would not escape death.
And so that the command would not be too heavy for him, and he could keep it gladly and willingly,
he gave him power over the whole delightful field, so that he could enjoy its good things and in that way keep this command.
The serpent persistently and deceitfully enticed them not to fear anything and to eat the fruit.
It said that they would not go into death even if they reached for it, nor fall into any danger because of that wrong.
So that he would not shrink from it, it told him of the benefits. It said that wisdom and all kinds of advantage would come to them from it.
It said that their beautiful eyes would then be opened, and they would see what had until then been hidden from them.
It said that they would then become like gods, not men, and would then know good and evil in their hearts.
He was glad of the apple. To our sorrow he chewed it, and to our pain he took it. What was the wretched man thinking?
To our woe we came to know that he shoved it into his mouth. Because he chewed and swallowed it, we now live in another land.
Woe came upon mankind then, because he did not spit it out or send it back, and so he sank us.
If only, before he swallowed it, he had sent it back, and had stuck what he left of it back
on the tree where she took it, we would not have gone so far astray. We bear very clear evidence that he did not leave it alone in time.
If he had let it be, or left it to God, the world would not have come into this misery.
He increased still further for us the many kinds of woe: the evil that clings to us and, alas, does not stop now.
He took our good fortune away from us when he touched it. He made us exiles from paradise,
from shining bliss. What a joyful life that was! He also took still more good away from us when he began to deny,
when God questioned him and he went into dispute, turned the blame from himself, and laid it on the woman.
If he had only confessed, admitted what he did, and taken it all upon himself, it would not have turned out so terrible at all.
It would then have come to a better end; God would have shown him mercy. Alas, that was not to be.
Since it was not understood then, now there is a better remedy: the Lord then sent his Son here from the kingdom of heaven.
No one ever saw love to equal it, or to equal the deeds he showed us, when we were in such great need.
He gave him without hesitation for us weary servants, his beloved head for us bondsmen;
Yet Adam too, as if by necessity, committed that one misdeed to this end: that such a ransom should stand for us before God.
Now we are spurred on to God's service; we know what the harm was, so that we love God all the more;
And by this reasoning we are in double joy: now we escape punishment and rejoice in the kingdom of heaven.
VII. JOHN WAS STANDING, AND TWO OF HIS DISCIPLES.
Here I now begin to tell how he began to preach, and began to gather the teachers whom he granted us;
Through discipline he made them devoted to him and filled them with wisdom; then he sent them everywhere, as far as heaven covers the land.
John, one man among men, stood with two of his disciples; he saw the very Son of the Lord coming toward them.
He was indeed God's renowned beloved one, who made God's ways straight in excellent fashion, as was fitting.
He pointed his finger and at once told the disciples, and straight away spoke to them of the blessing that was coming toward them there.
"Look here," he said, "where the Son of the Lord is going: he is his lamb, which he always intended, which the Law also signified.
If that lamb saved the people and protected them from hunger, this one with his words rescues the world from sins."
They took in the words at once and went after him; he immediately turned back toward them and said: "Good men, what is it to be?"
Then they said to him at once: "Master, we tell you truly, we wanted to know for certain where you always stay."
"I will do it," he said, "and give you an account, and show you my dwelling, and openly reveal to you all my private household life."
When they came there and saw the home, they gladly enjoyed the dwelling that day.
One of the two was closely related to Peter, his brother by the same mother; now he is a good servant of God.
He hurried at once to tell him about it, because Peter was dearest to him, so that he would not be [?] left without a share of these benefits.
"Dear man," he said, "we have found a great benefit for ourselves (and we know it is true): the Lord Christ himself!
Brother, I tell you truly, I could not hold myself back from hurrying here to you right away, so that you would go there with me;
So that I might urge you to it and lead you to him, so that you may see the man; he will please you very greatly."
He told him of it and immediately led his brother to him, as I have told; he did not delay in the least.

The married couple were very glad, and they could well count it an honour then: they had Christ himself there, who is the prince of all joy.
Then the drink ran short, and they were lacking wine. Mary noticed this and told it to Christ.
"I must tell you, my child, something very serious for the married couple, which I have just now learned: they are out of wine."
Then her son spoke to her sweetly and gently, with fine words above all, as a son should speak to his mother:
"Woman, I tell you one thing: what does such a matter have to do with us two? My time has not yet come so far that I should show what I took from you.
As soon as that appears, what comes to me from you, your heart will be very sorrowful all that day.
What you have now said to me, and the complaint you have made about it, such things must be done by divine deeds."
The mother heard that there; yet she knew in all truth that his goodness would not refuse her what she asked.
At once she ordered those who were looking after the drink that whatever he told them, each of them should do it.
Water vessels stood there, as was the custom in that land, for the people always to wash themselves.
There were six jars; there were enough of them for the deeds the Lord wished to do.
The measure that we often reckon and call a sextarius: each one held, by reckoning, thirty times ten
or twice a hundred; books record this. The vessels were of stone, so they could hold it all the better.
Then the Lord himself ordered that they fill them with water; they did that readily, up to the top.
Then he told them to pour it out and turn to the highest-ranking man, who was the chief of the table-companions at the feast.
He drank then as he pleased, but he knew nothing about it, and it never crossed his mind that it was made from water.
But the men who poured it knew very well that it was clear water when they filled the vessels.
He called the host over and brought him to himself; he was greatly amazed at the splendid wine.
"Tell me now, my friend, why have you dealt with the wine this way, holding it back like this and saving it so long?
Every man who likes to make his friends glad (I know you are aware of it) always gives the best right at the start.
When the men have then had their fill and begin to get drunk, he pours for the rest of the day whatever there may be.
But you have saved the good wine until now! I must also tell you now, I have never drunk its equal."
This sign the Lord Christ did first among people, after he came here into the world and took on a human body.
There he showed his power and his glory; that is true. Then at least his disciples, and they alone, believed.
IX. Spiritually (Spiritaliter).
As he drew the sword, the angel called out to him and ordered him to stop; the child lay there bound.
He said that he should hold back and do him no harm at all, and that he should spare him; he said it was enough as it was.
He said that in this it was fully enough for people to see that he feared God, since he did such a deed.
It showed too that he heeded God's words very closely, since he undertook such a thing and took it so close to heart.
He saw a ram standing there that was fit for the sacrifice; he saw it held fast in the brambles by its horns.
He caught it at once and offered it to God there: a welcome exchange for his good son!
Whoever wants to understand this, let them all listen here, and let them think about it so that they may drink sweetly.
Always do readily and for good whatever God commands you; always hasten to fulfil it with great willingness.
Always follow the example of this holy man very earnestly: then you will always drink gladly from the clear spring.
If you want to work it out more finely and taste it as wine, you must apply it to Christ, if you are able to choose that.
Read for yourself, as I tell you, in his gospels; there you will surely read of such deeds.
It would take long to tell how it all fits together, yet it can be explained in a few words.
Understand, in all truth, that God was the Father, and that the only child signifies Christ,
whom he gave over to death for our sake, as he willed, and did not spare even his only one, just as Paul wrote;
how he himself carried the cross when he suffered the punishment, and died there on the altar of the cross.
His body suffered it; his divinity did not will it [or: was not subject to it], just as the exchange was made there between those two [Isaac and the ram].
The people who seized him there fastened his arms to the horns of the cross, just like those same brambles.
They fastened him there with wounds for our grievous sins, and harshly mocked him with their abusive words.
Understand what I have told you about the son in this way: truly, you never drank a better wine of mine.
There is no need to delay at all. If you want to recount the whole world, you can think about all of it in this way and drink in two ways.
Always fulfil Scripture properly and with strength: then you will often refresh yourself from a spring of reason.
And keep the spiritual words firmly in mind: then you will give your thoughts the Lord's wine to drink.
The jars held two or three measures of liquid, so that you may take to heart what the holy ones do:
They write in a holy way of the Father and the Son, and some, as you know, also of the Holy Spirit himself.
