No one was found there then who wanted to resist, so that it came to the point of putting up a defence.
They clearly saw God's power shining in him, so that they were struck with fear there, and for that reason they also did not defend themselves.
Then the people spoke and asked what sign he would show them in answer to this deed.
"Destroy this house," he said, "and it will soon be restored as well; I will gladly set it up again within the space of three days."
The people quickly gave their answer, all the princes and the most important men:
"This has already been forty-six years in the building (we know the number for certain);
you promise in vain that you will raise it up right now, at this moment of need, within the time of three days!"
So that we do not go wrong or go astray, God's dear friend here explains the meaning to us very well.
He taught us and showed that our Lord meant the house of his body (may we never turn away from that!),
which the Lord holds as the foremost and dearest of sanctuaries, and also of wisdom, which dwells there in full.
Alas, they destroyed it with the bitterness of death; with weapons and without reason they destroyed that dwelling.
He raised it up quickly and very beautifully on the third day, as he had promised, and he also destroyed death.
He roofed it over completely and set it more firmly (that has truly been planned), so that it will never totter again.
When he had overcome death and came out from there on the third day (he brought us blessing and good when he rose up from the grave),
then his disciples very gladly remembered that he had meant this earlier, here, and this scripture shows it.
Then they fully believed the holy scripture and all the words that he had spoken here so forcefully.
And many of the people at Easter time also quickly came to believe there when they saw this.
Christ indeed did not entrust himself to the people's purposes [?] on that occasion; they were known to him.
He fully recognized in them their will and the thoughts that were in their hearts.
Know this without dispute: he had no need to ask, or for anyone to tell him, what a man's heart wanted.
For everything that a man's mind thinks over lies open to him, and also what he carries with desire in his heart.
XII. There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus.
There was a wise man, a good nobleman, who was also an honoured leader of the people.
I think he was deeply amazed at these deeds, and this marvel also took hold of his heart.
He came to him by night, and his intention in coming was very right; they spoke with each other in turn, with these words:
"Master, I tell you one thing: there is no doubt of it, we know that it is fitting that you have come from God;
There is no one who could undertake to accomplish such things, anything like this work, unless he works it with God!"
The Lord Christ recognized that he spoke the truth to him, because he came to him believing; therefore he told him all that was fitting for him.
(Not at all that he understood that he was God's Son; he understood only his power in this way. That is what the night signifies.)
"I tell you," he said, "truly a strange matter, which concerns every man who bears a body.
Unless he is at some time born again (or else he must forgo rejoicing in the kingdom of heaven),
he will not reach that entrance, nor can he boast that he rejoices in his heart in the eternal good."
Then the good man was greatly taken aback by these words, and he asked how it could ever happen; he very much wanted to find it out!
"How can a man," he said, "of necessity come back again, old and advanced in years, into his mother's womb,
so that in this way he avoids that peril and gains what he needs, so that he does not lack such a thing?"
He gave him an answer with great gentleness, and he made it all sweet for him in every way that he addressed him.
"I tell you in truth (you need not ask more about it; the whole world cannot undo anything of what I tell you):
There is no one who comes into the kingdom of heaven unless spirit and water give him birth; let him look to his beauty, so that he may make his way there.
Whatever has ever come here into the world from frail man is all flesh, as you know, and it needs cleansing most of all.
Water and the Spirit of God must bear them again above all, so that they may venture to rejoice in the kingdom of heaven.
Do not wonder at this, my friend, that it may well be so, and that it will come to pass at some time that the world rejoices in it,
and does not shun it, but rejoices with fair delight in this second birth.
The spirit blows quietly wherever it is his will; he does not turn away from where it seems good to him.
In the same way the Holy Spirit himself moves without your knowing it; his coming is in every way unseen.
Nor do you perceive then where he means to go, or from where his comings touch you.
Such is always what the birth of the Spirit does for those who come to it and are born of him."
Then the good man asked how that could ever be, and how anyone could understand so great a wonder.
He explained it to him well (as the Lord was always used to doing), and what he meant then, he showed him well:
"You are clearly the teacher of this people here; but now set your mind on this most of all: you know nothing of this at all!
All year long we tell you what we know in full truth, what we see rightly; yet you do not accept it.
"I declare to you," he said, "(as you have heard me say before, and I say it no less now) that I myself am not Christ.
I am his own messenger. My mission also goes before him, so that I, out of nothing [?], may direct the people onto the way.
Truly, he who has the bride is the bridegroom, and he keeps his love for his beloved.
His friend, who stands there at once [?], listens to his word and hears the bridegroom's voice with love.
He disregards nothing of what the bridegroom says to him, and always rejoices gladly at that voice.
That is my blessed state of mind and my joy, so good: in him all my joys are made full for me!
He shall grow greatly by his own deeds, so that my works dwindle before his powers.
He who is from the earth here shall speak from where he is; he will surely talk of earthly things.
But he who does not come from there, and came from heaven above, has power that extends mightily over all the lands of the world!
My preaching is nothing but what I have been commanded to preach. But what he teaches, he sees and hears it all himself.
Yet people will not accept that kindness [?] or practise it in their hearts, so as to believe in him.
Those who do come to it receive faith in him, and they make it widely known that he was always the Lord.
The Father loves his Son. He himself sent him here and gave everything into his hand, into his power.
He does not measure out his goodness to him as he does to us sinners. He shares it with him and imparts his Spirit to him,
because he is his own child. Whatever is dearest to him (I tell you this for certain), he gives him all of it entirely.
The man who learns this and turns his faith toward him makes his mind very glad for all eternity.
But whoever does not do this will come to a sorrowful mind, and God's wrath remains upon him!"
Truly, John was not yet lying in prison when this was preached in this way, all spoken by him like this.
XIV. JESUS, WEARY FROM THE JOURNEY.

He grew weary from the journey, as often happens to someone travelling. Hardships give no respite to anyone who is truly a man.
He travelled through Samaria and came there to a town, and in his haste he came to a resting place.
Then he sat down weary, as we told here earlier, by a well (which we also call a "puzzi").
The evangelist says there that it may have been the sixth hour, which is the hottest part of the day and the time of greatest hardship.
His disciples hurried off and fetched food by buying it, so that they could set about eating with Christ himself. Until [?]
Yet the time of that age is still to come, and it is also present now, when true worshippers will pray to the Father in the spirit from now on;
for he earnestly seeks worshippers who pray truly and rightly, so that they pray to him in the spirit at all times.
The Spirit is the Lord, with very great power; in truth the Spirit of God wills that people should pray to him above all."
She paid close attention to the Lord's words, and then turned with words to give this answer:
"A man has been promised to us, and he shall also be called Christ; his coming will someday make all this known to us.
His goodness will explain all these matters to us, and many things besides, clearly and easily."
Then the Lord kindly gave her an answer: "I am he, believe me, I who am speaking here with you!"
Meanwhile the disciples arrived. They wondered at this and were greatly amazed at the talk between the two of them:
that his majesty humbled itself so low that the Eternal Life was teaching a poor woman there.
As soon as she heard that, she immediately threw the vessel aside, hurried into the city to the people, and told them all this.
"Come," she said, "see the man who revealed all this to me; in words he told me everything that I have done in deeds.
Could it be Christ, my lords? I say it as a guess; and I say it because it is very much like him.
From the hidden signs it seems to me that it may be so; he understood everything I have ever desired."
Then everyone from the city hurried out, one after another; they all hurried in haste so that they might see him.
Meanwhile the disciples asked the master to sit down there to a meal and eat.
He said he had food, as he then told them there, with sweet delights, though they knew nothing about it.
Then the thought came to them that someone had brought it to him while they had been in the city buying what they needed.
"My food," he said, "is to do my Father's will fully, so that I always fulfil whatever he himself wills.
You say, truly, that there are still four months until it is, as people say, proper harvest time.
Now look, begin to look around with your eyes: there is no field here in the land that is not already turning white for this;
none that is not making itself ready for it, as I now explain to you here, so that the farmers may bring the yield into the barns.
I sent you to reap: you did not sow the grain then; out of necessity you have entered into other people's labour."
Then a great many of the people there believed: those who came to him there and heard the teaching.
Then he gladdened them and stayed there with them for two days; his kindness did this, because they asked him to.
And in truth many more of them believed then, because his own teaching meant far more to them.
Then they spoke joyfully to that same woman who had first made his coming known there in the town:
"We do not truly believe in him because of your teaching, now that the benefit has reached us, which he himself showed us;
Now we know in all truth that he is the Savior, that he came here into the world to save mankind."

XVIII. Do not think that I came to destroy the law.
"Do not think that it would be fitting, that I came for this purpose, that I took it upon myself to break the law,
or, as I now say, any of the prophets; rather, with patience I would fulfill them both well.
Truly, I tell you in all truth, and I will not hide it from you now: if you do not have greater goodness than these authorities have,

Do you know the saying (the books speak of it) of how strictly the law commanded the people of old?
They say it declared that one man should not kill another; it says God is very angry at such deeds.
But I tell you my own saying about this, my own command, which I order to be written in addition:
that every man take care not to grow angry with anyone, and also avoid bearing hatred toward any man.
Whoever controls that very deed keeps the other commandment better; by his obedience he shows what the law commands him.
If you are about to bring gifts, offerings given gladly, to God's altar,
and there you remember one man who is angry with you, even if the matter is so small that it had not come into your mind before,
do not offer it there any further; go and be reconciled first! Until then (I tell you this) it is very hateful to God.
XIX. Whoever looks at a woman; and: Do not swear; and: Love your enemies.
He also explained then, earnestly and fittingly, how the law commanded that no man commit adultery.
"But I," he said, "say to you: whoever looks at a woman in such a way that at that very moment he desires her
has truly committed adultery with her already, grievously, in his heart, with an unclean mind; it will not turn out well for him.
The law, I believe, forbids a man to swear falsely; my words forbid you to swear at all.
That is the greater caution, I tell you in truth; by it people guard themselves better and keep themselves better.
The law strictly commands that a man hate his enemy and that every man love his friend.
What I command you here always leads to good; I will not hide it from you now, it suits you far better:
Love your enemies, so the Lord God commands; love dearly whoever hates you.
Always pray gladly for whoever does you harm, so that in these deeds you truly imitate God.
Always be very gentle in your deeds, so that you may be God's children; let the Lord who dwells in heaven be your model.
He lets his sun shine very brightly, and rain likewise on all the earth;
Certainly, and I do not hide it from you: people are of many kinds, of hostile mind, evil and good.
If your love now burns hot toward those to whom you are very dear, why should you get a good reward for that? The heathen does that too.
Even sinful men themselves do that very fully: they always keep in mind anyone who does them much kindness.
XX. Take heed that you do not do your righteousness before men.
If you give comfort to poor people with honest righteousness, and you wish to give alms without boasting;
or if you always wish to do good works pleasing to the Lord willingly before God:
do, as I tell you, all those same things as hidden works, so that God may thank you for it.
If you do not do so, I tell you one thing: you have no reward for it, and without doubt no thanks for it will come to you from God.
If you give alms in righteousness (I am telling you what is fitting), do not do it for public fame.
Truly, those who make it public, openly among men, so that people will then praise them, are hypocrites.
Know this: they have the whole reward there. I tell you in all truth: no more will come to them for it.
XXI. How one should pray, and of the Lord's Prayer.
If you also begin to plead with God, and you intend to make your prayer:
let it be in your heart then, so that nothing of it slips away from you. Let it be secret in your mind, so that it turns out for your good!

Do not let your mind wander, as the hypocrite does: his mind turns about just as his neck does.
They do all this so that people will praise them for it and honor them because of it. Therefore they are not at all the better for it.
Do you know what I am telling you? That very praise is the reward. Certainly you know this: everything rests on it.
When you pray, know this: keep it short. The Lord does not much care for many words.
Pray earnestly in your heart, with short and pure words, so that God may hear it!
Leave all the reward to him, so that the prayer may be the better, and so that you do not lose your toil in that deed.
So you do not need to; God knows what is in you before you tell him everything you want.
Call upon his grace, as my words make it sweet for you, my own teaching (there need be no more of it);
as I shall now teach you here above all else. Each of you, receive all of it completely:
Our good Father, you are the gracious Lord, ever on high in the heavens; hallowed be your name.
May your kingdom come to us, the high kingdom of heaven, toward which we are ever going and in which we always put our hope.
May your will be done here below as it is up in heaven; help us here on earth as you now help the angels there.
Give us today in abundance our daily nourishment, and fully also (which is more) your own teaching.
Forgive all of us our debt, as we also are willing to do, the sins that we think and constantly commit.
Truly, do not let us fall into the snares of the Adversary, so that we do not go astray or fall into them.
Deliver us from there forever, so that we may be your servants, and by your grace may always escape woe. Amen.
If you take it to heart always to forgive sin, then his goodness will blot out your misdeeds;
But whoever does not do so (take this to heart!) will quickly have all his evil deeds counted against him.
22. No one can serve two masters; and: Take no thought for tomorrow.
No man can serve two lords in such a way that he ever fully carries out the will of both;
You need not even try to bring it about that you serve God and yet love the world.
Let it be fixed firmly in your minds that you will not lack food; and do not worry and deliberate over what you will clothe yourselves with.
The soul is of greater account, so do not let food matter more to you; and the body's condition [?] matters more than its clothing.
Look at these birds flying above us here: they do not go to the field, and they spin nothing either;
Yet they lack nothing (indeed they have plenty) to feed themselves and clothe themselves beautifully.
Look at the splendid flowers standing in the field, which people pass as they go along the road:
Solomon the rich, I tell you in all truth, was not clothed like one of those flowers there.
Now if he chooses to protect what will soon wither, and the birds too, truly, which are of little worth to you,
how much more will your Lord care for you? You are dearer to him than all the birds there are.
He sees to it (as you know) that you do not go naked, and he also gives you the food so that you do not die of hunger.
Truly, you cannot make yourself one hair less or more (consider this too), however you may dye it.
Therefore leave the worry (that is the right thing) to him who made you as you are; he will always protect you with clothing and constantly feed you.
He knows without a doubt that you need these things above all, and that you cannot do without them but must make use of such things.
Always seek with all your strength the righteousness of the kingdom of heaven; all the rest will come to you, I tell you that.
There is none among you (that is true) so very foolish that, if your child asks you for bread, you would offer him stones;
You also take care of this: if he asks you for fish, you do not offer him the wicked serpent at all;
Nor do you truly offer him a scorpion (that peril); you take great care about that, if he asks you for an egg.
Now you are accustomed to give good things to your children, and all that pleases them, so that you do not deceive them:
How very much more will the Lord give you good, if you follow him and are willing to ask him?
Ask diligently and very fervently: this I tell you in all truth, he will give you the good at once."
XXIII. ALL THINGS WHATSOEVER YOU WOULD THAT MEN SHOULD DO TO YOU; AND: BEWARE OF FALSE PROPHETS.
"Now I teach you in very few words how you may fully do the Lord's will.
Do not do (I tell you one thing) anything at all against any man in the whole world that you would not want done to yourself;
By this you then fulfill what the prophets sing, and carry out the law fully in every respect.
Always guard yourselves carefully against the words of deceivers, against lying prophets; you must always remember that.
They come to you, in appearance [?], in sheep's clothing; but inside them, in truth, dwell very grievous wolves.
They cannot slip past you: look to their works, and quickly observe their deeds;
It is not done among men that one gathers grapes from thorns, nor figs from briars, even if one should attempt it.
A bad tree bears what is always natural to it; so too does the good one; it happens just as is fitting.
The bad one they burn, as people indeed wish; but the good one, without doubt, they leave standing in peace.
Not everyone who calls me Lord goes into heaven (and God does not permit it; it will yet be made known!);
Know certainly, without doubt: those will be let in there who here fully work the will of my Father.
I tell you in all truth: many will lament there with manifold sorrows and grievous words;
Each will quickly say that he did signs in the name of my name, so that I should remember him for it.
Then I will tell them at once that they were not known to me, that I had long since hidden myself from them [?]; I care nothing for their affairs:
'Go away quickly, whoever has ever done evil, away from me at once, and do not come near me!'"
XXIV. CONCLUSION OF THE SECOND BOOK.
Christ taught this truly, and much more besides; I tell you in truth: you can read it yourself there,
all his admonitions and his very full teaching, and also very heavy threats; this I tell you in truth.
No one can recount it all, even if we begin it; the goodness of that teaching was very pleasing.
When he had then come to that point, he went down from the mountain; the whole multitude of the people followed him plainly.
He himself then intended, when he healed a leper at once with his words, where all the people saw it,
that they might take great delight in it, and that the teaching which they had heard in there meanwhile might be firm in them;
that they might wake early and think hard about it, and that it might be firm within their breasts;
that their minds might not waver, that they might be firm in their thoughts, in mind and in spirit, for every good.
Lord, make it useful to us, so that it may sit well with us; shield us from harm, do not separate us from your own;
so that we may not fall away from all your beloved ones, from your own dear friends; may we avoid that peril!
Purify our thoughts (we are your servants) with abundance of grace from the sickness of sins;
Hold us safe in our need from all adversities, so that we may shun perverse thoughts!
Shield us swiftly from all misdeeds, from terrible sicknesses, with your own power!
Your words here above, which tell us the whole account: for these grant us a very good mind and spirit;
grant us all, Lord, that we may always want what is yours, and always fulfil with deeds what your words tell us;
that we may think on it and lay it in our hearts, and leave out nothing of it, but make it cleave there!
Drive all misdeeds swiftly from us; fasten this in our minds, so that it may turn out for our good,
so that we may work at it with watchful thoughts, and always heed it with pure thoughts!
May harm flee quickly, and may this always draw near to us, and may we bring about by it that you may thank us for it;
that we may be joined, every one of us, to your own, who did you service here as they prayed to you, Lord;
and that we may be glad in the eternal life with your servants forever (we desire nothing more),
with your angels; that we may escape woe, in the kingdom of heaven, rightly, in your sight;
from age to age with the blessed souls, from world to world, may we be praising you forever! Amen. Here ends the second book.
I. Preface of the third book.
II. There was a certain royal official.
III. Morally.
IV. The Passover of the Jews was near.
I. Preface to the Third Book.
With Christ's own blessings I now wish to tell here, in a little book, especially of the wondrous miracles
(of the Wondrous One) which he performed here in the kingdom, while he was here in the world, before he tasted death for our sake;
the wondrous signs, some of them at least, truly, for even if he wished to, there is no man who could recount them all.
I do not write now strictly in the order in which they occur there, but as the deeds come into my mind.
With fearful cares I pray for his grace, that he may also work his sign in this work,
so that in these books I never go astray, and that I write the Lord's deeds here rightly and beautifully.
He made the lame run and the dumb men cry out too: may he see to it that I do not limp here, and do not waver in the meaning either.
Healer of lepers: may he also cleanse me here of pus and of wounds, of my grievous sins!
In them, alas, I remember much sorrow and pain; my heart weeps, their pain does this to me.
Lord, I must badly escape from the stench: take me (do not do it too late!), as you did Lazarus!
You brought him back to life from death, you awakened the body: bring to life in me (that is more) my weary soul,
so that I may come to understanding here in this life, and also sit at your table, as he did afterwards: may I hope for that;
that I may always be attentive and careful in the books, and in them also think fully of your own will!
And what I now tell here is entirely your gift; increase my understanding for your own honour.
Do not avenge my sin in this, Lord, but grant me understanding for it; nothing here gladdens our heart as your forgiveness does!
Gently, my dear Lord, let the chastisement be; soothe my heart, as a mother does to her little child.
Though she may beat it sorely, she never wishes (rather, she protects it) that anyone else should wound it.
She at once puts her hand in front of it if anyone aims at it there; she is at once mindful of the way of her dear child.
With her hand she shields it, the same hand with which she beats it; her heart cannot bear to see what an enemy does to it.
The father too does the same: though he grieves its heart sorely, he still keeps its noble inheritance for its benefit.
Protect me likewise, Lord, so that I may surely be your servant; may your hand also defend me, so that the enemy may not harm me!
Grant me also hope of my homecoming; be father and mother to me, you are my good Lord!
II. There was a certain royal official.
When Christ came into Galilee, the news spread, as was fitting, and his power was made known throughout all that land.
He said that his son lay in distress, dying, and was in that sickness with great weakness.
He gave him an answer with great kindness; with sweet words he wanted to mend the faith in him:
"Unless you see signs when such distress comes upon you, rare wonders, you do not truly believe."
For if he had believed fully, as it rightly should be, it would have come into his heart as was fitting before God:
He himself would then have believed, as befits a man of God, that the Lord is everywhere with his own power;
That one need not wait for him or lead him from place to place, he who is so mighty, who holds all that is in the world.
"Lord," he said, "hasten your going, if you will show me mercy; let me obtain your goodness before my son dies."
The Lord spoke his word to him, that he should go home, that he should go back there; he said he would find his son whole.
He believed the word and turned toward his land, at once on that matter, to his home.
While he travelled, pondering the power of that same word, his loyal servants came joyfully to meet him;
They also told him meanwhile very much that was welcome: that truly, in all certainty, his son had been saved.
Then he asked the time (he was very glad of it), and also exactly the hour when he had grown better.
"Lord, we tell you this: when it was the seventh hour of the day, yesterday, as they saw, he became whole all at once.
Do not doubt in your mind; you will find it done just so; you will truly find your dear comfort there just so."
Then the father at once recognized that it was truly the time when the Lord had granted it to him so, and had promised that same healing;
Then that same earthly king at once believed, with his household, in the heavenly King.
III. MORAL INTERPRETATION.
This is unfitting for us, as I now perceive it, and this good does not come into our wretched minds;
Yet he has shown us, and also commanded us by example, how we nevertheless ought to act, if we were willing.
Once a centurion came in urgent need and asked him to speak his word, that he might heal his servant;
He said he would come himself and take away the sickness, though the other did not ask for his own presence there.
The king asked him to come: that did not befit Christ. The centurion did not ask it: yet he wanted to go there!
Here his goodness strikes down in us our arrogance, our foolishness, wherever it ever comes to that.
We let the very rich man please us, and we utterly despise the poverty of others;
In them gold and costly clothing please us; we pay no regard to men of servile rank.
Some of us do not consider that we are all alike, all of one birth, though it later turned out otherwise;
In some people we bring the equality of creation too low; in others, because of their rank, wealth counts for more with us.
Therefore God himself has now set us an example here before this: not to flee from nature in ourselves, and to draw toward equality.
He was willing, of his own accord, to visit the servant there; but to the son, as was just told, he would not go, though he was invited.
But if some poorer man invites us home, then truly our mind at once swells with pride;
Yet we are grateful to a rich man for the same thing, thank him with grateful words, and bow deeply to him as well.
IV. The Passover of the Jews was near.
The time came round when Easter drew near; then the Lord, the Savior, went to the land of Jerusalem.
It is said that there was a fishpond there, as the books there tell; in Greek they give it a name;
For people washed in it from time to time the flesh that was meant for the sacrifice, whenever they wished.
Five porches surrounded it, and they were all full of sick and crippled people.
These waited there (know this for the truth); they were watching for the water to move.
A good angel of God went into it willingly; he stirred up the water and made it ready to heal them.
Whoever then sank into it and bathed in it first at once became whole of whatever had crippled him before.
There, among those just described, he saw an old man who had been grievously sick for many years.
Two years short of forty (I tell you this) he had truly lain in that same suffering.
Christ saw how long he had lain there, and he spoke to him himself, asking whether he wished to become whole.
Or the man thought and supposed that he was pointing him to the water; so he lamented his misery in this way:
"Lord," he said, "good Lord! None of my friends is here to help me with this and throw me into the water;
I hurry there quickly, but my weakness makes me late; others rush there before me and take the bath from me."
"Stand up," he said, "listen to me, and take your bed with you. Dare to do it at once, and go on your way!"
As soon as he took in his words he lifted the bed, and he carried it away the moment he heard them.
He stood up quickly, as was Christ's will; he took hold of the bed at once and went off with it.
That day was truly a Sabbath holiday when the Lord took the infirmity from the sick man.
Then the people said he had done wrong and needlessly profaned the holy day.
"The one who healed me," he said, "he ordained it all this way; I tell you this for certain: he commanded me to walk with it."
They pressed him to say who it was that had commanded it; at that moment he said at once that he knew nothing of it.
The Lord himself had in truth gone off at once to a place apart, he and his disciples, away from the crowd.
After this he found the man, when he came into the house where the people always prayed and sought the grace of God.
"Now you are healed," he said. "Sin no more, so that your mind may guard itself and nothing worse befall you."
Then he made it known in all truth to the people that it was the Saviour who had freed him from his affliction.
V. MORALLY.
Here we may understand (and we have also found it so) that infirmities come from the sickness of sins.
When he forbade him those deeds, telling him not to sin, and to take heed that nothing worse should happen to him:
this saying teaches us to guard ourselves against that, so that sickness may not harm us further, in our limbs and in our soul.
Because of such deeds the people persecuted him, and each of them wanted vengeance on him because he had broken the Sabbath.
He ruled over the holy day as was fitting; none of them perceived that he, with his powers, was lord of that day.
They persecuted him all the more for this, because it grieved them sorely. They called it an outrageous thing that God was his father,
and that he necessarily made himself equal to the Lord, always alike in his works and different in nothing.
It is certainly so, even though they took it amiss in this way, and though the hardness of their minds always resented it,
and they always twisted the Lord's deeds, those very glorious signs; know this for the truth.
Lord, deign to heal us along with your dear beloved ones, and make our great needs sweet for us,
so that it may not be too hard for us always to bear with one another here, and to love one another fairly among men always!
VI. JESUS WENT ACROSS THE SEA OF GALILEE.
What I now tell here, the whole world knows: a very famous and very strange wonder,
how Christ took five loaves and two fishes besides, and from them gave five thousand men their fill of food.
The Lord and his followers crossed over a lake; the books tell of it there and call it Galilee.
Because of many strange things and wonders, truly, a great crowd of people went there to meet him.
A countless host truly went there to meet him, a great crowd as was fitting, women and men.
The Lord took his disciples and went with them from there up a high mountain, and he sat there with them in a fitting way.
These same deeds also certainly took place before an Easter, before the holy season.
When he then began to look at the people with his eyes and saw that same multitude, he spoke to Philip like this:
"Where can we now start to buy bread, so that the people may sit here until they have eaten?"
He was testing the state of their weak faith. Yet he knew, as he should, what he meant to do about it.
He said it could not be done, getting it for them by buying, even with great wealth, so that the people could sit down to it
and each one would then get even a mouthful, stretch out his mouth for it, and taste any of the bread!
Then Andrew spoke, one of Peter's kin, his dear brother, the good thane of Christ:
"There is a boy here, and I know of nothing more here, who is carrying five barley loaves for his own needs,
and two fish with them. But that is nothing at all for offering to such a great crowd."
"Have the people sit down here," he then said aloud. "While they rest here, they will not lack bread."
In truth there was also suitable grass there, pleasant enough. The books tell us this.
When the host then sat down, they ate the blessed bread. It grew there at that time, in their mouths and in their hands.
It grew suddenly, while they all looked on. It multiplied abundantly until the people were satisfied,
to their sweet delight, so that none of them lacked any there, old and young, and even all the women.
He himself also then shared out the fish and handed them out there, and they too grew, necessarily, just like the bread.
When those who sat in the grass had eaten there, and everyone there was satisfied as they received the bread,
the Lord then ordered his disciples to hurry and gather up what the people had left, the crumbs there,
so that they would be kept and would not go to waste. Then they all gathered twelve full baskets there.
When the people there suddenly saw this sign, they began to thank the Lord with grateful thoughts:
"This," they said, "is truly the famous prophet (it is not otherwise in any way at all) who is to come here into the world!"
Later he gave four thousand men their fill, kindly satisfying them with seven loaves and also with fish;
and there were leftovers of the fish and the loaves (they did not eat it all), seven baskets over and above!
VII. SPIRITUALLY.
My good Lord, now guide me kindly. Turn my mind to this for me, and my heart as well,
so that I may show here, in spiritual words, to your dear thanes what your purpose means.
The exalted servants of God gather up the words for them; they fix in writing what people like me leave behind.
Wherever it happens that someone like me does not understand it, they collect it into books, to be kept and held there,
so that it may be read there, preserved, year after year: what they finely told us and laid in the baskets.
By this they have shown why they are called baskets: because their goodness endures poverty here.
A basket is a servant's vessel; yet they do not mind it if people ever call them baskets in this way,
for they are all full of Christ's teaching, that same subtle wisdom which they write down for our benefit.
The grass is the vices, the lusts of the body; they bloom here in a person, soon to wither.
We must set about always subduing such grass and treading all its sweetness under foot,
so that by this deed it withers away completely beneath us and does not rise up again against us, contrary to what is right.
We cannot sit down at Christ's feast, even if we want to and even if we make a start, unless we ourselves understand [this].
As I said, tread all that sweetness under your feet, so that it does you no harm at all and does not hinder you at the feast.
When you have done that, Christ's food will grow for you in mouth and in mind, for your own good.
Read gladly in the hardness of the letters, and dig carefully into the plainness of the scripture:
there you will always, without fail, find very spiritual bread under the crust, so that you will take great delight in it.
If you do this very often, Christ's food will grow for you continually; that is how it does a person good.
If you keep sitting longer up there at those words, then perverse thoughts will wither away in you more and more, without fail,
and the grass under you will rise up against you less; the evil lusts will give you respite from then on.
And there you will also, without doubt, find a very precious treasure: the famous prophet who made the bread multiply.
The people proclaimed that he was a prophet; but faith has come to us that he is himself the Son of God.
May he deign to gladden us always at his feasts, keep us from hunger and also save us from death!
VIII. THE PEOPLE WANTED TO MAKE HIM KING, AND HOW HE WALKED ON THE SEA.
Then the people wanted to seize him by force (truly, I will not hide it from you) and make him king over them.
He fled into the mountains to hide himself there. He certainly did this because his time had not yet come
for him to be king with power, openly and in truth; that is why he fled from them there.
He then commanded the disciples to go to the other side, to stay watchful, and to cross over the sea.
The wind drove the ship along, with the waves beating against it; the weather was very hard for them on that voyage.
The Lord then went after them, once the crowd had dispersed and those who had sat there at the meal had left him.
He went after them at once, there over the water, walking firmly on the wave as we do here on land.
He went straight on his way and sought his followers, his dear thanes, there on the waves.
He reached them as it was turning toward day, before they came to land, while they were in very great distress.
They were badly frightened when they saw him; they thought for certain that it was a phantom.
Then they cried out loudly because of their heavy fear and because of the great and monstrous thing, for no one had ever seen such a thing before,
that anyone had ever thought of this, that anyone had ever achieved such a thing, or had done this: that he trod the water in this way.
Meanwhile the Lord spoke and said: "Do not be afraid at all; take heart boldly. It is certainly I myself!"
When Peter saw that, he spoke to him from the ship. He boldly greeted the master (I tell you this), as he was accustomed to.
"Lord," he said, "if it is you, and you yourself are walking there, then," he said, "command me to come there to you."
"Come!" the Lord truly said to him. He did not delay at all, but quickly set off from the ship to walk.
At first he managed well. But when he saw the wind, and what the waves were doing, fear gripped him.
Then at once the fears sank him, because his mind wavered. Doubt did not carry him up, as faith does in every case.
"Lord," he said, "help me to get through to you, so that I do not perish here now and am not lost!"
Then he stretched out his hand and saved his servant there, and with his words he rebuked him sharply for his unbelief:
why should he ever think such a thing and waver in spirit, and fear the heaviness of death, while he was with him?
Then he went into the ship to them, and they were no less afraid because of it. Then in that moment the weather became very still.
Then all of those he had saved from danger worshipped him, and they said, as is true: "You are God's own Son."
IX. They brought to him all who were sick.
Then the people learned that the Lord had come there. They went out in crowds to meet him, to see the wondrous works.
They all came together to see the signs there, many wonders. Because of this it became so famous there.
They brought the infirm and all crippled people, and also those badly afflicted with hernia (hórngibruader [?]). I tell you this truly.
The blind and the deaf as well (let everyone believe this), and also those who were out of their minds came to him there.
They wished they might touch even a single thread of his garments. They asked for nothing more.
Whoever touched him carried away benefit from it; blessing and healing were shared by all of them there.
Those who called on him with faith always obtained healing there, and an abundance of every good thing, for he is the sustainer of this world.
For he created this earth and the bliss of heaven, and also the sea here below; that is why he walked on top of it there.
The reason was this, truly: that very wave was his, and that very sea, that is true; that is why it did not give way under him there.
At that time it always stayed firm under his feet; it never gave way under him as he walked.
X. Of the Canaanite woman.
Then a woman came along the way. She was weeping, and she followed them as they went, crying out loudly.
Never before had such crying out come to the Lord from a heathen woman, whether he was walking or running.
She came calling out, made her need known, and lamented her grief over her dear daughter.
In great sorrow, as women are accustomed to do, she told him her pain more and more.
"Have mercy on me, Lord," she said. "That is why I call to you. Give us your help, son of good David!
My daughter is truly in pain and out of her mind. The devil is inside her, the one who is always mankind's enemy."
She went on speaking like this, crying out after him, and continually lamented her daughter's wretched state.
The Lord in his mildness gave her no answer. The woman kept speaking like this, and the Lord himself stayed silent.
Then, as was fitting, the kind-hearted men there, his own dear followers, spoke up and helped the woman.
"Lord, help the woman, so that she leaves us in peace, and does not run here like this and call after us.
You always willingly help all these people, rich and poor; let her also move you to pity!"
"I was not sent here into the world," he said to them, "except to bring my Father's people to understanding [?].
Many of them are lost, and they have not yet been found. I came because of that need, to gather them together."
She was eager for it and fell at his feet. She kept lamenting her pain, so that it would move him to pity all the more.
"Lord," she said, "help me! I know that my comfort lies in you. Have mercy on your weary handmaid in this sorrow!
Heal my daughter by your grace. Do me this kindness out of your own goodness!"
"It is not right," he said then, "to snatch the food out of the children's hands and throw it out to the dogs."
"Lord," she said, "it is all just so; we know that for certain. No one denies what your words mean.
Yet the whelps lick it up (that is life and help for them too); they fill themselves with the crumbs that fall from the tables,
where the wise masters sit at their meal, yet they still taste the substance [?] of those same leftovers."
He saw how firm the faith in her heart was. It pleased the Lord, and he praised her goodness in these words:
"Because your faith in my works is so strong, now let everything be done just as you have asked me here."
Then at that very moment the daughter was healed. Good Christ commanded what the mother had asked for her.
XI. THE MORAL SENSE.
As he knew, she had very firm faith. She showed it there; I tell you that in all truth.
In this matter she acted far more wisely, and better in her need, than the king did.
He asked the Lord to go to where his son was, and to be minded to heal him there.
She, however, asked for none of this. She only lamented her pain and her many sorrows, and held back nothing of it.
It is true that she did not ask him to go there at once. Nor did she even hope that she might bring him there.
Instead she prayed in this way: she begged for his mercy, believing that he would heal her if he intended it there,
and that if he did so and spoke his word, what was fitting from him would come to the daughter at once.
You certainly know this, because she showed it: she went home at once, as soon as he had spoken his single word.
In that hour she also had very great patience, a patient heart beneath her pain.
Christ himself, as he chose, counted her among the dogs, yet she never once stopped crying out.
Nor was she at all ashamed of what he said. In her need she did not stop following him,
but rather she chose to tell him her need and lament her want to him, calling after him all the while.
There she prayed to Christ himself and also praised his word, and took it in good part with a gentle mind.
Therefore she obtained there (know that in all truth), because she had such a mind, the good thing for her daughter.
With zeal and great diligence she won healing, at once, at that very moment, without delay.
And she went home rejoicing at his word. She fell silent at once and believed what he said.
XII. JESUS CAME INTO THE REGION OF CAESAREA PHILIPPI.
Once the Lord began to speak in a friendly way with his followers, and asked them kindly about the people of the world.
He promptly asked them what the world said, what people said about him, and how they spoke of him.
"Hide nothing from me," he said, "of what I now ask you. Tell me truly everything that I am about to ask you here.
"What does the people say of me? Tell me that now plainly: who do they say I am, or what my nature may be?"
They told him what they had all heard and reported the various talk: how the people spoke of him.
"Some," they said, "declare that you are Jeremiah; some also name John and count you as him.
Some say for certain that you are the famous Elijah, who afflicted this land so, who shut up heaven so;
who long ago let no rain fall on the people in their need, and truly oppressed them very grievously.
And some of the people here in the kingdom also say that you are surely one of the holy prophets,
who long ago, in ancient ages, told the people wonders, future deeds and the counsels of the Lord."
"Now," he said, "do not hide from me how you have understood me, since they speak of me in this way and disagree so greatly!"
Then one of them gave answer to this and spoke for those same men. Peter, the foremost of the Lord's beloved ones, spoke out aloud there:
"It is certain to all of us that you yourself are Christ, who came to us here from God, the Lord's own Son."
He thanked him warmly for those very words, and, know this, honored him very highly beyond that as well.
"My Father," he said, "has now put that into your mind for your good; it was not anything a man did that made you say this now.
Now I will promise you: you shall be called Peter, because, I tell you, in faith you shall always be as firm as a stone;
on it I will build my house, all my beloved ones, so that they do not go out from it.
Know this: the gate of hell, the devil's armament, will not prevail against it; it stands firm.
To you I will give the keys of heaven within, so that you shall have power over all that entrance,
so that the door is closed to those who are not to go in, and you also unlock it for those whom you admit.
Whomever you bind with words, let him remain in those bonds; nor will I go against you in the case of anyone you choose to release from his bonds.
Whatever you decree and determine here on earth, let it be wholly so in heaven; let no one oppose you in this!"
XIII. He commanded them to tell no one that he was the Christ; and the rebuke of Peter; and of the vision on the mountain.
Then he commanded the disciples that they must keep it hidden, so that it would not become known that he was Christ.
Then he told them his will fully, and also very plainly why he had come here into the world.
"I shall be seized," he said, "hung on a cross, spat upon and scourged and violently reviled.
These princes and the highest men will do it: they will hand me over by force to a foreign people.
After that I will rise (do not be afraid of it; truly, it will not be long) at once on the third day."
When Peter heard this, he took him aside and rebuked him, and very harshly too, with words like these:
"Lord, do not speak of it any further; have mercy on yourself, so that the world never sees such a thing happen to you!
Lord, you should not want to fall in this way; and you yourself should forbid the people to do this to you.
Do not betray us like this by ever failing us; God forbid that such a thing should ever happen to you!"
Then he gave an answer that seemed harsh to Peter, and it certainly stung him very sharply.
"Get behind me, then, you satan of a man! You know nothing of the counsel that the Lord himself wills most.
He has resolved that the world be healed through me. It cannot happen any other way, and you say you do not want it!
Human deeds matter more to you than his counsel. You go by what seems right to you, not by what he intends.
Whoever wishes to follow me gladly at all times must utterly deny his own self-will,
and take up his cross as well, and then always follow me wherever I go before him.
What does it help a wretched man who rules so widely here that all the ends of the world are in his hands,
if in the meantime he loses his soul and inevitably damns himself through sins?
In all the kingdoms he cannot find anything to give in exchange for it (that is all worthless), and that is true; he himself must be there to pay.
For when the Lord passes judgment, he repays everyone according to what they did and worked here.
Some of those standing here among you (I tell you this for certain) will not taste death or suffer its pain
before they see the holy Son of God in his glory, shining like the sun in his kingdom."
Eight days after this (I mention it here so that you may read for yourself there about the marvellous wonder
that he soon went on to do), he went up a mountain. There you will also read, without doubt, that he told three to go with him;
and there they suddenly saw his glory, and how he also wished to bless them there with things beyond words.
The Father made it sweeter still by greeting his beloved, saying that he was his only one (you know more about this).
Moses the faithful and the renowned Elijah came there to meet him from the holy multitude.
Luke tells you what their business there was, and what his servants spoke steadfastly there with Christ.
Then the disciples were suddenly startled by the radiance, and they were greatly afraid of what happened;
He himself commanded them that they must keep it hidden until he, in his goodness, rose up from death.
XIV. A brief admonition concerning the signs.
There is no number or count for how many wonders are his, how many marvels are famous across the world.
The four writers who write the gospel make this widely known; read for yourself what I am telling you.
There you can find how he also brought a man back to life on the bier; I tell you that truly.
Because he had the power, he also brought the ruler's daughter back to life in the house, to the joy of her family.
While the Lord himself was going there, a woman interrupted it; she went away whole as soon as she touched him.
Yet there had certainly been no physician before this who could help her in her distress, though she had spent everything she had.
As the Lord was going there, as her father urged him, to act for the daughter, as he had begged him there
(the crowd that was there before him pressed upon him, where those same people pressed hard upon the Lord Christ!),
she began to think and to consider in her mind how she might get close enough to touch him
(but by this she meant only one of the threads of the fringe). She set her mind on this, so that she wished for nothing more —
that she would at once become entirely whole, and that it would come about that her bleeding would stop!
She brought it about and drew near to the Lord, and managed to touch the fringe of his garment.
With great speed she was healed at once, immediately and in every respect.
At once — this is true — the fountain of blood stopped and ran no more; so she immediately felt the benefit.
The Lord, who had brought about the healing there, turned back and asked insistently who had touched him.
"Why, Lord," said Peter then, "do you ask about this now, and inquire so urgently about this deed?
People are crowding you one after another on this very road, all these people — and you ask who touched you?"
"I," he said, "felt that someone touched me; I tell you, I perceived the power go out from me here."
When she then heard him answer this way, and her deed could not stay hidden,
and he spoke openly about the benefit she had stolen there, at the very moment when she thought he did not know of it,
she came at once, full of fear, and told him what had happened there, and spoke willingly there of her own deeds,
of the Lord's works and of her own thoughts: why she had become so bold, and why she had come there,
and why she had gone to touch the fringe. Faith truly did it; she did not dare touch any more of it.
"Go," he then said, "go home now, daughter, in peace and in good, healed in this way by faith.
Truly, your faith made you whole here; it did what was fitting, so that you received the benefit here." You can
read in this account a great many miracles, certainly, as I tell you, all of which he performed:
How the devils went out there at Peter's house, when the Lord resolved to heal his mother-in-law.
Then in the evening all the sick came; he drove away all their sicknesses and their infirmities.
He commanded the winds and the stormy waves; as soon as he spoke of it there, they immediately grew still.
When his disciples called to him while he slept in the boat, terrified with fear, he worked that miracle.
He also healed the blind, who were mourning and who came hurrying to him on the way.
Those who struggled with the devil also came hastening to him, and lepers too; he healed them all at once.
Read for yourself Matthew's part, how a leper was healed; and in Luke's part, how ten were healed.
Old bedridden people are also told of there, sick men; he healed them all, as was fitting.
Above all he wiped out their sin, which was a wonder; in his goodness he forgave them their misdeeds.
Add to these a great many blind people, a multitude of lame people, and a gathering of crippled people,
whom I cannot list in full, even if I spent the day on it, or the whole year, and my life beyond that.
This happened in the settlements [?] and out in the countryside, wherever they cried out and hurried to meet him:
the Lord healed them all at once; I tell you that in all truth. Whoever approached him went away happier.
Whoever cared to seek help from him (know it in all truth) lacked nothing there;
for he himself is joy and the fountain of all good; truly, all good flowed from him there
in abundance to all people, to whoever spoke of it there, to whoever ran there for this purpose and called out to him there.
In this manner he sent out twelve disciples (yet not for worldly glory), to work miracles as well;
so that they would put devils to flight in wretched sicknesses and always help the people in all their needs.
He commanded them to take heed and to take nothing with them at that time as provision for the road,
neither purse nor bag, and to set out from there in this way; nor to carry any penny with them on that mission;
that they should undertake it in this way and go with staffs, with rods in their hands, in great haste;
and that they should not care to seek two tunics for themselves, nor many kinds of shoes in that haste.
He did this for their benefit, so that they would go on their own among worldly people for such matters.
"I tell you one thing," he said: "take no treasure for this; let the wages of worldly people mean little to you.
Before this I did this work for you freely, of my own will, and you (you know this) gave me not a drop for it.
So you too must not want to go about it, or run after it, in order to sell any part of it!"
Because of such deeds the people watched him closely; meanwhile his enemies were after his life.
And they spread it about that he was out of his mind, and that he had the devil, and that this was how he did all these things.
He bore all of that, and more besides: all this ill-treatment, because of his goodness.
In his mildness he was gentle to them, and he always showed them great sweetness, without fail.
He kept showing them more and more why he had come here into the world, rightly, with works, through his righteousness.
He did this with works in great abundance, even though the crowd kept showing ill will against it.
He endured all of that very heavy envy, for an envious mind always hates what is good.
Out of arrogance it always hates goodness; wretched hearts take no delight in it.
XV. JESUS WALKED IN GALILEE.
So because of their great hatred he then avoided the Judeans, for they were firmly resolved on his death.
He stayed in Galilee, though not out of fear; he waited, as he was meant to, until the time he chose.
A time drew near when people had to keep a week-long feast, as the law commanded,
when the people were to dwell outdoors faithfully for a week, with plenty of food, as the Lord had once commanded them.
Without doubt, this had been set up long before as a remembrance, a reminder for the community,
so that they would remember and keep reminding themselves how their forefathers had journeyed out of Egypt,
and how for this reason they had been without a home and had in fact lived in tents for forty years.
Then his kinsmen urged him, as relatives often do, since the good fortune of those closest to them always pleases them.
They advised him to win fame and glory for himself, saying it would be fitting for him to go to the feast,
to show his manly greatness there, and to do signs so that the people would recognize him,
and so that the people would also see his own goodness, and the disciples would recognize him by these same deeds.
"No one who means to make himself known does that," they said: "no one like that plans to do such works in secret."
The people who wanted this from him did not believe as they should have; this world mattered more to them.
He refused to do what they thought fitting. His time, he said, had not yet come for him to show himself in glory in the kingdom.
"Certainly you know this: Moses formerly did not do this, that he would wish to oppose me with deeds or with words."
Then the same crowd spoke against him again; they let out from themselves, truly [?], the pain of that same mind.
"You have the devil in you; certainly we perceive that! Who here is thinking of this, of bringing about your death?"
He gave an answer to the people, though they did not honour him; he told them why they were so zealous about it, and what they all reproached him for:
"I did one great work, certainly you know that, which I intended for one man: I healed him on the sabbath day.
Moses commanded, and you do not neglect it, that your children be circumcised; yet that command came rather from the old forefathers before him.
This is also, without doubt, often done on the sabbath day, so that they take care not to break his command;
and also so that healing may then come to the man, and ample blessing too, because the law mentioned it.
Now, since you do not refrain on the sabbath day from circumcising your children, so that it is fulfilled of necessity as the law commanded:
why then is this same goodness offensive to you, that I made a man entirely whole on that day?
Do not judge unjustly, so that anyone has regard for rank; give a right judgment here, common to us two!
You do not grow angry with him if you do that on the sabbath day; so do not be angry with me either if I do the same."
Some from that same realm said: "This is the one they speak of and whom they want to kill!
He speaks openly here now to them and very boldly among them; he carries on the dispute here among them, and none of them says anything against it.
Have they turned away [?] from this, that they had at hand the one whom they earlier wanted to kill, and have now fallen silent [?] like this?
Do the authorities understand that he is truly Christ? That is great folly; we know well where he comes from.
In that respect we know all his family, father and mother; should he be the good Christ?
When Christ comes to us, no man knows, as befits his nature, where he himself came from."
Then he cried out loudly where the people heard it; he said that they recognized him among them: "And you know well where I come from.
Know this also very well, that I did not come of myself; he who sent me is true, and you do not know his ways.
I know him for this reason, because I also come from him, and he sent me here for this purpose; yet you do not believe because of it!"
They wanted to seize him, and yet they held back from it; that was indeed fitting, because his time had not yet come.
Many of the people then believed in the Lord, and they also asked, with reason, how it could be
that Christ's own goodness would do more wonders, more fitting signs [?], as soon as he himself came.
The chief men heard that and made a plan, with plenty of words, that he should be seized.
XVII. Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
After many words and many very weighty teachings (that was a mighty work), he went to the Mount of Olives.
Very early he came into the house [the Temple] and taught them again (as was fitting for him) with beautiful words, very many and varied.
Then he gave all the chief men a beautiful sermon in full words, and all the people heard the speech.
Then, being ill-willed, they came in there and brought an adulteress, as they had wickedly planned.
They brought her into the assembly, into the middle of the circle, in the midst of the people, so that he would pass judgment on her.
They asked our Lord directly and at once about this very deed, and what he would say about it.
"Master, you know that this woman has forfeited her life; she has been caught in the very act of the misdeed of adultery.
Moses himself said long ago that a woman who does such a thing here should be pelted with stones, and no man should help her in it.
Now tell us fully here what your will is, what your counsel is, what you would say about this,
so that we may know the thought of your mind without any doubt. Do not hide any of it from us, and instruct us in it!"
They really said this as a trap. They wanted to arrange things there so that they could accuse him,
and so that they would have to slander his goodness and his wise words in this way:
for our Lord always spoke of mercy in many ways and with merciful words. We feel it deeply!
If he had said that they should let her go and free her from the sentence, because mercy is sweet, it would have gone no other way than this:
they would have accused him of speaking wrongly against the old teaching, the law, as people had heard it.
If, on the other hand, he had said that she must be stoned, then he would have contradicted his own teaching;
or they would have said that, although he was merciful, he had turned what he had taught as sweet into harshness.
The Lord himself looked down when they said this to him. Then, as is known, he wrote on the ground with his finger.
Then they asked him urgently and again insistently. He straightened up patiently and gave this answer:
"Whoever among you," he said, "is without sin, let him throw the first stone at her, I tell you."
As soon as he had said this he bent down again at once and wrote with his finger again, and each of them slipped away at once.
No one stayed there while he was writing down there. Each one went his own way while he stared down like this;
And each of them then set about it; one after another they went and took themselves out of that place when they heard this;
for each of them there now understood that the man ought to be good who would count himself among the good and would torment the sinful woman in this way.
In truth they were not that. So they shied away there, and at once, on the same path, they withdrew from the matter.
The Lord was left there, and she was alone; her heart was sore within her, and she still stood there in the middle.
"Woman," he said, "now tell me: where are those who were against you, who gathered here for this purpose and accused you so hatefully just now?
Does anyone here condemn you now?" She answered as was fitting: "No one, Lord," she said. "That is all through your power!"
"Nor do I condemn you," he said. "Now go forth, and see that you always take care that you sin no more." — Mercy
on me too, Lord! I am your sinful servant, sinful in thoughts and in hateful deeds!
What would my punishment be, were it not for your mercy, because of my evil deeds and my manifold wickedness?
Help me, Lord, in my need, as you did here just now for this poor woman, so that the lust of adultery may not cling to me;
so that I do not go astray, and always place my hope in you, and so that I may always be, my Lord, your constant servant! — Again
the Lord told them that he is the chosen light, and wholly without blame in his deeds.
He showed them much good there, but none of it went into their minds; nothing of the Lord's teaching went into their ears.
XVIII. WHICH OF YOU CONVICTS ME OF SIN?
Among many words and very weighty matters, the Lord, by his own power, then spoke to them thus:
"Who is there here among you," he said, "who can accuse me of this? Who among you will charge me with sin?
If I tell you the truth here, why do you not believe me at once? Why do your minds not open when I tell you what is good?
Know this: whoever is from God hears his word, and always turns his own heart to it very readily.
In truth you are not from him. That is why you do not hear it at once, and why his manifold goodness does not come into your minds."
They began to answer with very harsh words, and to argue with him there with base words.
"What," they said, "do we say wrongly if the devil is in you? We will tell you something more as well: you are an utter foreigner!"
"Know," he said, "that I certainly do not have the devil. I am wholly safe from that; he has no part with me.
Rather, I honour my Father above all, as I ought. I do not hide this from you: but you dishonour me!
I do not seek dominion here now, nor my own glory. My Father looks to that, and he himself judges!
Know this for certain: those who keep my word, who willingly fulfil what my words tell them — Not …
they feared the woe. They will not die for ever, and that misfortune will not come upon them, as I have just said here."
They gave their answer with great indignation; with great hatred they grew angry:
"Now we know what this is: you are out of your mind, and the devil himself rules over you completely!
Abraham the renowned is certainly dead, and the good prophets are all dead as well;
and then you say that whoever does what your word declares, whoever strives to gain it, will never die!
Are you then truly greater than Abraham? Greater also than the men we have just named here, all of whom death overtook?
Now start explaining to us whom you want to compare yourself with. Without doubt, whom do you count yourself among, when all of those men have gone that way?"
He patiently gave them a gentle answer to this. He truly set them right, though they understood none of it:
"If I set about glorifying myself alone with concern, and also do it with anxious care, that is all nothing.
My Father is the one who does that. He furthers the good for me, and he fully furthers my will.
He is the one you say is our Lord (know this further). That is why you name him, and yet you know nothing of him!
I have always known him. But if I spoke otherwise, then I would be lying, like your talk.
I certainly know him. It is not otherwise but just so, and I truly keep his teaching!
Old Abraham rejoiced greatly that he might delight in this: seeing my day.
He saw my day, and his mind was glad of it; his heart rejoiced at it. Be certain of that!"
They took the meaning in a bodily sense and looked at his age; so it seemed very strange to them.
"You certainly are not yet fifty years old here among the people of the world. Where would you have seen him, then?"
The Lord answered with sweet mildness. He wanted to start bringing their minds onto the right path.
Then he lifted up their minds, as he always does for us, to the goodness of the Godhead. That displeased them.
"I tell you truly," he said, "my being is thus before him: I have existence before he ever came to be.
My times were before his ever came to be. My being, know this, is far, far before him!"
Then their minds could not bear the eternal good, the eternal teaching. Know that for sure.
Then pain touched the stony heart. This same grief touched the heart that always shunned what would do it good.
At once they picked up stones, meaning to act quickly and throw them at him,
to cool their tempers, as people do with enemies, and in this way take revenge for their anger. They had been planning this long before.
He truly hid himself, and at once he went out, out of their hands, away from his enemies.
XIX. In the moral sense.
Here the Lord Christ admonishes us, as is his custom; here his deed teaches us that we should be patient.
There is no one among us who can bear it when anyone rebukes us; at once he is very ready for us to answer back.
Nor are we willing, moreover, to endure any anger; it seems to us for certain that it would be a disgrace
if we were to begin this: to put up with insult, or in the battle of words to keep silent at all toward anyone.
Pride does this to us, not at all our goodness; great boastfulness and our foolish heart.
Learn here the goodness of how our Lord acted: his own mildness and gentleness of spirit.
Here it is found that he was reviled here, and that he was greatly dishonored here by their words.
They kept insisting that he had the devil; all this he endured. You can read that for yourself.
He did still more: he showed them his teaching, surely, in answer to it, there to that same crowd.
Those who heard it there took it all amiss; he always wished, willingly, to calm them gently.
He showed them there in all truth his eternity, his high birth; that displeased them all.
At once those wicked men ran to their stones; with them at that time they wanted to torment him!
Then he avoided them with patience, so that it would be to our benefit, so that we would always do the same in times of distress.
He would say nothing about it, though he could have avenged himself and, if he had wished, cast them into the abyss.
We, however, do from the start the worst we can; if we lack the means to act, then we threaten fiercely.
The Lord's teaching is truly far better; as I mentioned here earlier, he endured his enemies.
Let all imitate this, whoever wishes to do well, whoever thinks of it, so as to thwart the devil!
That is pure and also good. Have a gentle mind, and do not waver in it, so that God may thank you for it,
so that he in turn may spare you here in life, since through his example you endure the insolence of men.
XX. Of the man born blind.
Then the Lord saw a man born blind; he had been in that same misfortune from birth.
Then his faithful disciples asked about it, whether this blindness had come from his own sins,
or whether his father and mother had earlier deserved it, having been so very sinful that they bore such a child.
Then he gave his own a kind answer in words and explained to them the strange case, the matter of this man:
"These infirmities are not because he deserved it, nor, truly, did his forefathers' deeds cause it;
Rather, it happened for this reason (I tell you this for certain): so that through him God's work might always be shown clearly.
It is my duty to be mindful of doing the works of the one who sent me for this purpose, who sent me here into the world,
while the day shines and night does not touch it, and no one has to suffer the helplessness of the dark night.
The night comes after that (you certainly know this), so that there is no one who could quickly set about any work,
or even think that he could do anything in that darkness; let them always be sure of this.
While I am here in the world, I am a light that leads all people to divine things."
Then, truly, he at once made mud with his spittle. He smeared it on the man where his eyes should be, though the man had not asked for this.
He told him the name of a body of water and told him to go there and wash it off, washing properly, so that he would take the mud away.
He went at once, as he had been told, and washed the mud away. In this way he did himself a good and fitting thing, for now he could see clearly.
Then the people who had seen him before were suddenly amazed. They would not recognize him, and they began to speak like this:
"Is this really the beggar who sat here blind for years, who called out to us here because of his need?"
Some of the men said: "It is the very same man (you certainly know it) who sat blind among us."
Others declared that it was not he. Each of them said that it was someone who looked like him.
"I am the one," he said. "Know this: I am the one who sat here blind and begging. I always had to grope my way with a staff
along everyone's walls, always begging for bread, always lamenting my own poverty because I had to."
Their poor minds were curious about this. They marveled greatly and asked about what had happened:
"Tell us truthfully now: how do you see so well? And who gave you the power to see so clearly?"
"I will tell you how it happened," he said. "It was the one we call the Saviour! I said nothing to him about it. When he saw me here,
he immediately spat on the ground, truly made mud there, and smeared it on me at once.
When I washed the mud away, as he himself had told me to, my sight came. Thanks be to God and to him!"
"Show us," they said, "where this man is." At that point he said at once that he did not know anything about it.
Then they led him over to the place of authority, to the court, to the assembly of the leaders.
The books state that it was the Sabbath when Christ chose to do this very miracle.
Then the leaders and the elders asked how he had come to see so clearly so suddenly.
"I tell you," he said, "and it is true: he smeared mud on me there. As soon as I washed it away, I could see at once, as it should be."
Some said that he had acted against God and broken his commandment: "his folly so ruled him that he did not keep the Sabbath."
Then others from the crowd spoke against this (they judged the matter more purely and much more carefully):
How could a sinful man do that, or be capable enough to perform such a sign in this time of need?
There was strife about it and fierce dispute; the wicked and the good could not agree there.
Then they began to quarrel about it and to question the man again, and they began to address him with harsh words:
"What do you say about that man who has made himself so dear to you, who has pleased your heart so much by bringing light home to you?"
"He is," he said, "God's beloved; I boldly declare it of him. My heart assures me that he is a good prophet."
They could not believe this deed about him, that he had suddenly gained his sight so newly,
until those who bore him were present there: father and mother, where the good son also was.
They ordered them to come forward at once to tell the truth, and not to say anything other than what they knew of him.
"Look," they said, "with truthful eyes: is this your child, who was born blind?
You both made it known that he was blind then, and that at that time he lacked sight.
Now tell us quickly: who did this, so that he can now see with such clear eyes?"
Then they began to answer with fearful words; they told them there how they had understood it:
"We know, and we tell you one thing that cannot be denied: such as we were, we bore him blind.
We do not know how it came about, or who opened his eyes for him; nor do we wish to [?] about it, as we now tell you here.
Ask him about it truly; he is already old enough to speak for himself in these matters!"
They gave these answers out of necessity; they were very much afraid because of this deed.
The people had made a great vow, as is known, in which they stood firm against Christ himself:
whoever chose that and joined himself to Christ would at once, by necessity, be cut off from them forever.
Therefore they put those answers onto him there, because they feared what they had earlier decreed among themselves.
They were then greatly distressed by this deed; it was very displeasing to them that the blind man could see.
Then they summoned again the man who had gained his sight, and told him to confess the deed still more fully.
"Give great thanks to God for it, and do not credit it to this man; we know him to be very wicked in his deeds."
Then he answered the people with dignity, and told them what he had felt and what had touched him there;
They were truly enraged at the lordly teaching, at those fair words; so they also spoke harshly to him:
"You are utterly despised, born in sins, with every kind of wickedness; and would you then preach to us?"
Then they quickly cast him out from among them at once, truly, so that from then on he would be forced to be without them forever;
And that, because of that affair, he would be excommunicated, cut off forever, because he had made the day hateful to them.
The Lord then heard how he had been rejected [?] there; and he learned all of it, that they had cast him out because of that.
When the Lord then saw him, he himself at once spoke to him (he joined the healing of the soul to that of the body):
"Do you believe in the Son of God, who came down here from heaven?" He then gave an answer (he was very glad to have his sight):
"Who is he, Lord," he said, "so that I may become his through faith?" He himself, as was fitting, instructed him kindly about it:
"You have seen him close at hand, and, believe me, he is the one who is speaking with you here now."
"Yes, Lord," he said, "I do; I firmly believe in your glory!" Then he fell down there before him and worshipped the Son of God.
They fiercely persecuted him for such deeds, and his very lofty teaching made their envy even greater.
Soon after these wicked intentions they wanted to stone him; all of this happened every time because he told them who he was,
He declared it with words and showed it with signs. All of this was for their good, but they did not care about it.
XXI. Spiritual interpretation.
May Christ himself, who is our dear Lord, now grant that I may explain here whom that man signifies
