who was born blind and could see nothing before the sinless man smeared the mud on his eyes;
Before he brought it about, he touched the beggar's eyes with his hands so that he could see afterwards.
All mankind suffered great misery and, besides many evils, grievous darkness;
Very heavy sins, I tell you truly, did not let us have the joy of seeing the true light.
This blindness came to us, I think, through descent from Adam, and also to all people through the sins into which we fall.
Then the Lord saw the need, our wretchedness, our blindness from birth, and he took pity on us.
I call it "need" here because there was no remedy then, no relief or fitting help, unless it came to us from him.
Then his Word was made a body, made a fleshly creature with all its powers.
When he brought it about in this way, and touched us with such things, with his birth, so that it would be to our benefit:
Those deeds did us much good, and afterwards [we] could see, surely enlightened out of the old darkness.
Let everyone now run to the beautiful baptism, to which Christ then directed him and himself sent him there.
Know this in all truth: the water there is also called by this name, because Christ rules it, who was sent here;
No man would ever be healed of his sins if the Father had not sent him and turned him here into the world.
He enlightened us very greatly, and he came here into the world so that his goodness might open our eyes;
So that we might recognize where we should go, on straight paths, to his glorious righteousness;
And that we may behold him with open eyes, face to face, unveiled, so that it may be well with us;
With an open mind, so that it may turn out to our good, may we forever behold him with the eyes of the heart! Amen.
XXII. The Feast of Dedication took place.
Around that time came the dedication of God's house; the people celebrated those same high feasts.
The gospel says there that it was in wintertime, above all this deed that I am now to tell you here.
Then the Lord went inside, into the porch of the house; its name made it famous: that it was Solomon's.
That may truly have been because of its splendor, that people attributed it to him and chose that name for it.
The Jews surrounded him; they did not know what they were doing. They spoke to him treacherously, as they were accustomed:
"How long shall we endure it that you lure us this way toward you, and thus take [?] one by one [?]? Will you forever [?] in this?
If Christ is your name, then let that be made open; tell it to us here, right now, so that we may know it to be true!"
"If I tell it to you," he said, "you still will not believe because of it; your mind does not grasp it when I tell you what is good.
The works that I do in the name of my Father bear witness to me in every way, very fully.
Yet you still do not believe, though it has often been told to you; surely you are not among those whom I choose for myself!
Those whom I count for this and choose apart for myself always have love for me and hear my voice;
I also know them, and they follow me with love; and I truly give them eternal life.
They will never perish; they also escape woe; they are held firmly, without end, in my own hands.
No hatred of men (surely you know this) will take them out of my Father's hand until the end of the world!
What my Father has granted me is the foremost of all good; there is nothing that ever equals the benefits of his gift.
"I and my Father, and his eternity (I hide it from none of you): the being of us two is one."
The people could not bear these words at all when he spoke of this; then at once they hurried eagerly to stone him.
Then he answered the people patiently, taught them the good once more, and turned their minds onward.
"I have shown you," he said, "many pleasing good works, sweet deeds from my Father's goodness;
yet you hate and persecute me out of envy because of my works, every one of you, man by man, with your stoning!"
With ill will and with their minds very full, they began to defend themselves and spoke to him again:
"We do not show you this hostility because of good deeds; we do it rather because you say what you should not.
You are only a man, and yet you say you are God; your folly makes itself equal to the Lord's goodness!"
Our Lord nonetheless spoke what was right to them there, and he reminded them there of what the Law said.
"Your books," he said, "know that men too are called gods; I certainly tell you that they are named so there.
Now those who dwell here in this world are named gods, those to whom God's word told what they were always to say to you;
and no one denies what the Scripture says to you there, and it stands very firm forever, for all the ages of the world:
he whom God named holy and sent here into the world, and into whom he gave all his blessings in full abundance:
do you say that my words are against the Lord, that I dare to call myself God's Son?
If I do not do his works before you, then do not believe on that account, and do not go that way or turn yourselves toward it;
but if I take care to work his works, then even if I am not [?] to you, at least believe the deeds,
so that you may recognize this and also be willing to believe that we are to be one, I and my Father!"
When his words said this, they wanted to seize him, but at that very hour he went out of their hands.
When all this had happened, he went across the Jordan, so that they could be there at home until his time came.
XXIII. THERE WAS A CERTAIN SICK MAN, LAZARUS.
The Lord's deeds are very many, and too many and varied for anyone to recount them all;
yet here I will now tell one wonder in particular. It is, I will not hide this from you, unlike all the others.
Lazarus the good was very sorely afflicted by a powerful sickness and great weakness.
I tell you here openly: he was very dear to Christ; he was his beloved friend. You may believe me in this.
He was from a village, as we all know, where Martha and Mary lived, and it is called Bethany.
This was, as you know, the one who once unbound her hair, and to whom it was sweet to wipe Christ's feet with it.
What more can I tell you about it? These were his sisters; they had Christ's love and were his own beloved friends.
They sent word to Christ about the brother, to make their grief known to him; it was enough for them if someone merely mentioned it to him,
so that he would know of it at once, at that very time: the sickness that the one he loved so much was suffering there.
"This sickness," he said, "is not brought upon him so far as death, but truly for the Lord's glory,
so that through this sickness the might of God's Son becomes very famous. Know that for certain."
Truly he held him in dear love, and the two women as well; believe me in this.
When the Lord heard that he was so ill, he held back and stayed there two more days.
Then he spoke to the disciples: "Let us visit the Jews! Let us go back there to them, into their land!"
Then his dear, faithful followers spoke with love (they were quickly frightened [?] at the earlier deed):
"Master," they said, "think about this: they are seeking your life, to stone you themselves; and now you are going back to them?"
"Yes," he said, "there are of necessity twelve hours of the day, which run their course and follow the day.
Whoever walks by day certainly does not stumble, because he can look ahead with his eyes.
So do not doubt this: if he sets out at night, he cannot help going blindly and stumbling badly!
Whoever wants to walk rightly," he said, "let him follow me; let him always look entirely to my guidance!"
Then the Lord spoke openly about his sick friend, and also with cheerful words to his disciples:
"Our good friend is now sleeping peacefully; we must wake him and rouse him from sleep."
"That is good, Lord," they said. "Then he will get better; now his spirit is getting relief, as often happens to a sick person."
They thought the Lord meant that he was talking about his sleep; but he himself meant that he had died.
Then he at once made the truth about him plain: "I will tell you plainly first," he said, "Lazarus has died.
Yet I will truly rejoice in it now for your sakes, so that you may believe, because I was here with you now.
And I know the circumstances, his whole case, how it all went there; I tell you this truly.
Though he is now dead, let us still go where he is; to this end it will now come about, even though he lies buried."
Thomas, one of the disciples, said: "Let us go too, rightly; since he himself truly wills it so, let us die there with him!
Since he is now seeking death and does not care for life, let us all be ready to fall with him!"
XXIV. So Jesus came and found that he had already been [in the tomb] four days.
Then the Lord, the Saviour, came there into the land of the Jews, where his friend had been before; he had lain buried for the fourth day.
A crowd of the Jews had come earlier. They comforted the sisters there and begged them to cease from their distress.
Martha the good, when she heard of his coming, at once left the crowd and hurried to meet Christ.
The other sister sat at home and lamented the pain; she wept continually and piteously for her brother.
Truly there were painful tears among them, with grieving hearts; yet it turned out well for them.
Then Martha, when she had hurried to Christ, lamented with painful words; it moved her very deeply.
"Lord," she said, "if you had come earlier, we would not be suffering this pain; your grace would not have allowed death to come upon us like this,
that it should ever come to this, that it should seize us so closely, fill us so with sorrow and with such painful distress!
Yet I know for certain, though your coming is now late, that God grants you everything, whatever you ask him for;
and all your counsel takes effect at once, everything that is dear to you and whatever you yourself say."
"Do not let it grieve you," he said; "your brother will rise. He will be brought back to life in such a way that your heart will not be grieved."
"It is so, Lord," she said; "I certainly believe that it will not pass him by either, when all the world rises up."
Then the Lord said to her at once (which we believe as wholly true, and which all the world everywhere shall always hold in its heart):
"I am the resurrection, know that for certain; I am also life, very firm, for all eternity.
Whoever believes in me (that is the head of all good!) will still attain life, though he dies here;
and all who believe in me, I do not hide it from you (have no fear of woe at all!), shall never die.
Do you believe all these words of mine, as I tell them?" "They are, Lord," she said, "firm in the breast of my heart.
I gladly believe that you are Christ the good, the fitting Son of God, who came here into the world."
When she had said that, she at once fetched her sister. "The master is here," she said; "he bids you come."
She rose up quickly; her will made her do it. She made no delay at all, but hurried swiftly to him.
Our Lord had not yet come into the village; he was still staying where Martha had met him.
The Jews took notice that she rose up so suddenly; they too set out and went after her.
They said she was going to run to the grave to weep, that she was eager to do so and to weep her fill there.
She fell at Christ's feet as her heart surged so; she poured tears over them as she wept for her dear brother.
She then showed her grieving heart, as women often do in such things (she could hardly bear it), and spoke to the Lord:
"If you had been here, Lord Christ, we would not now be suffering this death; my brother would be alive now, and I would not have this sorrow!"
Then he felt the sorrow, when he saw her weeping; and all the people who had come to the gathering were weeping too.
There the sisters stood together and wept over their grief; there they showed their anguish, their aching hearts.
He who is the prince of all good was then troubled in spirit; he did not hold back his tears where the brother was being mourned.
The Lord also showed what he meant by this: that the dead man moved him so deeply to pity.
He told them to tell him where they had laid him. "Lord," they said at once, "you can see for yourself there."
Then our Lord came there weeping, to the beloved man, to where he lay buried.
On top of it lay a rock, as is still the custom in that land, a very heavy load; I tell you that truly.
A very great crowd was present there, a great many people; in the middle lay the dead man.
Those who had just come hurrying there saw all the grief; the sorrow touched his own friends so deeply.
Then the people considered how much he had loved him, when they suddenly saw the tears on him.
Then some from that country also spoke (they took it the wrong way when they heard this;
they considered his grief): why had he not thought of it before? Why, alas, had he not protected himself from this sorrow beforehand?
Why had he not arranged that his friend should not die, he who had been so mighty before, who had made the blind see!
Then the Lord began to look at the grave with his eyes, and he spoke cheerful words to his own people:
"Take the stone away at once and quickly set it aside; uncover the chamber for me, my friend's bed!"
"Lord," said the sister, "the body is already rotting (that is why I am telling you this beforehand); it has been buried for four days."
"I told you just now," he said, "that if you believe, you will see God's power and the Lord's own might."
Because they had to, they took away that very stone, as he had commanded; there they opened the grave, as his words had said.
He stood there below and raised his eyes up to heaven, far up into the Father's bosom, from which he had come here into the world.
"Father," he said, "I thank you with words and with deeds, that you always fulfill my will completely.
I have always known it for certain, Father, I tell you, that you would never do otherwise than all that I asked of you;
yet I speak of your goodness for the sake of these people, so that they may know that you sent me and turned me here into the world."
Then he spoke in a loud voice to the dead man, to the rotting warrior, that he should stand up from his bed,
and that he must turn back here from the pit of hell, from the people of hell back to this light.
At once life returned to his spirit, and he stood up from the grave wrapped in sheets and bound likewise with [?].
Then the Lord withdrew from them. He no longer went openly among them, and he went away from there with his followers into a wilderness.
XXVI. Moral interpretation (Moraliter).
Now Christ, in this account, performs so many signs, and yet, as the priests said, they took it all in an evil sense:
Let us now put that doubt away at once and entirely, and let us believe in the deeds; that befits us greatly.
Let us turn God's deed over in our minds, always for our own good, from now on, as it stands written there:
They deliberated very earnestly about what they wanted and what they ought to do concerning that same deed of God;
But they did not say truly that they would believe God at once, that they would teach it to their hearts and from then on turn it to good.
We must gather ourselves to more righteous speech; we must make ourselves dear to God and believe more rightly;
And let us say rightly that all his deeds are praiseworthy, even though they are hateful to them.
They said about this that if no one killed him, they would be forcibly made exiles
and would lose the path to their home, and with it, forever, the journey to their own land.
But we must take care, lest we fail to think it through well, that we honour the works and take them into our hearts, so that
we do not become exiles without end and lose the beautiful kingdom, the high kingdom of heaven,
and end up mourning in grievous exile, in captivity. Of this let us always be certain!
Let us also reflect on this for our good, with a sound mind, and from now on turn to good what Caiaphas meant to teach.
He advised that they bring it about that the one man should die, so that by his single death he would save the whole people,
and that through his single wound the whole people would be preserved and would live in peace once he had given up his life.
We certainly know that it served us very well, and that it profited us greatly that the Lord came here into the world;
He was willing to die for us and alone to bring it about, through his own single fall, that we should never again perish at all;
And his goodness gathered us all together, when we had always gone astray and had been scattered.
That is now a wondrous thing throughout this world, a wondrous plan beyond all deeds.
When worldly kings die for their thanes, falling valiantly in battle in the same way,
then all who followed him there in that peril are thrown into confusion and their fight is broken up;
And they fall by force before their enemies, under their hands, by spears and by swords;
They are altogether in flight from that deed, terrified by the works of their fleeing thoughts.
But he died for this need, so that he might gather us, and by the goodness of his death joined us together;
And through his pain we have had a bold heart, ever ready then to stand against our enemies;
So that, glad of that death, we travel homeward into our own estate after this misery.
After they condemned him, as Caiaphas told us, and they put him to death, as he declared there:
Now we are glad in mind because of his one good deed; with his one fall he has redeemed us all!
Now let us dwell boldly in that kingdom of his, joyful in righteousness in his sight.
That same joy his goodness gives us, for he alone achieved this: that he died for us.
Now let us hasten to think of this and work constantly, so that it may always please him, toward the high kingdom of heaven,
And that the Lord may count us all there by name, and name us all there, man by man;
So that his death may not, above all, be in vain in us through our wickedness and our manifold presumption;
But rather let us be bold in this: to rejoice forever with his own, to be glad forever with his own, and not to shun it!
That is made certain for them, that they lack nothing more; so may it also be for all of us, by the will of Christ himself! Amen. Here ends the third book.
