II. SIX DAYS BEFORE THE PASSOVER JESUS CAME TO BETHANY.
When the Lord intended this, that he would heal this world and also show mercy to mankind in its need;
When he had brought it to the point that the time drew near when he would comfort us and redeem us from the enemies:
Six days before that he came to Bethany, where he had awakened Lazarus from death and brought him back to life.
Then in the evening they promptly prepared his meal there; they were glad of him, and their goodwill made that very plain.
Martha the good served there then; she arranged it all beautifully and brought out the food.
I do not think she fell short in anything when she poured the drink there, so that it was all fitting and proper for the Lord.
Lazarus was one of those whom good fortune favoured, so that he sat at the table there and ate together with him.
Mary took nard of very precious worth (that service was sweet to her) and poured it on his feet.
When she had done this anointing, she wiped those holy feet with her hair, with her beautiful locks.
The costliness of the ointment gave off its scent on every side; its goodness filled the whole breadth of the house.
Judas, who was always on the worse side, found fault with that; he said that it could quickly have been sold for a very high price,
So that one might choose to feed the poor with it, and to give thought to clothing the naked as well;
And also those who travel through the land as pilgrims, that one might help them in their need with it.
Though he said that, he did not do so out of goodness, nor did poverty move him to any pity.
He was a grievous thief and the keeper of his purse; he wanted to skim off something there, and for that reason he began such talk.
"Let her," said the Master, "do the work she has begun, so that she may carry it out for me now; she will not be able to once I am buried.
You always have plenty of poor people with you; but me, truly, you do not have here forever."
III. WHEN THE PEOPLE HEARD THAT JESUS HAD COME.
Then the people heard that the Lord Christ had come there, and a great multitude came there to meet him,
Not meaning it for the Lord alone; rather, on that journey they also wanted to see Lazarus;
Because the Lord's word had led him back from death, the people came truly [?] to look on the marvel;
So that they might also see this: that the man who had already been dead was, by a great wonder in himself, living a second time.
The chief priests commanded with their words that no one should mention it before he had been killed;
For many people there truly believed because of him, because of these deeds of God's own goodness.
Why did they not consider that, even if they did it, he could without any doubt command him to rise up again,
and bring him back to life again with the same power by which he had earlier taken him from death and commanded him to come out of the grave!
Then in the morning all the people who had come to the Passover (there was a great crowd of them!) went out there to meet him.
The whole crowd of the country people went out there to meet him when the people learned that he was to come there.
They carried palm branches in their hands, spread out widely before him, and also twigs of olive trees.
By this the people meant that he had won victory over death, and that from then on he gave people the joy of peace for ever.
IV. WHEN HE HAD DRAWN NEAR TO JERUSALEM.
Then he wished to begin making his way to Jerusalem, so that he might bring it about that he would die there for us.
That was five days before he suffered the pain, before it came to the point that they seized him.
Then he began to give orders, since he wished to ride there, that they should hurry and fetch him a donkey.
He ordered two of his disciples (I tell you this) to set out and go to the village.
"There you will find a she-donkey tied up. Untie her there, and bring the foal too at once.
If anyone starts to refuse to let you have it, tell him truthfully of the need; then he will let it be at once."
Then they went on their way and found everything as he had said. They saw to it and brought the foal.
Then they took their garments and laid them on it in a fitting way, gently and pleasantly, so that he could sit on top.
Then the great crowd streamed toward him there. They called him king and covered the road for him.
They did this out of necessity, so that the beast would not stagger or stumble when he began the journey;
and truly they also did it in lordly honor, for his glory. He was very dear to them!
No one in all the world has ever thought that any king travelled with such splendor,
or that the deeds of people ever honored any king so beautifully, truly serving him with such a procession.
These same people (that is true) spread their garments there, so that they made the road soft with clothing.
They quickly covered the road for him there, very beautifully; the men hurried eagerly to do it with their garments.
They strewed the road there especially for him, which was a wonder; a strange thing: they spread out their cloaks.
Whoever lacked one at once broke off branches, so that he made the road straight and smooth with them.
They saw to it and broke off branches from the trees there, so that they might gladly strew the road for him.
Many men went there ahead of the king, and a host, also full of eloquent speech, followed behind.
He rode in the middle, as was fitting and as it then fell out on that journey, with honour, as he wished and as a king himself should.
Then they raised a lofty song, very beautiful, fitting for him and very eloquent:
"You rule many people, son of King David; you are also clearly king of the people of this land!
May he have salvation forever, and blessings shared by all, and benefit in glory over all his kingdom!
May he be greatly blessed, for he came in the name of God; Christ the good himself is a king dear to us!
Hail to you also in the highest, with the same blessing; extend your kingdom also into the high kingdom of heaven,
so that you keep us safe here and also rule over the angels, and shine forth there in power over paradise itself!"
Those same good people, all of one mind, sang the delight of this song with a single voice.
The people in front sang it eagerly over and over, and the host behind answered with the same words in turn.
They came with a throng in that same procession, and with that force went straight into the city.
All who were inside were alarmed; it stirred the hearts, I think, of the townspeople themselves.
"Who is this man," they said, "who presses on us here so boldly, crowds us here like this with a host, and pushes us out of the city?"
The people at once gave answer: "This is truly the prophet! The Saviour from Nazareth, who came from there into this land!"
He went into the house of God and drove them all out of it; he forcefully scattered all their wickedness.
By day he taught them and preached in person; by night he always stayed on the Mount of Olives.
It was an unfitting and terrible thing that they begrudged him in their hearts and refused him lodging.
The chief men saw this and were greatly alarmed by it, and they also talked a great deal about these deeds:
"Our cause," they said, "is nothing; it does not prosper any further at all. It can never prosper in the face of this same man.
If this is allowed, this whole world will go after him in a single moment!"
V. Spiritually (Spiritaliter).
Here we must explain the spiritual meanings of the journey and the going and the people's song:
what the beast means, what the garments signify here, and the branches that they scattered and laid on the road.
We ourselves are that beast. See it for yourself in your own case: because of our dullness we are necessarily so!
He also told how each of them made a point of adorning his garments, and demanded of the people that they bow to them without fail.
Then he also warned his own disciples separately and in earnest that they should avoid this and not be like that.
He said that they should seek high rank through humility; any other way would not be fitting, nor could it come about.
He held back nothing of this then, and told them of many woes. They had to hear it, as Matthew relates.
He told them some seven woes. Even one is too much, alas! But they had in truth earned them many times over in this way!
And right away he also told them why this had to happen to them: because they all neglected what the book commanded, though they told others to do it.
They also did whatever they wished, everything they ought not to do, against God's law. Therefore he told them of the woes.
There he also rebuked them about his prophets: how they had killed them and tortured them all.
He also told the men how he had always wished to love that very same people, if only they had not resisted it.
7. On the Lord's teaching to his disciples on the mount.
Then the Lord went away from there, and his followers went with him. They showed him the buildings of the house [the Temple].
He said: "Truly I tell you, these stones will yet come to this: they will lie here so worthless, all scattered."
After that walk he sat on the Mount of Olives. They asked him privately, because they wondered greatly about it:
"Tell us then, master, how the time will run its course: the sign of how you will come, and how the world will also come to an end."
"Take heed of these things," he said, "and be very watchful, so that the many liars do not harm you by setting snares for you.
Grievous things will arise over this circle of the world: hunger and sickness, and wretched flight."
Then in his goodness he told them of the hardships that they would have to suffer for his name;
and of the hatred of many men that would be laid upon them, and very fierce envy, as far as these could carry it;
and how people would seize his dear followers, drag them before governors, and bring them bound before kings.
Then he gave them comfort for all their deaths. He said that it would be for no other reason than hatred of him alone.
"Do not be anxious before the people when you stand there in distress. Do not be afraid about what you will answer them.
I will fully provide you with wise words and righteous speech. You are my followers."
I myself will be there for that purpose, and there I will also speak out of you. Be watchful in heart, good, and very steadfast in mind!"
He also told them truly about the last day, and he spoke to them carefully of the time of the Antichrist.
"The affliction the world will suffer then, alas! I will certainly not hide it from you: it will be unlike any other time!
They will then be in woes and grievous hardships, such that no such disaster ever happened before, nor shall one ever happen again.
The Lord will soon shorten it by his grace for the sake of his beloved ones, for the sake of those [?] of God.
The moon and the sun will be joyless in darkness, and the stars will fall to earth from very far away.
Then all that is here on earth will weep over that destruction; all this human race will weep over that same misery!
Then they will see the Son of Man himself coming down here from the clouds with power, to the judgment.
His angels too, in truth: they will blow their horns there, and every one of them will blow very mightily,
so that they may diligently gather all his beloved ones there, and these will come to him there, wherever in the world they may be!
As for what any of you now says about this last time: there is no one who can make it known except my Father alone.
Nor does any man in the world know when it will happen, when God wills that the whole world should fall to ruin.
Yet before it there will certainly be a great calm, as there once was among the people in the days of old Noah.
As the water overtook them there as soon as he had gone into the ark, so suddenly will the Son of Man himself come here.
Therefore always be careful and very watchful, for it is hidden from all of you when the Lord will come!
If the man who is at home in his stronghold knew all the outrage, and how the thief would come,
he would have to keep watch at that time, drive the thief out of there, and not let his house be broken into.
So he keeps watch all night, even though it is beyond his strength, so that he may save what is his and defend it against enemies.
Do as he does, for you do not know the time. Always be watchful, as I have commanded, so that you escape the distress!"
He then told his beloved ones a parable about the ten maidens, one that was apt and fitting for this:
how the five who were unprepared fared, who were not properly watchful, and so failed there;
and how well it went there for those who were always watchful here, who ruled their hearts here and kept them pure.
He also told another parable, so that they would be on guard all the more: how a rich man went into another kingdom;
how, as he had planned beforehand, he divided his treasure among his servants to be worked with carefully.
"He commanded them to look after it and to earn fitting profit with it until he came back.
The two worked hard at it and increased it well; the third was not at all eager, because he was cowardly.
He was rightly condemned to the place where he is tormented, and truly rightly so, because he was not watchful.
The other two of his servants he made very glad, and greatly rejoiced their hearts, as a good lord does;
Then he set them handsomely over his cities and made them very rich, so that they were pleased with the service.
Therefore be always watchful, all your life here; day and night always think on what is right,
so that you always hasten toward it, avoid the peril, and always hurry to escape the terror,
so that you may be found worthy as soon as my judgment comes, and stand upright in my sight!"
By day he taught all the people aloud and openly; they came to him eagerly and promptly, at the proper time.
Then at night he went with the disciples to the Mount of Olives; he stayed there overnight, as was mentioned here before.
VIII. THE FEAST DAY OF UNLEAVENED BREAD WAS DRAWING NEAR.
The high festival, which we told of here before and called Easter, was drawing near, as it had to.
The priests began to plot with cunning words; they made an agreement on how they might seize him.
They gave very strict orders, in their own words, that wherever in the land he went, he should be captured;
that whoever sought him out should take up arms against him and slay him before he could ever escape;
that wherever he was, he should be under ban; they were to think of nothing else, but all were to persecute him.
They took plenty of counsel about how he might be slain; but inwardly they feared the multitude of the people.
They said they would not do it during the high festival, so that the people themselves would not rise up in fighting over it.
"We must take care," they said, "that they do not snatch him away from us; therefore it must be done at another time." Judas
also arranged it and plotted it with them: he wanted to win himself a name [?], as the devil enticed him.
He was in counsel with them that he himself would betray him and go with their messengers to the place where they would capture him.
"I will arrange it," he said, "truly, so that there will be no more men there except exactly his usual company of disciples."
At once they promised him a great treasure for it, in return for his doing this and handing him over so intimately.
He promised it firmly and did not abandon it; he set his mind on it and carried it all out accordingly.
From then on they watched for the opportunity; and he too was on the lookout for a time when the people would not be there.
IX. THEN CAME THE DAY OF UNLEAVENED BREAD, ON WHICH THE PASSOVER HAD TO BE KILLED.
The good time came when the offering was to be made, and when people were to sit down to eat the lamb at night.
Then he at once sent Peter, and John with him as well, truly, and commanded them to hurry and prepare the Passover for them.
They began to answer: "Where can we turn, that we may go there for this and begin such a thing?
We have no house at all, and that is the main thing, as you know, and no dwelling of any kind that we could make ready properly."
"That will not be lacking," he said to them. "Go into the city. A man is making a place free for us; he lends us his upper room."
Both of them hurried, and they found everything just as he had said. The man had seen to it and lent them the room ready.
It was ready and finely furnished with covered seats, and as clean as could be, as was fitting for such guests.
They hurried at once to do his service there and always made it their earnest concern; they were glad to see to things as he had commanded.
When they had prepared everything and he sat down to the meal, he told them to sit down and all eat together with him.
Happy that company, that table fellowship, which then enjoyed the sweetness of his meal! Well might they be glad of it!
Never was any meal shared with such companions, and never was a table so surrounded on every side, except, again, with these same people.
There sat the eternal sun, a great joy, and not far from him were eleven morning stars:
truly the Lord himself (what more should I tell you about it?), and those who were travelling with him through hardship.
After God they are the foremost princes among men, and in the kingdom of heaven too, that is true; they earned that by their service there.
By their service they earned great and manifold benefit: the same honour I have just told you of, and eternal friendship.
Now their fellowship is for us, whenever need comes, a strong and very manifold intercession with God.
We cannot tell their praise in full, even if we want to; so let us now go on joyfully with the story.
X. WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED [TO EAT] THIS PASSOVER.
Then the Lord began to speak to those twelve followers who sat around him there and ate with him.
"I have longed for this meal so that I might eat it with you before I suffer punishment and die for you.
Truly, I will not drink any more of the fruit of the vine, of that growth, from now on; believe me in this,
until, as I intend, I drink it new again together with you, to your delight, in my Father's kingdom."
Then he himself took the bread, blessed it and gave it to them, and told them to eat it, just as they sat there.
"Without any doubt," he said, "you are eating my body. I tell this to all of you; you may be certain of it.
Now take the cup as well and share the drink among you. In it you drink my blood, which does you good for ever.
It heals people's wounds and the sins of many; it is a thing of many powers and redeems this world."
XI. BEFORE THE FEAST DAY OF THE PASSOVER, JESUS, KNOWING THAT [HIS HOUR] HAD COME.
When they had eaten there and were still sitting at the table, the devil spied out Judas himself there.
He did as he always does: he turned it over hard in his mind, how that night he could arrange to betray the Lord.
Christ loved his own to the end of his life, those he had taken to himself to teach when he first began to preach.
He knew that his Father had given everything, as far as heaven reaches around, into his hand and into his power.
He himself also knew, as was fitting, that he had come to us from God, and that he must go back to him again, as he wished.
Then in the evening he rose from the meal and laid aside his garments, and he performed the mandatum for them.
There he took a linen cloth and girded himself with it, truly. After that he took a basin and poured water into it.
Then he began at their feet and told them to sit still. His precious hands washed them all the way through.
The Lord himself did this, and he also wiped them with the cloth. His high goodness taught them humility.
When he first began it, he came straight to Peter, who shrank back very much from such deeds.
"Lord," he said, "is it fitting that you should now wash me? I am your own servant, and you are my lord."
"Because of your lordship it does not sit well with me that your hand should ever touch my feet for this purpose."
He answered him with gentle mildness, went on with the work there, and spoke to him sweetly:
"What I mean by this now is quite unknown to you, but at some time you will come to know it."
"I refuse it from now on," he said. "It can never be, it must never come to this, that I should allow you to do me this service."
"If I do not wash them for you," he said, "you will have no part at all with me, and in that sense no fellowship at all!"
"Lord," he said, "wash all of me, head and feet, if it must be so. Being near you is sweet to me.
May it never happen that I go without you, nor, my dear Lord, that I should ever be without you!"
Then Christ the Lord said to him: "A man who has been washed needs to wash no more than to clean his feet, truly."
When the Lord had done this, he sat down with them again and quickly showed them what he meant by it.
He first took up his garments, and then at once he explained the deeds to them and the goodness of that work, though Judas did not hear it.
"Understand this deed," he said, "for it concerns you. This example shows you that you must not be arrogant.
You always call me Lord and Master, and you speak rightly in this, for so I am. That is true.
Now since I, who rule you, endure such things toward those I rule, and humble myself this way, in such a manner, before my own:
how much more fitting is it for you, since you are equals among yourselves, that each should gladly wash the other's feet,
and show humility among yourselves with kindness, and from now on show it to people with great love?"
XII. Jesus was troubled in spirit and spoke to them of his betrayal.
When he had shown them this there, he at once became sorrowful; he who is the joy of all good was troubled in his spirit.
His goodness grieved for those wretched people; nor was there any delay then in this account to the company of the disciples [?].
"I tell you," he said aloud, "you were all dear to me; I counted you, the twelve, and chose you out for myself
from the multitude of the world; you were my retinue, so that I also made all my counsel known to you;
and so it came to this, that you show me loyalty; for that reason I raised you up above all others, so that you would not do me such wrong.
Yet one of you has it in mind to do me violence tonight and to give me into the hands of my enemies."
They looked at one another; there was anguish in their hearts; in their minds they were sorely shaken by the Lord's words.
Those terrible deeds weighed grievously on their minds, and they urgently asked about whom he said such a thing:
all around among themselves, from whom such a thing could come, such deeds and such an assault!
Then they all spoke, each for himself: "Surely it is not I, Lord? Surely my heart is not moved to it, nor does it carry such evil!"
Though they knew themselves to be pure, all except the one, they trusted his words more strongly.
Then Judas, who had plotted it and brewed up all this harm, spoke with scorn: "Master, surely it is not I?"
"You say it," he said at once; "yet I tell you in all truth: that man will suffer forever very many kinds of pain;
he will suffer such mighty woe in eternity that it would have been better for him if he had never been born a man."
Peter asked John to find out who the man was, to ask him who was plotting such evil.
(He signalled this to him plainly; he was seated nearest; truly they held the master in great honour;
for Peter sat there and kept silent, as I have now said; the foremost of the friends did not dare to speak aloud!)
Then he asked about the deeds and the assault, and begged him to tell them, to rescue them all from their worry.
"It is he, without doubt," he said, "to whom I offer this bread." Then he took a morsel there and offered it at once to Judas.
After that food Satan clung to him, and the devil himself at once ruled over him entirely.
When he had come to the point of swallowing the morsel there, the devil's companion at once went quietly out.
Then the Lord at once spoke to him (not that he truly commanded it!): "What you carry in your mind, do it quickly."
There was no one there who understood what he meant by this, nor did anyone in any way recognize the intent.
Some took it to mean, because he was the treasurer, that with those words he was telling him to give something to poor people,
Or they thought he was concerned with what good things they should have at Easter, and that he should provide for them for the feast day.
As soon as he went out, dark night took him in; from that light the man was cut off forever.
He went in haste to the leaders of the people and eagerly set up the attack on Christ.
Then the eternal King began to rejoice quietly, although he was to die the next day for the sake of his kingdom.
For this speech he had no one but eleven retainers; I can say it plainly: the twelfth had deserted.
The power of the battle did not lie in the size of the army; it rested entirely on his own strength alone.
He came into this land like a giant, a mighty giant; in single combat he struck down the one who was harming his kingdom,
seized the prince of this world by force and laid him in bonds, so that he could not harm us any longer!
XIII. He said that Peter would deny him.
The Lord took up his discourse after Judas had gone out from there; that night he told them many things.
"Truly," he said, "know now, my little children, that I am with you only a little while longer,
then you will seek me fervently and very eagerly; but your haste will not help you at that time.
I leave you, I tell you this, an entirely new commandment: that you love one another, as I showed you by my example,
so that everyone, and the whole world as well, may recognize by this love that you have me as your master."
He also spoke separately to Peter, his retainer, who was there, and spoke words to him that went deep into his heart:
"Simon, above all, pay attention to what I am about to tell you, and think hard about it; do not let your mind be idle:
The Adversary himself has strongly desired you, so that he might sift your hearts the way grain is sifted in a sieve.
It was very terrible; so I myself prayed for you, that you would not waver in faith and that you would strengthen your heart.
And as soon as you have turned back, be a comfort in sorrow to your brothers, so that they may escape harm."
He spoke boldly and very valiantly, and said he would always stand firm with him in that time of need:
"With you I am ready, Lord, in heart and in strength, to go into prison and even to taste death;
even if they all desert you, I will never want to do this, but I will keep faith [?] above all things, as one should with a master!
Do not let it enter your thoughts that I would ever turn away from you, my dear Lord; I assure you of this!"
Then Christ answered the firmness, the boldness of his heart and his good courage, saying it would turn out otherwise:
"Peter, I tell you this: the struggle is so severe that this very night you will firmly deny these words;
There are truly many dwellings there (remember these words!) and many mansions.
If it were truly otherwise, I would have told you so at once; it would never be fitting for me to hide it from you.
I am going now to prepare a lordly place for you there, where you will dwell with me forever. Do not doubt this.
Where I am present, may you always be nearest. Since you know where I am going, know the ways as well."
Then Thomas, who was one of the eleven, spoke to him: "We do not know the way, nor do we know where you are going.
Show us all of it: where you mean to go." He told him the truth at once and spoke to him truly in this way:
"I am the way of what is right and of everything rational. I am also life and truth, so you will not go astray there.
It is true that there is no man who comes to the Father, however hard anyone may press for it, unless I lead him.
If you knew me, you would understand for yourselves, and without long delay, what my Father is like."
Then Philip, one of them, spoke. He was in doubt about this very thing and held the mistaken belief that the Father was greater:
"Lord, let us see the Father alone (may your words often be remembered [?]), and then we will have all we need."
Then the Lord removed that same foolish notion. Because Philip had understood it wrongly, the Lord turned his mind another way.
"I have been here with you in the world for so long, and still you do not draw near to me in your minds and do not yet recognize me?
Whoever wants to see the Father should look closely at me. I am not hiding this from you.
In me he sees the Father's nobility and his very image. Let him look at me and be sure: my Father is just like this!"
Above all, he also told them there how the Holy Spirit would increase their wisdom through his own teaching,
so that no one would be without knowledge of every benefit, all that is true and good, as the Spirit of God himself does.
He also told them truthfully beforehand about the hostility of worldly people and the many hardships that were then waiting for them.
He taught them in words how they should endure this, and said that after this suffering it would turn to joy for them.
"You have no need to worry about this," he said. "I leave peace with you, and joy enough. Do not worry at all about that!
I will not leave you orphans. I will come back to you and comfort you soon with complete joy.
It is no wonder: you are truly my special friends, my beloved ones. That is why I chose you at once.
This is my commandment to you: love one another, and let each of you keep this in mind and never turn away from love."
Then the Lord told them this, because he himself had chosen them. That night he urged them to much righteousness.
There he promised them much comfort out of his own goodness, as soon as he would rise again.
He said that after that time they would never lack him, and that it would ever after be so for them that they would live in joy.
When he taught them in that night, as you can read there, he then himself drew them fully into his will.
He then looked up to heaven and spoke praise of God himself; then he commended the disciples to his Father's blessing,
so that he would protect them for him until he rose from death, before he would then send them out and turn them to his service.
XVI. After this he went out across the brook Kidron.
After these words, after these things, he went into a garden across a brook.
They too set out for it and went together with him, full of steadfast spirit, his companions in distress.
Consider it all from every side; that was now a pitiful thing: he who saved the whole world then had no more of it with him.
He made all that is made, and gives them all their sustenance, yet now, alas, he had no larger following!
Judas himself knew that the Lord was accustomed to this, that he was often wont to go in there with them.
At once he quickly took to himself the men of that same commander, a very large troop, and led them there.
And the priests duly lent many servants, and also enough of the Pharisees for that same fight.
They began to equip themselves with their lanterns, with many torches and with weapons at the ready.
Truly, an unbeaten army went out against him there, a great multitude of men (and they were only twelve!),
with spears and with swords; they pledged with words that they would seize him, so that he would by no means get away.
Some of the comrades also carried great staves, and clubs in their hands too, so that they might carry the deed through.
Then Judas, who was their guide, and truly also the leader of that wretched expedition, spoke to them:
"So that you do not make a mistake (I don't think you would recognize him), watch the one I kiss, then you will be certain of it at once;
he is the one, I tell you truly; seize him immediately, in an instant [?], so that he does not slip away from you!"
(Or else he had quickly heard from those who saw it how he had changed his appearance and was transfigured on the mountain;
so he thought that in that danger he would make himself look different, so that no one would recognize him, and for that reason he said this;
he also thought that his power, which is written down for us, was a sorcerer's trick, with which he would defend himself against them and save himself from them.)
Christ went forward, as was fitting, and came toward them; at once he quickly spoke to them: "Whom are you looking for?" he said.
They told him at once and named him himself, but they did not do so because they recognized him.
Then he said to them at once: "I am he myself, that is true; you do not seek me for any good, yet I am the one you are looking for."
As soon as they heard it, they staggered at once; they went backwards and all fell down.
He questioned them again when they had recovered; he asked them again at once whom they were looking for there.
They gave the same thing in words as their answer; they told him the same thing that they had said here before.
"Indeed I tell you," he said to them, "that I am the very man for whom you have truly undertaken this journey."
Judas, who had brought them, then came near to the Lord, so that he might carry out everything he had promised here before.
"Hail, master!" he said, and kissed him at once. Out of his mildness, the Lord received him patiently.
Those who had come there with him then recognized the sign, and each of them remembered what he had told them before.
Then they stood there ready and seized him at once; they laid their hands on the Lord to bind him.
XVII. How Peter cut off the ear of the priest's servant.
Peter was present, and he quickly drew his sword. He hardened his heart and at once wounded a man.
I know that he intended this too and aimed at the head, so that he might settle the matter and rescue his master.
The other man (I think) meant to dodge, but even so Peter truly struck off his right ear.
There is no one who would defend his lord like this against an army, who would act so boldly when he was unarmed and in danger;
who would run so far forward into the fight without shield or spear, so close into the crowd of his enemies!
He certainly defended him very fiercely, until the Lord himself, out of necessity, forbade him to fight.
As a man ought to defend himself and save his lord, so he kept pressing hard on Christ's enemies,
until the Lord himself spoke to him: "I could obtain an army, a host of angels, if I wished to do it.
Heavenly warriors, many thousands of them, would quickly come here and stand present,
so that they would speak for me here, avenge me at once, and rescue me with swords from these men's hands.
Understand these words for yourself and put the sword back. It is fitting that I should will this and fulfill the scripture."
There was no delay: as soon as he touched the man's ear, he made it whole again. Yet they did not believe because of it!
The people then took out their anger, as they had planned to do long before. They bound him as soon as they found him.
The disciples saw this and quickly fled from him. Shamefully, they left the master there alone!
They saw an unfitting and terrible thing: their Lord being bound. They did not dare to turn back to him.
There was a man there named Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, I believe. They led the Lord Christ himself to him first.
XVIII. Of the denial of Peter.
Peter then followed him at a distance, far behind, so that he could see what was done to him.
In his grief he wanted to see the end: how they would carry it through, and what they intended for him.
When he came to a door (I think he went too far forward), the woman who kept the door spoke sharply to him there:
"I think you are truly one of this man's servants, one of his followers, as I believe you will now find out."
Then he quickly answered her in front of the crowd. He denied all of it and said he knew nothing of the man.
There was a fire there, because it was very cold. Peter stood there among them and warmed himself there with them.
At once some of them said: "What are you doing here, man? You are truly one of this man's company!"
Then he swore very readily and said he was not one of those men. He confirmed with an oath that he did not know the man.
"I tell you," he said, "in truth: I am not one of that company. I do not take that vow [?], and I know nothing of such things either!"
Then his companions also made him greatly afraid. They said (some of them insistently) that they recognized him.
A kinsman of the very man whose ear he had struck off brought it up there. He said he had seen him in the garden in that sudden rush:
"I tell you truly, you did that very injury there, for I stood there in the garden watching you.
You started the fight there and caused plenty of trouble. You attacked us fiercely. You will not get away from this!"
"You need not deny it," they said. "Your speech will give you away. Your words now truly betray you!"
Then he began to swear (he wanted to save himself), and he told them firmly that he did not know the man.
He swore to them again and again, insistently, that he did not know him at all and had never had any dealings with him!
Then it was the time when the cock crowed, so that the bird announced the coming of that same day.
As soon as it first crowed, Peter at once came to himself. The Lord's own words brought his mind back home.
Then he earnestly remembered that same moment, and that everything the Lord had told him had now come true for him here.
Then he began to weep and to cry out to the Lord, because the pain of weeping so stirred his heart.
For the Lord truly looked over at him at once, and began to look at him with gracious eyes.
XIX. The words of the high priest to Jesus, and of the false witnesses.
Meanwhile the Lord truly stood there before the high priest, so that the eternal Wisdom had to give an account there.
He stood there under force among enemies, in the bonds of their ropes. He was alone, without his friends.
also sitting gloriously and very splendidly, after this speech, at God's own right hand!"
The high priest at once burned with hot anger, and he tore his garment and made his mind known,
so that the people would know that he was very angry about it, and so that they too would become enraged and be angry along with him.
I tell you this without dispute about this same matter; understand it in your mind: he did not do it out of goodness.
He did it to give the men a [?] ("frístfrangon"; perhaps a prompt or pretext), so that, as I explain to you, they could fall upon him.
"You have heard," he said, "the outrage, how he spoke against God; truly we now need no more witnesses.
What he himself now says here, you have heard; let everyone now consider what he thinks of this!"
The people then at once agreed and condemned him to death; they said that he deserved it and was very guilty.
Then on top of that they also spat in his face, and they did not hold back, alas, from striking him on the neck!
They blindfolded him (they made a game of it) and kept asking him who it was that struck him.
He endured that from them in those hours for our sins, all this insolence, because of our wickedness!
XX. They led him to Caiaphas, where Pilate also was.
Then the people led him to where the authorities were; the high priest Caiaphas was there, and truly the governor as well.
The governor himself went out there to meet them in front of the palace; they were not allowed to go so far as to the heathen man,
so that at that time they would not become defiled, but could feast in purity and celebrate the Passover.
Yet they did not fear this at all (they were plotting murder!), nor did they hesitate to slay Christ!
The governor spoke to them as he went out to meet them: "What accusation, then, do you bring against this man?"
The hardness of their evil will gave him an answer: "If he," they said, "had meant well, he would not have come to this;
if he had not gone about among the people with great misdeeds, we would not have thought of bringing him to you."
Then with many words they began to accuse him of very grave matters and very many sins.
They said that he claimed to be called the Son of God, and also made it known that he was their king;
that he also says with certainty that he himself is the Christ, goes so far in this boldness, and takes the name for himself.
They said that he did not want the people to pay tribute any longer in honour of the emperor;
and that he had stirred up all the people to strife, to great rebellion: "lest he be let go!
He never left off until he had truly and gravely troubled this whole land with his own teaching;
there is no limit to it and no turning back, the way he leads the land astray, the way he throws it all into confusion and disturbs this world!
He began such things at the far end of this realm, and from there he went through the whole land, until he was seized here just now!"
"Take him yourselves," he said; "why did you bring him to me for this? Judge him there as your law teaches.
If you all find out there how far he seeks what is right, you carry out all of it yourselves; it is known to you, not to me!"
That, they said, was not fitting for them, nor could it be, because their books warned them against killing a man.
By this the people signified what the Lord had said before: that he was to end his life at the hands of heathens.
Yet I tell you truly: they were his killers; they brought him to death with the sharpness of their tongues!
XXI. Pilate's address to Christ in the praetorium.
Then Pilate went back with him into the upper hall and spoke with him at length; he was troubled about these matters.
First he asked about what he feared most: "Tell me now at once," he said, "whether you are their king.
Were you consecrated to it, as the people accuse you? Did you set out with that intention, to seize the kingdom like this?"
Then the Lord said: "Tell me, do you say this of yourself, or did others tell it to you and report it to you about me?"
Pilate wanted to rid him of that idea at once, so that he would not think Pilate had thought it up himself.
"People know of themselves," he said, "that I am not a Jew; your own nation has handed you over to me in this plight.
The people who handed you over to me laid the charge against you; those same people all told me of this boldness of yours.
But if it is true that you are not their king, why is it that they seized you and handed you over to me bound like this?"
"I tell you this," he said: "my kingdom is not from here; it is not, as I explain to you, of the things of this world.
If it were from here, my thanes would strive with their courage, so that my enemy would not overpower me like this
and would not handle me like this in this plight; they would act with valour to rescue me from them.
But I give you the reason: my kingdom is not from here, so that I would defend myself now with an army of my own."
Then Pilate spoke again, because the matter weighed heavily on him; again he asked urgently about his lordship:
"Wherever your kingdom and your glory may be, are you nevertheless truly a king, as I hear?"
"You say," he said, "that I am a king; for this I came here into the world, and for this I was also born, that I should suffer such things among you,
that I should at once bear witness to the truth, and that I should also spread true things throughout this world!
Whoever is of the truth always hears me at once; he hears with love the voice of my very self."
"Tell me," he said bitterly, "what you mean by this truth; make me certain of it, what this truth is!"
XXII. How Pilate wanted to release Christ in place of Barabbas.
When he had said that, he went away (I know he was not worthy to hear what the Lord would say about it;
I also believe he hurried off because he was thinking of the robber: he meant to arrange an exchange so that he could rescue Christ himself).
Then he spoke to the people, hoping they would decide otherwise. "I find," he said, "this man guilty of no crime at all,
nor do I know of any reason why he should forfeit his life, though I questioned him closely about his own deeds.
Indeed, you have a custom at this time that I release one prisoner to you from punishment;
now consider what you want and which of the two you choose: whether you take Barabbas for yourselves, or now choose Christ for yourselves!"
But that robber was, in his view, a grave criminal; he lay there in bonds as punishment for his crimes.
The whole crowd of the people shouted back against him; they said it would truly be dear and sweet to them to have Barabbas released to them!
Then he had him bound, as he wished, and he himself had him scourged, the Lord himself. What was the wretched man thinking!
Then the governor's soldiers took him away from there; to mock him, they wove thorns together there,
and they set that ring of thorns on his head, eager to mock him: a crown of thorns!
As part of this they took royal garments of deep red purple and dressed him in them;
then they fell on their knees, mocking him all the while; through such deeds they heaped great scorn on him!
"Hail, Christ!" they said. "You are king of this people; you are dressed for the part, too, and very kingly!"
They said such things to mock him; they kept eagerly thinking of ways to humiliate him.
At the same time they struck his holy cheeks, and they beat him about the ears with hard blows.
As I said before, he endured such indignity for our sake, in blows and in words, because of our grievous sins!
XXIII. Pilate led Jesus out to the people after he had been mocked.
After these deeds Pilate went out to the people; he wanted to calm their wicked will.
"I am bringing him out here to you," he said, "so that from this you may see that I find no wrongdoing in him at all."
Then Christ went out in that procession in a red garment, crowned with thorns and scourged and mocked in this way;
He was forced to wear purple clothing then, and a crown of thorns: that was done to him in mockery.
"Behold," he said, "now the man: he has been condemned to the utmost! You see his disgrace; what more do you want?
He has been harshly reviled, with mocking words as well, and has also been punished very severely for his misdeeds;
He has been scourged," he said, "and set about with thorns as well; now that such things are done to him, let your anger cool!"
When they saw him, they all cried out at once (their hearts burned against him, as enemies' hearts often do),
Then they demanded again and again that he be put to death, and cried out very fiercely: "Crucify him, crucify!"
"Take him yourselves," he said, "and crucify him among you; I cannot find in him that he is so very guilty."
The high priests answered him harshly, out of their old hatred; they could not restrain themselves:
"He must die, as our law shows, and die by his own words at the hands of these men;
For he proclaimed here that he himself is the Son of God, and he truly spread such reports everywhere.
The law teaches that whoever presumptuously claims such a thing for himself is to be hanged on a cross."
Pilate was then greatly afraid at these words; he left them and went with Christ into the praetorium.
"Tell me now at once," he said, "what land you are from, and of what birth, that you have ever come to this."
He stood, kept silent and quietly held his peace; in his patience he gave him no answer.
"Will you not speak to me?" he said. "Do you not know what I am telling you: that your end lies in my own hand;
And that I also have power over everything that concerns you, over life and death today, whichever of the two I command?"
Then the eternal emperor, the heavenly king, gently answered the governor there, truly:
"I tell you, and I do not hide it from you: you would have no power over me if it had not been granted to you from heaven;
Therefore the one who gave me into your hands bears the greater sin, as does the one who brought matters to the point that I am treated like this here."
XXIV. Pilate wished to release Jesus, and how he handed him over to them.
Pilate was then eager to release him: he wanted not to listen to them, and to take him out of that danger.
When they saw this, they raised their voices; the whole crowd of people shouted fiercely against him:
"We accuse you of disloyalty, a grave offense, because you are letting the emperor's enemy go free and unharmed like this.
He has stirred up this whole land; that is why we handed him over to you. He has incited the people to rebellion, and now you are letting him go like this?"
"A man who dares to call himself king truly sets himself against the emperor straightaway!"
Then Pilate came out to them, bringing Christ himself with him. "What more can I say?" he said. "Here is your king!"
The crowd of people shouted back loudly; they screamed at once when they saw him:
Then a great multitude of the people came out to meet him, and they all followed him to the fall of his own death.
The women of the people of the land then wept loudly, for they too lamented what, alas, they held against him;
They wept loudly then and cried out very bitterly; the wretched grief there touched them in their hearts.
They beat their breasts in their anguish and kept lamenting in their distress over the miserable deeds;
They began to ask why they should torment the one who always meant good for them and healed the whole land!
"Whoever touches him carries good away from him; whoever ventures to come to him goes away from him glad.
He healed lepers as soon as he willed it, all by his powers; what do they blame him for, the Lord!
Blind men seeing and the crippled walking; yes, and dead men too, indeed, came alive at his word;
Yes, it is said in truth that they rose up from the bier, that they began their life again and rose out of the graves!
There is nothing good in the world that he did not do here among us; now shall they destroy him, sinless as he is, so senselessly?
Why do they now crush him like this and put out the good that was in him? If we must now do without him, may God have pity on it!
In him there was great good of many kinds, always plenty of every good thing, for any man who asked for it!"
They wept a long time, [their weeping] reaching up to heaven [?]; the Lord himself looked at them then and spoke to them like this:
"Listen here, women," he said, "do not weep for my life, do not lament my death! I am not to escape it.
Do not lament my suffering; something else will come upon you, more [than this]. Weep for yourselves; you will have great need to.
Weep also, as I tell you, for all your children, because of such distress as the world has never seen before!
For the time is yet to come when every woman will say of another: Happy is she alive who never had children;
Truly blessed is she who is without a child, who never brought one forth from her womb and never nursed one at her breasts!
The times of misery are yet to come upon you, such pitiful conditions of wretchedness;
Such things will yet come home to you that you will waste away to the bone, and such pain will touch soul and heart,
That in your sorrows you will call out to these mountains and ask them (this I tell you) to fall on you;
And you will also ask the hills to cover you from above and shield you in your distress from such times!
Then you will begin to cry out, and to sleep inside the earth, and you will waste away terribly because of such deeds.
Now that they bring things to this, destroying the green tree like this, burning it here like this with the fire of the cross:
What do you think will then become of the useless wood, when they begin to harm the dry tree?"
I know that they also wanted this: they counted him among sinners, and by that was also signified what the old scripture shows us.
They nailed him to the cross, as they were accustomed to do, by the feet and by the hands, with very hard bonds.
Truly, they raised up there the heavenly king, the emperor with the powers, our Lord himself.
He was there in power, though he suffered such things; he endured it for our sake, as I told here before.
With that precious body he redeemed the kingdom of the world, and all mankind as well, through the fall of his death.
For our sake he shed his blood here, which no other will ever do: he made it firm here, so that we would never lack good.
They did as I told: he was nailed to the cross as firmly as they could, and they raised him up there;
Then his own hands showed the ends of the world, the head the heavenly [?], and the feet this ground of the earth.
Truly, all of that was his, the whole circuit in four directions, above and below; how blessed are his thanes!
Pilate raised in writing words of his own over his head (which all the world believes):
"The true Savior, the famous one of Nazareth; he is plainly king of the Jewish people."
Then the priests said: "Do not write it in those words; write that he said it and declared such a thing himself."
Then he gave answer and said it would not be otherwise: "What I wrote, truly, stands written for him there!"
XXVIII. Of the division of the spoils and the lot cast for the tunic.
They took the spoils (believe the books on this), then agreed together on it, and divided it into four;
For there were four of them who were in that deed, so that they shared it thus and divided it equally.
Then in that division the tunic was left over; it was of very rare workmanship:
There was nothing sewn or patched on it; it was woven skilfully and beautifully throughout.
Then the companions advised that they cast their lots, so that it would be fitting which of them should take it.
"Let us not," they said, "alas, damage the work; the lot shall decide everything for us, whose it is to be.
So let us not set about breaking it, nor strive among ourselves to tear such work,
For it is so fine and very rare; let us settle it by lot and keep it whole."
One can say plenty about how the old scripture mentioned this; truly, it would take long to tell, so read it rightly there yourself.
Count off twenty psalms, believe me, from the beginning of the Psalter, if you are so eager for it;
Now I will show you: the one that comes first after that (there is no doubt about it), there you will truly find it;
You will find plenty about these same things in the Psalm, words of this kind; there he tells all of it.
XXIX. Mystically.
This tunic signifies a precious thing. Be quite sure of it: it truly is so.
Its weave signifies Christ's own disciples. They are always whole in goodness and very steadfast.
They are all of one mind in every good thing, and they are always evenly interwoven, all of them, with love.
He wished to gather them together with very fine threads. He himself watches over them, and so nothing there is [?].
Nor does anything come near it that is sewn (of a discordant mind), nor anything that is [?].
They always believe rightly in Christ's body, in his humanity, and with that they cover him all around.
God's beloved servants are the beautiful threads. With them the tunic is always evenly woven.
The good tunic, for which the lot decided, so that it would be kept whole with [?];
so that it was agreed that nothing would be broken, and that none of them would be the one to tear any of it;
and it was fitting for them that one man alone should take it. Care was also taken there that nothing would be torn apart.
It was utterly unworthy of those words for anyone there to say that he would break any part of it,
because holy Charity spun it beautifully. She supplied all the threads and wove it herself.
Truly, as I tell you, she watches over all works. She arranges everything for God and always shows it to his own.
Do not think I am boasting to you: she herself spun the tunic, she herself wove it for Christ, and that is why it is all so whole.
And she measured all of it to fit Christ's body. She fitted it beautifully, just as the Lord himself wished.
She shaped it as was fitting and as suited it best, with very fine threads and an unsewn weave,
of fine yarns. She did that gladly for Christ. It was woven throughout as is proper for the only one.
She watched over it constantly and very lovingly, attending carefully and eagerly to the wondrous garment,
so that nothing in it would [?] when he put it on, and that holy garment would fit him beautifully and without a flaw;
and so that, as was fitting, there would be nothing of [?] there that might come to touch Christ's body.
It would also fit beautifully throughout, as one thread should with another, touching each other and joined together.
She herself wanted this, since she owed it to Christ: that she would inspect all of it herself, from close up,
so that it would match his body completely and nothing would fit badly, since she had spun it herself;
so that no one there could cry out that anything there was ill-fitting to the fullness of the body, since she herself had shaped it;
rather, she herself looked quickly upon Christ and herself gazed at him unwaveringly when she shaped the garment for him.
Good Charity herself fitted it together in this way; even today she unfailingly weaves Christ his garment.
There is nothing so worthy of account (do not doubt that; let it come into your mind) as what Charity does.
She [?] it all out from there to the Lord's house; she is in it always, at every time, forever.
Sometimes her two sisters go away from there, but this one, truly, is always there continually!
30. On the mockery by the priests and by all who passed by.
Then the people went thronging around him and harshly dishonored him with their abusive words.
Many stood there and held him in scorn, mocking him harshly with their own words.
All who were there, and also those who passed by, railed at the whole matter of his own cause.
They shook their heads and spoke evil with it; then they spoke out their spite fiercely:
"Well, woe! This man once boasted in anger that he could undertake to tear down God's house,
and that he could then build it up again at once by himself, and that his goodness would make it stand on the third day!
Look, he hangs there, and he can neither accomplish anything with the house nor come down here.
Now let him help himself up on the gallows, in the shame of this death; the torment urges him to it!
If you are God's son, come down here now; and work hard at this too: free yourself from this torment!"
The priests themselves mocked him with words and zealously reviled him in that same torment.
Their wretched minds [?] heaped reproach on him; they brought it all out just as they had thought it then.
There was very much blasphemy against him there; they let out all the abuse that came into their minds.
"Indeed he healed people," they said, "by his own deeds; now he cannot manage to heal himself!
Make us know it even today: if you are our king, then truly come down here, and we will believe you at once!
Come down from the tree so that people may believe you; unnail yourself from there, and we will become your followers!
Indeed, he trusted in God; let God protect him, now there is need, as you all see here now; let God help him now if he will!
This comes from nowhere else than from his own speech; he himself declared that he was God's son."
That was a pitiful thing now; among the people who stood around there, there were none who grieved over such things!
XXXI. AND THE ROBBERS ALSO [DID] THE SAME.
One of the robbers (I tell you this), since he [Christ] hung between the two, heaped the same reproaches on him, as one should know.
"If you are Christ," he said, "help yourself, now that you are in need; and show your goodness there, and help us here in our distress too!"
The other one, who understood much more, gave an answer; he rebuked him sharply for his foolish words:
"What sort of man are you, that you still do not fear God? You are indeed suffering the same torments by force.
Truly, our deeds are meeting us here, and our misdeeds are now quickly catching up with us.
What we often did, and did not fear such things before, alas, I and you: we are now suffering that same thing!
This other man has no word that is not good and sincere; he was always kind, beyond all these people.
He always did good everywhere, in villages and in towns, to men and to women, while he was here in this life!"
Then he turned his own thoughts, as best he could, as far as the strength of his limbs allowed, and also addressed our Lord:
"Remember your servant with honour, Lord, and let my life enter your beautiful kingdom!
As soon as you are there, Lord, remember me here too, and then think also of your poor servant!"
"I will do as you say," said Christ, "though you are not worthy of it: today you will truly be together with me there.
My messengers will come to you and lead you to me, in my own way, into the beautiful paradise." The
grace that you in your goodness gave to the robber, Lord, work that in me too with your might.
Without doubt, Lord, I am very wicked; I have imitated him and outdone him in sins.
My misdeeds are utterly beyond measure; your grace, in truth, is very much greater,
for it easily overcomes it all, as I have often seen shown; it has always led me away from harm, as I have often felt.
Lord, make it firm now, so that it never again fails me; be gracious to me for ever, so that I may be your servant for all time!
XXXII. AND HIS MOTHER STOOD BY THE CROSS OF JESUS.
His good mother watched all this; these same torments struck her breast
and her tearful heart, and it was for our good; it could not be otherwise than that the pain should strike her.
His beloved friend also stood there alone, pure in virginity; he too happened to be there and saw the misery that had come upon him.
Out of his goodness, then, in this distress, the good son entrusted his mother to him,
so that he would take her to himself and she would not be without comfort; in exchange for her child, he was to care for her in all things.
He provided for his mother while hanging there like that; let us also carry out his command and think of our mother.
33. The sun was darkened, and Jesus gave up the spirit.
The sun was greatly angered at such deeds; she would not let the people of the world see her lordly light.
She quickly withdrew from the wretched deed; in her grief she would not look down on them there.
She would not let them enjoy her beautiful face; for that reason she would not let her bright countenance shine on them.
The brightness I have now told of, in which the world always rejoiced, she denied them, as she had to, for three hours of the day.
That was, in all truth, from the sixth hour to the ninth, which truly should have been the brightest part of the day for them.
She withdrew her bright light from them entirely; she turned it for them into fearful darkness,
for she saw her Lord seized and hanged, the very one who made her, and she was greatly afraid at that.
Then, when the ninth hour came, he cried out very loudly, and his voice addressed his Father's love:
"My Lord, my Lord! Why have you forgotten me, so utterly forsaken me and abandoned me to my enemies?"
They tormented him further and pressed vinegar on him, a bitter drink; they did all this out of malice.
Soon afterwards the Lord cried out again (you can read it there) with a loud voice, which the people there heard:
"Into your hand, Father, I give my soul; I commend to you also, as you know, my own spirit!"
At that very moment he released his soul into his own Father's hand, as he had said just before; so it is told.
One of the soldiers saw this and pierced him to the life; he hurried up with a spear and opened his side.
In this way the meadow, the entrance to the kingdom of heaven, was opened to us; the side opened for us what we had waited for so very long.
Blood and water flowed out of it at once; I tell you truly, we were redeemed by these two.
Then at once the curtain of God's house was torn, the one hung there for the purpose of separating off the cherubim,
the precious altar and indeed the table, and all the lampstands; the curtain fared no better:
it was torn apart then and left nothing covered, because these things were to be made known to us as signs.
Whatever all this signified and always meant for our good, the Lord Christ did it there and then, so that it is open to us.
XXXIV. THE EARTH QUAKED, THE ROCKS WERE SPLIT.
The earth trembled, for the power of God compelled it; and in the same way the stones split apart.
The graves opened, and the dead came out, here into the world: the bodies of the blessed.
I shall tell you a wonder: they went out of the graves, into the city to the people, and showed themselves to them,
so that this news would not stay hidden, and the people themselves would come to know all these deeds.
I tell it here openly: many who were dear to God rose then together with the Lord himself, his beloved servants.
All this was done when the Lord himself chose to rise, and for this we are now glad; he was the firstfruits.
The gospels tell it just as I recount it to you; those same holy books tell it very beautifully.
The centurion himself was greatly frightened by it; after these works he stood there giving thanks to God.
He said that without doubt this man had power over all things, and he declared publicly that he was the Son of God.
The people turned back at once in great sorrow; late in the day they went home from those wretched deeds.
Then they regretted those deeds and beat their breasts, and at once they set off homeward, all full of sorrow.
All those who knew him stood far off, with grieving hearts; yet for them it turned out well in the end.
Those same women who had been with him, and had come to the Passover, then mourned him who was their very life.
XXXV. HOW JOSEPH AND NICODEMUS BURIED JESUS.
Then a noble man came boldly, as was fitting for him; he was angered by these deeds, as a good man should be.
He had not taken part in those deeds or in the plot itself; it had not been his will to carry out such a thing.
He went boldly away from them, in to the governor, and asked that the man be given to him, even though he was now dead,
so that he might take him away, take the body down, and also see to it that he was laid in the grave.
Pilate said he would do just as he asked, and ordered that the body be handed over to him there at once.
Read all the books there are: you will not find, by my faith, that anyone ever did such a thing, or asked for so precious a treasure,
or that anyone in the world ever laid such a treasure on a bier or a litter, I tell you truly.
It was worth more than the angels and the whole kingdom of heaven, the earth and the sea, even though they treated him like this, alas!
Nicodemus the good, who had once come to him by night, came there willingly while he [Joseph] was taking him down.
He truly brought with him a very precious ointment to anoint Christ, as was then the custom there.
Then the two noble thanes took him down from there, the Lord's faithful followers and the dear friends of Christ himself.
The women stood close by and watched all this; they were waiting to see where he would be laid,
so that they would find out whether the men carried him away from there, or whether, as they had arranged, they laid him there properly;
so that they might carry him, handle him tenderly, and anoint the beloved man on every side;
and might take pains over it, tenderly mourn over him, and also tenderly attend to the poor one.
Then they wrapped that same holy body beautifully in linen cloth and with careful concern,
in a linen shroud, there to bury him, with very fine cloths and very pure ones.
Then he alone laid him in his own pure tomb, which was also entirely new and hewn in the rock.
Before they went home, they rolled a great stone in front of it, so that they hid the treasure there, and they turned homeward.
After that journey the women at once went homeward, also to make their ointments for these things.
Truly, the earth then held the most precious of treasures for us there, the treasure hidden there until the morning of the Sun's day (Sunday);
then joy rose up for us, the eternal sun, and also blessedness over all, as will be told hereafter!
XXXVI. HOW THE CHIEF PRIESTS SEALED THE TOMB.
Those same priests still could not give up their wretched will, and they showed it then in words.
Then they went gladly, with their old hatred, truly full of malice, straight to the governor.
"We must not hide it from your lordship," they said. "That wicked man always said something that our minds now recall.
He always told the people a great wonder, in private: 'I will rise,' he said to them, 'on the third day after I am dead.'
Now command that the tomb be watched and kept safe from his disciples, so that they do not deceive us or creep up to it;
so that they do not uncover it or snatch him away by stealth, or steal him from there and win the people's favour;
for then they will tell of his goodness, that he rose from death, and the people will go more astray than even over this deed."
He told them then to work out for themselves how they would guard him; he said the matter concerned him no further at all.
They quickly set about it and sealed the tomb right then, at that time, with great security,
at once, in those very steps [?], with armed men, so that no one would steal him or take him away by force.
The more they then had charge of it and the better they guarded the tomb, the more certain we are ever of the resurrection;
for then those who did the evil bore witness to it, and so did those who were guarding it there: then one could be confident of it!
XXXVII. MORAL INTERPRETATION.
If we wish to keep watch with very right thoughts and to guard Christ's tomb with good thoughts,
then we must hasten to undertake it with other counsels than these deeds;
Let us keep the watch with a different will and a different mind, so that it may turn out for our good!
We must bear weapons and give up sleeping, and remember what he won for us, that he died for our sake;
Let our thoughts be set on true virtue, and let faith stand very firm in the breast of your heart;
Let Christ be held fast with it; do not let him go out from you. Set your mind on it, and do not let him be snatched away from you;
Make sure that you keep hold of him and guard him well by living rightly, so that it may turn out to your joy!
Let your faith be strong, so that his death may profit you, and with his blessing may it prosper for you from now on, forever;
So that God's messenger may set us free with comfort as he did, and always draw us lovingly to him,
As he looked at the women there and spoke lovingly to them with a gentle mind; he did that for their good;
So that fear may not cling to us here in this life, and we may be steadfast in all that is good;
So that we may be certain of his resurrection, that his life is new; the angel announced this to them then.
Let us not do as those advised who bribed the soldiers with money and with words, those very priests,
With plenty of persuasion, so that they would not mention it, so that it would not be found out that the Lord had risen:
Instead, let us take it up very early with faith, eagerly and in earnest (may a good will make us do this!);
Let us truly make it known to people, so that the world may know the good news that Christ rose from the grave;
And let us bring the news to those who are hoping for it, and to those who are willing to heed it with right thoughts;
So that they too may take courage, rejoice together with us, and not hold back from it either, but be glad together with us
Forever, for their good, with a whole heart and with right thoughts, through all the ages of the world;
In which they may dwell from now on, praising the Lord forever, and always giving thanks for his grace,
For his glory and his might, who gave us this joy through his goodness,
So that we may be certain of the resurrection! For the Lord is so good, and therefore let them always have a joyful heart;
Let them always have fitting, beautiful joy through his mercy, without any end! Amen. Here ends the fourth book.
