I. WHY THE LORD BORE THE SHAME OF THE CROSS FOR US, AND NOT SOME OTHER DEATH.
Many people wonder, and I will now tell of it here specially, why the Lord here in the world chose the death of the cross,
when he saved us here in this way, rescued us from the enemies, and took us out of hard bonds, out of the hands of the enemies;
It is also for this purpose, in the end, that our mind may rejoice in such armour against wickedness.
We do it, I tell you, with our two fingers; and there are also two beams of that same cross, take note of it.
Believe me: carry the battle-banner on yourself, on your head and on your breast, and in the desires of your heart.
There is no enemy here in the world who does not give way before it. The devil himself must yield as soon as he looks upon it!
By it we were avenged and his power was pierced through; by it he was wholly overcome, so that he will never recover.
By it the adversary himself was very grievously wounded and condemned far off into eternal torment!
Let it shine on you and let your limbs bear it. Believe me truly: he shrinks from you greatly.
III. The sign of the cross.
Give, Lord, its blessing to my body, and let it always cling to my soul here in this life!
May its blessing, Lord, be on me on every side, so that truly no enemy may attack me anywhere.
May I be fortified by it all around, through Christ, in body and in mind, against every assault [?].
May its sweetness shield my eyes and my feet, and may it also guard my heart, so that the enemy may not harm me!
By it may my breast be firmly blessed, and my head and my hands, and all my limbs to their ends.
May I be surrounded with purity when I make the sign on myself, at once all around, on every side.
May it shield my breast from wretched desires, and my heart and my deeds from evil thoughts!
By it may I always be blessed all around, as I must be, so that the enemy may not rejoice in ever finding a place in me.
By it may I always be enclosed and escape from enemies, entrusted to its blessings and to all God's servants.
So may the enemy, with his malice, always keep away from me, and may good always cling to me here in this life!
IV. On the resurrection of the Lord on the evening of the Sabbath.
Through the power of the cross and the might of Christ himself, may it now come further into my mind how he rose from the grave,
and how they saw him as a friend [?], and how he spoke with the disciples, how greatly he gladdened them and told them good things!
All this misery and the dreadful deeds that we told of earlier here, they did on Friday.
It was truly the morning of the Easter feast, and the glory of that day was very great and famous.
On the evening before Sunday the women rose up at once. They did not delay then; they hurried to the tomb.
Surely each of them hurried then because of the late hour. What the holy day had delayed, love made good for them.
They carried their ointment with them on that journey, to anoint Christ, the beloved man.
And as they went they reflected that it could not be that they would roll the weight of the stone away from the tomb.
They thought they would ask men to do it. Their strength was too little against the heaviness of the stone.
They hurried quickly on the way and saw the tomb. To their great surprise, they found the chain [?] unfastened.
Then at that moment there was a great earthquake and a very great terror, so that they were frightened.
The whole earth shook mightily, and quickly it gave up there the treasure that lay in it.
An angel came suddenly from the height of the kingdom of heaven. He rolled the stone away at once, as soon as he touched it.
(Not that he hurried there to clear the way, but so that people would recognize the wondrous deeds,
and also so that people would know that Christ had risen from his resting place. He gave them the empty tomb to see in its bareness.)
His appearance was (what joy!) as beautiful as the sun ever is. All his clothing was the color of white snow.
Then those who guarded the tomb were struck with terror there, all at once [?], and they suddenly became afraid.
In that same distress they became like dead men. Then the angel at once spoke to the women about one beloved person:
"Women, I say to you: do not be afraid at all! Do not let your hearts be troubled; you came here for a good purpose.
How could it ever be that you should be afraid of us? Truly, we are your own neighbors.
I know why you have come here: you are looking for our Savior, whom these people killed and also buried here,
whom they put to death here, tortured on the cross, on whom they took their revenge, and whom they pierced with their spears.
Truly, you have no need. You have nothing of him here. He left nothing undone, just as he himself promised.
He has escaped from hell and has risen up from death. You have no need to mourn him; indeed, this was promised to you.
In the kingdom of death he won the victory mightily. He fights with it no more and no longer rises against it.
I also tell you lovely good news: there he took his spoils, after he had overcome death there, and led them into another land,
into heavenly glory, his own kingdom, mightily and very far, as was fitting for him.
As was fitting for him, he took everything from death. Believe my word: he left nothing of his there.
Here everyone may see where the body lay, and where the men who arranged it had buried him.
Now you must hurry at once to his disciples and gladly tell them my words.
And do not now keep this message of mine from Peter [?], lest he fail to join them. Gladden all their hearts, for he rose from death today.
None of them set about it, just as that one did not go into the tomb, so as truly to pay heed to it and look upon the benefit there.
Peter, however, came no less for that, and he went straight in. In the same way the heathens became believers at once, as soon as they found it out.
Then the other one went in after him; he had held back from this before. He went in after him in hope when he saw him go in there.
So the times will yet come (this is what these deeds signify) when the heart of the Jews will believe fully in Christ.
They will believe in the cross and in Christ's own suffering, and they will also be certain of his resurrection.
Each one will come to himself as soon as the heart opens itself, and their breasts will soften from the firmness of unbelief.
Then pain will touch the heart of stone; it will begin to sweat and to wet itself with tears.
Then it will begin to soften and to grow pale with remorse, and they will hasten straight to the confession of Christ.
Then that resolve will seem very late to them; truly, many a Jew will then be in very great sorrow.
They will turn to the good with a tearful mind; then they will begin to repent and to beat their breasts.
They will weep with good reason for their long misdeeds, because they did not lament them before, while they lived so wretchedly.
Then they will take heed of their long unbelief and lament the very long hardness of that course.
Then they will begin to wail and to call to God with great haste, so that they may blot out their sin.
Certainly it will then come to pass that they all believe, and that they are of tearful mind in their longing for that good,
as soon as the number of the heathen peoples is fully completed, of those who are to go in there.
Just as the one who went in after Peter set about it, so that he too beheld the deeds with him.
There they saw a wonder: the cloths lying apart, and the sweat-cloth itself truly lying separately there,
wrapped together there out of the same linen, found apart from the cloths in which he had lain wrapped.
The cloth certainly signifies the Godhead, which is in power without any end.
The cloth, which is found wrapped together: know this, you cannot see either of its ends.
So the Lord is in power without any end, and he is without beginning; there was no point at which he began.
In his good things he is far removed from our toils, set apart and wrapped up, just as the cloth was found there.
They will believe these deeds, though it be late, and their minds will recognize how the Lord himself rose,
and how his grace brought it about that he died for us. Then they will lament with good reason the earlier times,
because they followed these deeds so late and paid no heed to what the books told them.
VII. BUT MARY STOOD AT THE TOMB.
Mary, however, never grew weary of it. She stood outside the tomb and wept earnestly there on the spot; she loved him dearly.
Truly, upon my word, she had great love for him, great affection; believe me in this.
Great love above all things, as I shall now tell you here: the disciples went away at once, but she still stood there weeping.
She did not yet give up the place, and she looked into the tomb again; she searched there once more, so deeply did she care for him.
A man who is looking for something he cares about deeply will truly turn back to the place where he just missed it and search there again.
This woman also did as is the custom here. She had already searched it all, yet she searched there no less, and then she looked into it again.
Then she saw two angels sitting there in beauty. They were very glorious, as was fitting in Christ's own tomb.
One sat at the feet, where Christ alone had lain dead, and the other at the head, where the body had lain before.
They spoke to her about her distress and what she wanted there; and by asking her this they also pained her heart.
"Woman, why do you come here? Whom are you looking for? What is your trouble, that you weep so beyond measure?"
"Alas," she said to them then, "I may well long to weep. Pain and sorrow beyond anything I expected have been dealt to me heavily.
I have so much to lament and so much grief to tell that, alas, I do not know in my haste where I should begin.
The pain that touches me here is unlike all other sorrows; it far surpasses every hardship.
For me there is pain upon pain. I will never get over it, and I do not expect ever to find comfort for it among men!
They have taken my dear Lord from me, my dear heart; that is why this pain touches me.
It was not enough for them that they killed him; they also contrived to hide him,
so that no friend would know how he was killed and how he was destroyed, to my sorrow!
Therefore, my lords, as I tell you, I cannot recover enough ever to let joy into my breast again.
And, as I now tell you here, love has brought me woe, because I let his love into my heart, if I may not enjoy it!
If only someone would tell me where they put him, or let me know where they laid him,
so that I might still do some service for the dear man in his death: what that would mean to me then!"
As soon as she had said this, she at once looked back. There she saw the Lord standing, and she had found him.
Yet she did not recognise him at all, and she was quite sure that he was in fact the gardener.
He asked her at once why she was weeping there, and what she was seeking so earnestly with such words of lament.
"My lord!" she said, "tell me, if you took him away, and where your kindness laid my beloved;
I promise eagerly, and that is true, that I will fetch him from there; the labours of love will not be too hard for me [?]."
She had not named him at all before this, because of her great grief; she fully believed that everyone knew whom she meant.
Then he called her by her name, and she at once recognized him; she hurried straight to his feet, but he told her to wait.
"Hold back," he said to her, "do not touch me! I have not yet gone up there into my Father's presence.
Tell my brothers in your own words that you have found that I have risen from death,
and that I am going straight into his own sight, into the glorious presence of my Lord.
Tell them, since you are the messenger, that he is God and their Father, so that they may truly put away their unbelief."
She did not wait at that, but hurried at once to the disciples and told them that she had seen him, and told them the words he had spoken to her.
VIII. SPIRITUALLY.
I want to explain here what the angels signify, the beautiful ones, the ones in white, who sat in Christ's tomb;
who were so beautifully fitting there in the Lord's resting place; they shone out, as well befitted God's messengers.
And it is a great wonder that they sat apart like that, and so agreed together on that good place.
What we call "angels," the Frankish people call, as we say, "messengers" in their language:
those who always choose to announce at once, in quick time, whatever they are commanded.
These two, his angels, stand here for something (they make us certain of the resurrection):
they are those same thanes of God who write down Christ's sayings for us, who write down for us his deeds and his very counsel.
It is shown to us that God is Christ's head; know this gladly: he is our good Lord.
The one who sat at the head proclaims to us with certainty (know this) Christ's divinity.
The one who was seen at the feet signifies another fitting thing: he signifies the beautiful event, the birth of that same body.
John, you know, sat at Christ's head when, gazing so high, he began the gospel;
when he carried it so high and touched on the divinity with very deep words, the divinity to which we always call out.
He also took thought for the feet, for he wrote sweetly for us, very openly indeed, how he came here into the world;
how the Lord did what befitted him and took on our body, how he also became eager to come here and now dwells in us.
The Lord called her by her name, as I told here before (the one whom you call by name is dear and known to you),
It was as if he said to her: "You must recognize me; let it burn warm in your heart, because I know your name."
She recognized him at once when he spoke her name. Before that she had wholly lost that knowledge, while he still called her "woman."
In the same way it was spoken for good to God's beloved, to Moses in truth, the giver of the law.
"I," said the Lord, "know you by name; I do not hide that from you. I know you fully by name, as one should know one's beloved.
I do not mean that I mark you out as one with the common world; I know you specially, in your own affairs."
So it happened here too with the woman who was then seeking the Life. She recognized him as he wished, when he spoke her name.
It was as if he said to her: "You must recognize me; let it burn warm in your heart, that I know your name!"
Then the woman hurried off and made it known to the disciples. So the woman was the very first to tell them of the Life.
Now pay close attention here to the wondrous deeds, the fitness of the Lord's plan, and how remarkable it is:
Long ago a woman gave man the bitterness of death; the serpent enticed her to it.
But now, in truth, this woman came and at once announced life. A woman, I tell you, was the first to announce it to men!
It is just as if the Lord had said this, and he arranged the message so specially for this purpose, so that it would be a greater wonder:
"The same hand that once poured out death for you and gave man woe to drink:
from that hand, and it is also a woman's, you now receive eternal life and joy for your life. Do not be angry with woman!"
IX. TWO OF JESUS' DISCIPLES WERE GOING TO A VILLAGE.
When the eternal Good rose out of the grave, the Life that died for our sake here came back from hell.
On that day two of his beloved followers set out from there. They were two good companions, and their minds were full of sorrow.
As they went, they kept talking about the pitiful deeds and the grievous things, all along that same journey.
They walked along lamenting him and always speaking of him. His manifold goodness came strongly into their minds.
Then the Lord quietly joined them as a companion on the road. He went along with them on the journey, talking with them.
But they did not recognize him, nor did they truly know who he was.
"What is this talk of yours," he said, "and this unhappiness, that you go along so sorrowful in your words?"
One of them answered, as if he were angry that the other did not feel the grief that moved him himself:
"Are you the only foreigner here, from another land, so that what all this world knows does not burn in your heart?
Do you know nothing at all of what has just been done among the people here? We may weep over it forever!"
This happened as they said and also asked him then; as they pressed him, they led him into the house.
Then, I think, they sat down so that they might eat together; they offered him their goods, as one does for someone dearly loved.
Then he took that same bread and offered it to the disciples; their eyes were opened, and they recognized him at once.
Then all of a sudden they could no longer see him at all; at that very moment fear stirred in them.
It grieved them very much that he withdrew from them so soon, when they could have rejoiced in him and looked at him for a long time.
One looked at the other, and quickly they grew afraid; they were dismayed beyond measure over their dear table companion,
that they had lost him like this without knowing anything of it, and that the one they were just looking at had suddenly slipped away from them!
Then they began to talk it over among themselves: how he had walked along talking with them, what the books said about it, and yet they had not recognized him at all;
how the heart had burned in them while he talked with them, out of fear and out of the longing of his love!
At that very hour they turned back at once, so that they might betake themselves there [?] and proclaim it to the disciples.
I tell you one thing for certain: the disciples at once told these two that Peter had seen him, and that he himself had also spoken with him.
Then the two gave them an account of how they too had recognized him, and how they had walked along talking on that journey.
XI. Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples.
The disciples were then gathered in a house for fear of the Jews, because of great distress.
You can see it in the books: while the doors were shut fast, he stood in their midst on that same third day.
(No less on the octave day did he come to them again in the same way, for, I tell you truly, they were gathered there together again;
they were fleeing the same danger then too.) And at once he offered them peace; he gave peace (as I am telling you) to his beloved followers.
He also breathed on them (as you know) that same Holy Spirit, that same power of his, which he had promised them a while before.
"Whomever you promise it to," he said, "you release from his sins. Know for certain, without doubt, that it is at once done on my part.
But anyone you hold guilty and do not release from his sins: that too stands firm above all, without any doubt!"
He granted them this as an honour: that it would be in their power, so that they would govern it all, however they decided it;
that they would govern it very excellently, as befits God's followers, and that at that very moment it would stand very firm.
Then they became troubled, with doubting minds; they did not believe these words because of the joy in their hearts.
He did not delay over it then: he told them to touch his side; they also touched his hands, so that they would not doubt.
The Lord did this because he had been wounded, so that they could not do otherwise than recognize him by it.
When he was willing to die for us, so as to gladden the world, so that it might enjoy him in the frailty of the body:
What wonder is it that he who was to live forever chose to do this, and went in unhindered through doors so locked,
When he became man in order to die for them, the good Son of God, from an untouched mother,
From a virgin kept intact, he, the very Son of the Lord? He did both of these things, since it was in his power.
Here you also read, fittingly, another rare thing, a very great wonder, and this one of Christ himself in particular.
This is as certain as day: whatever can be touched can (as I say) suffer injury.
Here our good Lord graciously showed himself to us, to be touched all over, he who will yet live forever;
To be touched, and his wounds also to be seen, though death (believe me) was never again to touch him,
Nor was any injury ever again to overcome him (surely you know all this, as I tell it to you);
That would be a wondrous deed, as it stands written there, unlike in its goodness any of his other deeds,
Unlike them, as I tell it, all these things, all these deeds, the Lord's plan;
So that they might perceive glory in that body, and something so fitting for a lord as no man had ever seen before;
And so that all his faithful ones, those who were there then and those who came after, would know forever
That by nature he was truly himself, of the same being as before, as his followers had seen him before.
There is still more here of the Lord's teaching, of the Lord's deeds, which we greatly need:
That we may all understand what the account means, what it signifies here, and what it intends for our benefit,
Those same two gifts (we have great need of them), the two gifts of comfort, of the same Spirit of God.
Here his voice teaches us two loves, since he gave them the Holy Spirit twice (as you know);
When he breathed it upon them here, which he had promised them before, he later also gave it from heaven, as he had granted it to them before.
First he gave them that good gift while he stood present before them, and afterwards he sent it to them again when he sat in heaven.
That is the Holy Spirit, with which he comforted them most afterwards, once he had taken his presence out of their hands.
By this men are shown that they should always love one another, and also that their love (as you know) should always be greatest for the Lord.
On earth he gave them the Spirit, so that men might understand above all that love should be enough for them, and that charity should join them together;
Afterwards he gave it from above, so that men might understand from this that they must love God, as he commanded.
By this he also makes known to men here that they should first love one another, so that in this way they may fully come to the love of God;
As he first gave the Spirit here on earth, as I tell, and afterwards from heaven, as I also relate to you here.
There is no wisdom for people, and neither is of use without the other; and a person makes himself hateful to God if he separates the two.
Therefore let us always be eager toward God, with love among ourselves, and love him greatly; then it will go well for people!
This love, which we call caritas, is in no way like other powers (surely you know that).
It is greatly praised in Paul's own words, in his own preaching, this caritas of which I tell you;
The famous preacher truly praises it in many different ways in his own words.
Yet although he was so famous and also so wise, he did not fully recount its disposition, its manifold goodness,
Or its virtue; he could not come to the end of its excellence. That is why it is so glorious.
He recounted many kinds of good about it, and plenty of them, and laded it richly with a good and gracious disposition.
The greatest thing of all is how the Lord speaks of it, as you know, of that same love which he taught the whole world;
How he taught his beloved ones here in this worldly life, how he told them of love with his own voice;
He said that one should recognize that whoever would love it, and would willingly and always fulfill that commandment —
That they were good and very dear to God; for this he brought up his disciples here in life.
Therefore let us always keep in our minds this very great good, this very beautiful joy; and that is called love!
XIII. Jesus showed himself at the Sea of Tiberias.
Here, for our benefit, I tell of a fishing: how they also fared there and recognized Christ himself.
Peter truly went fishing (you can read it there yourself; believe my words) with six of his companions.
They toiled all night in vain: the fish all escaped them, and they caught none.
Then early in the morning he stood there on the shore, and from there he spoke to them where he saw them fishing,
Asking whether any of them had anything that had succeeded for them in their fishing, caught with the nets, for the benefit of friends too.
They told him at once that they had nothing; they said, as I have just told, that nothing had succeeded for them.
He told them to move and turn to the right, so that it would then succeed for them, as he himself told them.
Then they cast their net to the right into the sea, and at once a great multitude of fish came toward them.
Then they hauled with effort, for it was very heavy for them, to the shore and the sand, onto dry land:
Three times fifty (the books record this there) and also three, as I tell you (the Gospels recount this).
The net did not tear or burst, though such a load was in it; it all came whole to the shore, well and as was fitting.
John, God's beloved, spoke aloud to his companions and told them in all truth that it was the Lord himself.
Peter at once began to swim that way, with love and with eagerness; he could not hold himself back.
The others came to land by boat; he could not wait, because he loved him so much.
Then he also went very quickly and eagerly to meet his companions; as you read there, he drew the net to the shore at once.
When they came to the shore, they saw a fire there, and bread ready at hand, and fish roasting.
He told his fishermen to eat their midday meal there with him at once, truly,
and he also told them to bring some of the fish they had just caught on that trip.
XIV. Mystically (the hidden meaning).
It means something very good that the Lord stood there on the shore and did not walk on the waves any more, as he had done in front of them before.
It is very hard to tell all the fine detail of this in Frankish words and to explain it.
Yet I will gladly tell a little of it here, and also show you truly where you can read more about it.
The shore means the joy of the firmness of his life, which he took into his hand when he overcame death.
The sea means deeds and the instability of the world, which always moves here, tossing violently.
The disciples were still out there in hardship; they still had to feel that same worldly pain.
The eternal Lord had overcome that by his powers, and that is true; that is why he stood there on the shore then,
just as if he were saying plainly by this very act: "I am no longer with people in these waves of the world;
I tread the surge underfoot, it can no longer harm me, and now I stand with joy in eternal firmness!"
What the net means, what the number of the fish means, and the group of disciples, that there were seven of them;
the bread on the table with the roasted fish, and also that the same net did not burst under the load;
that Peter drew it to the shore, that no fish escaped him, and that Christ here sat down for the last time with seven servants and ate:
the good Gregory explained this gladly, and very beautifully, by my faith, as is his custom;
Augustine explains it and uncovers it very finely, he who does much good for us, openly and beautifully.
They both deal with this and make it very sweet for us; of what I have mentioned here, we find more than enough there.
XV. So when they had eaten, Jesus said to Peter.
When those who sat there with him had eaten, his dear beloved ones with the Lord himself,
then the Lord himself said: "Do you love me, Peter? Do you love me much more than your other companions do?"
"You know this about me, Lord," he said, "that I have love for you, and in my love you come before all the people of the world."
He said: "Keep firmly in mind what I command you, and always hasten to carry it out with an obedient will."
"Keep my sheep for me (mine, not yours at all), and always truly feed them with my own teaching."
The Lord spoke to him again and asked so often, something no one had seen before, that he alone should do:
"Peter, let me know whether I am very dear to you, and whether with the love of your heart you wish me every good."
Peter answered again with assurance and told the Lord his thoughts:
"You know, good Lord, that I love you greatly, that you are dearer to me, and that no one else comes before you for me."
"Do without fail," said the Lord, "as I commanded you here above. Let it be held fast in your heart, and do not let any of it slip away."
"Look after my lambs for me (mine, not yours at all). Through them let the world know how very loyal you are to me."
He spoke to him a third time, because through this he made amends for the fact that before, truly, he had so often denied him;
he who had so often slipped away should confess three times and declare his love here, as was fitting, after he had so sorely shrunk back in fear:
"Peter, tell me again, am I very dear to you? Is your heart truly loyal to me?"
God's repeated question troubled him. He was very unhappy about it, and then he answered again:
"You yourself are Lord of all and know everything that is in the world. You yourself know my love for you in me."
"Take note," he said, "of the words I told you above. Let what I want, as you know, always matter most to you."
"Now feed my sheep (mine, not yours at all). Through them make it very plain how dear my favour is to you."
"Pay close attention now to my words, and let them cling to your heart at once, for I tell you in all truth:"
"While you were young, you were free to put on your own belt and go wherever you wanted."
"You will stretch out your hands as soon as you grow old, and then another will put a belt on you. I will certainly not hide this from you."
"Many men will lead you where you do not want to go. Yet you will have to go through with it against your will."
Before that, he had told them what was still to come: that they would seize him and hang him on the cross.
XVI. On the Ascension of the Lord.
When the Lord wished to set out on a journey to visit his own kingdom, after the victory, as was fitting, that he had won over Satan,
from whom he rescued us, and whom he laid low in hell, and also won us by force into his own homeland,
he then gave his disciples a command with these words, that they should understand it well and come to meet him.
He commanded them to hurry, at those same fair times, to the place he had in mind and had himself pointed out to them.
They hurried there without fail, as he himself had commanded them. They made the journey just as they were used to, and worshipped the Lord himself.
Then he came closer to them and welcomed them sweetly, though first he rebuked them harshly with his own words
for having hearts so hard in that adversity [?] that they did not at once believe those who had seen him risen.
Since he was about to leave them, he told them a great deal, so that it would stay firm in the breast of their hearts.
There he also told them many things in a wealth of words, and the Lord also spoke thus:
"In heaven and on earth I rule over all of it. All the ends of the world are given into my hand.
Now I shall send you out and turn you to my service. Tell the peoples of the world all that I command you.
Go out preaching as far as this world extends, and proclaim all these things over the whole circle of the world.
Tell them also very boldly that I myself came here into the world, so that my presence might soften their hardness.
Make my own teaching widely known among them. Baptize them and preach, so that they believe in God.
Go to the poor and the rich alike, to whatever has life on earth, whether man or woman.
If they hasten to it and take hold of the faith, let them all be baptized; then that is their salvation.
But whoever does not hasten to it and does not consecrate himself through baptism, and therefore truly does not believe, is already condemned.
You have power to work signs throughout the lands of the world, the ones you saw me do while you were with me.
Heal lepers as soon as you resolve to; drive sicknesses away as soon as you touch them.
Raise the dead wherever you pray to me for it. Old bedridden people are to be counted among these too.
This power is shared among you, so that there is truly no sickness in the world that you will not heal at once.
The devil cannot stand against it wherever you name my name. Wherever you begin this, you are wrestling against him.
So you have no need to fear: I am always with you. You will not lack me any more. Do not fear the pain at all!"
Chapter 17. So those who had come together asked him.
When those who had come to him there had heard all this, they asked him together and very carefully:
"Lord, will you restore the kingdom to this people by your own power, right now in these times?"
This may well give us fear: he sees our deeds, and the mind within its thoughts; we cannot escape that.
Our words lie plain in his sight; whenever a man's mind thinks anything, he makes him give an account of all of it!
XIX. On the Day of Judgment.
For this he has appointed over the whole circle of the world a day of assembly, a very weighty assembly; we have good reason to be anxious about it.
I tell you this here aloud: there is no one, not even one of his own beloved, who can do anything other than come to that assembly.
All the wretched will come there too, all those who here fully did their own wilful desires.
It is grievous to tell! There is no one born of woman (my mind is startled by it) who will not have to be there,
and they will have to give a strict account of their deeds there, all of them surely and in full. That is a very pitiful thing!
It will go well at that assembly for those people who are fully secure there about their deeds.
in whom there is then no evil to be counted against them, so that they may defend themselves and somehow be saved!
For there is no further way out, believe me, by which he might get away anywhere (if he is caught there),
but he must of necessity (if he is convicted there) suffer then forever the woes of the torment of hell.
In those proceedings it goes well for those people who are fully secure there in their deeds!
Do you know what God's prophet says about that time? He speaks of that same assembly, that there will be great distress there.
In him one can read that it is a day of wrath, of tribulations, of destruction, and of many anguishes.
It is also a day of the horn and of the angels' sound, which they blow here on earth so that the world may rise up.
It is also a day of darkness and of whirlwind, alas! Those two will then curse all sinners.
Of great griefs and of deep misery (what more can I tell you here?), the day is entirely full of these!
Have you ever read the passage in which the Lord threatens about it? There he calls to mind that he will then shake the heaven.
Who among men on earth will then withstand him, when he brings it to the point that heaven itself moves,
when he in his power is rolling it up (that may well come into our minds!) as one does with one's book?
That day is not at all like other days, so that a man might escape anything there in his thoughts.
Here and now people take little care about hidden deeds; there even that same little thought will show itself without fail.
It will go well at that assembly for those people who are fully secure there about their deeds.
in whom there is then no evil to be counted against them, so that they may defend themselves and somehow be saved!

20. How he will judge the world.
I will now tell specifically of that terrible wonder, the judgment that is shared by all the world.
He himself meant it this way and made it known to his disciples, and he himself told them fully how terrible it will be. When the Son of Man comes to his throne.
The Son of God himself comes here from the kingdom of heaven with great power and the host of angels,
with great majesty, and all his retinue with him, so that with terrors he may examine whatever people have ever done.
This is what the two meant here, the white-robed, beautiful men, who said that whenever he wished, he would come in the same way.
I will now tell this here to all our dear ones, so that everyone [?] may likewise always be anxious about it and fear it.
That same mighty king sits in glory; he is high, as I tell you, and the whole world sees him.
His throne is unlike any other; I tell you, there has never been anything like it, nor ever will be!
His beloved ones sit there, whom he himself trained here during his life, and they also have great authority over these matters.
The whole multitude of angels goes there to meet him; every one of them comes there in fear.
All people stand before his eyes, the evil and the good; their hearts are heavy then.
There is no man who has ever been born, or is being born now, or truly ever will be, who will not have to be there.
All of them rise from the fallen state of the body, from the foul bed of the grave, to give an account of their works,
Out of the ash, out of the embers, whenever it may happen, out of the earthly ground;
with the same bones, and no others, with flesh and with skin, even if he never wished it!
These he separates, truly, to either side of himself, as a herdsman does who keeps watch there and rules over his cattle.
You need not ask about it at all: they will not begin to quarrel there, to be angry at it or to avenge it, or to say anything about it,
nor will the multitude murmur anything against it; rather, at once it hastens to do as the Lord decrees.
The throngs at once part on every side (no one is united with another there [?], so firmly has his power determined it);
Those who were dear to one another here are parted there for life, for ever more; believe me in this.
The mother is parted from her child, so that she never finds it again, and the father, that is true, is parted from them there;
Lord and retainer are truly parted there from their old affection; believe me these words.
Kinsmen, very dear, who here in life were joined in very tender love, cannot show it there [?]!
As the Lord himself has commanded, so it must of necessity be; there is no one in that judgment who will struggle against it.
They cannot bring it about that what they always loved and continually did will be accepted there:
much pleasure, which they served here; they do not enjoy it [?], and afterwards they weep forever.
Thus, as I tell you, the whole world is parted, friend from friend, in great distress!
Then he sets the good, with joyful hearts, in the circle on the right at that same judgment;
There all the others are in a wretched plight, who cannot escape the left side, who stink just like goats.
The King begins to look with gracious eyes on those who, on the right, of necessity await his word:
They too turn their eyes to him and stand in fear; it weighs heavily on their minds what he will decree concerning them.
With hands and with eyes they begin to look toward him, waiting to hear how he will pronounce his word and what he will judge for them.
He begins to greet them with very sweet words, with great love, in his own voice:
"Come," he says to them, "you who are the blessed of my Father, his blessed ones and my beloved friends;
receive what he has made, the kingdom that he prepared before the beginning of the world, before he called you to it!
You have earned it; you have fulfilled my will; there I will reward you for it with love, truly.
Truly, you relieved my thirst and hunger for me; you also took me into your house, so that I did not go about as a wanderer;
for God's sake you did not allow me to go naked; for God's sake you also eased the sickness in me;
"If I was in prison, you bore with that, and you visited me there too; I never lacked anything from you;
And it also happened that I died: each of you took care that I should be lifted up and buried properly."
They humbly answer the king (they see his kingdom, the high glory,
and are shaken in mind): "Who could expect this, Lord, that anyone at any time [?] saw you in such a state;
that anyone ever carried you as a dead man [?], and that nakedness, thirst and hunger touched you? How can it ever be true
that it came into our thoughts that you suffered weakness, bitter exile or harsh prison;
that this could ever happen (it is far beyond what we imagined!), that anyone ever served you in such need?"
The glorious king says: "I tell you truly, I shall declare it to you above all else; know it without doubt:
My limbs felt it, and the deeds touched me, when you did it to my dear brothers."
He also addresses those on the left there and reproaches them for their wickedness; he begins to attack them with terrible words,
and also to assail them with terrible charges, with grievous force and heavy onslaught.
Woefully he says to them: "You are cursed by God; go from this sweetness into the eternal punishment!
Know this for certain: it is prepared for the devil; with him let those who did his service be forced to share it!
I found in you nothing good, nor any comfort, dear to me, for the suffering that I endured, which I here counted as done to my dear ones;
You did not relieve my thirst and hunger, that is true, nor did you clothe me, nor did you give me comfort in sickness;
And if I died, there was no one who buried me; nor did you lead me into your house, nor did you wait on me with kindness;
Each of you always failed me in what I hoped for from you; for that you shall now truly be repaid very grievously!"
They begin to be in anguish and want to excuse themselves; he drives them all away from there, and their pleading counts for nothing.
With very sorrowful hearts they begin to turn away; Satans drive them into torments that are not pleasing to them;
In truth they have a twofold misery: they lose the kingdom of heaven, and they dwell in the pitch of hell.
XXI. HOW STRICT GOD'S JUDGMENT WILL THEN BE.
Now pay close attention to the Lord's words, bind them firmly in your heart, and see how very terrible they are.
He does not punish them severely for their crimes, but because they forgot and so neglected his service.
If he who does not break bread for the poor is to be in hell, what of him who, beyond that, did not let the poor man keep what was his own?
Now if the man who begrudged the poor a shelter is punished, how far driven out of heaven is he who takes another man's house!
If even the one who does not clothe the naked falls, what do you think will happen then to the one who robs another?
If the one who does not visit the prisoner must burn, the one who binds the sinless will not escape from hell!
Now if the one who does not bury the dead here burns there in pitch, what do you think will become of the man who took another's life?

All the world prays for what I am now telling you here; whoever wishes to become blessed must always be intent on it.

Lead your faithful servants there, Lord, by your own power, to that beautiful life,
so that we may enjoy that delight under your protection, in our hearts, forever, for our good!

so that we may enjoy that delight under your protection, in our hearts, forever, for our good!

so that we may enjoy that delight under your protection, in our hearts, forever, for our good!

XXV. Conclusion of the whole volume.
By the steering of Christ himself and by his grace I have now been brought to this point, moored here at the shore;
I have now turned homeward with my words, and I wish now to make an end of what I have been carrying across like a ferryman.
Now I want to take care to let down the sail, so that my rudder may now rest in the firmness of the shore.
With God's help I have come to the end of the labors that friends asked of me; they did so out of love for God;
They earnestly asked me this by the very words of God: that I should write, for our salvation, a portion of the Gospels;
That I should undertake it in our own language; and I would do it for God's sake, as I was asked.
I could not refuse this; rather, I had to take care to do everything that Charity asked of me;
For she is truly my Lord's beloved; she is the foremost in the household of his service.
Authority over that same service passes through her hand; none of it is pleasing unless it is done with her!
Now, as I tell it, it has been brought to an end with the blessings of Christ himself and by his power,
Written as they asked; their love brought it about, and dear brotherhood too; that I tell you truly.
Here now I wish to ask all the servants of God, all his faithful ones, and my dear friends:
If there is any benefit in these works, let them thank God for it; let them choose to count it as God's gift,
All that was conceived, as the work of his might; and to him, as I say, all these very words.
If there is anything in it that is not fitting, as may well have befallen me, attribute the folly to my dullness,
To my own wickedness, that I was ever so presumptuous, and very much to my own badness, that I paid no heed to it,
The great Jerome also speaks truly of this; in his words he mentioned that same old envy.
He says there are some, those I mean, who even though the work pleases them still pay attention to what is bad,
so that they are always searching for ways to speak about it perversely, and always strive to turn it backwards!
Now since they do not hold back from this, attacking such great men, and do not hesitate to rebuke God's beloved friend in this way,
what then will their insolence and their evil will do to my lowliness? May God protect me first!
So it is with all things, as I now tell you here; so differently minded are the bad and the good:
the one group truly wants to reveal the good at once; the others hasten to destroy it at once.
The good begin it at once and bring it forward, and are very glad of righteous deeds;
all the others grumble bitterly at it very early, and it pains them sorely at that time that it is not covered up.
Now I truly commend myself here to all the better ones, to all God's servants, with Christ's own blessings,
so that this same lowliness of mine may stay in their minds and memory, and so that with abundant words they may commend me to the Lord,
right away at that time, to the ruling Christ, to the ruling hand without any end.
To him be glory over all his kingdom; may his majesty dwell forever over all ages,
on earth and in heaven, and also here below in the abyss, with angels and with men in eternal songs!
He comforted me so here and released me from my labors, so that he remembered me and brought me to shore.
Though I think about them, though I look back on them, I am rejoicing as I stand on the shore.
Glory be to the grace that always granted me this, and praise also to the power without any end,
on earth and in heaven, and also here below in the abyss, with angels and with men in eternal songs! Amen.

Now, gladly, consider that same beloved of God; think about it now, willingly, in Saint Gall himself.

Let us bear it in mind now, for the good of us all, and let this same goodness of the Lord come strongly into our minds.
Here, always and of necessity, we are shown in both, in evil and in good, the deeds that teach us how to live.
Always pay close attention to the better deeds; look all around you at all these worldly things.
All the damned who were wicked, truly avoid them always, and all their ways.
Take into your mind those who are better; then (as I must tell you) you will be God's beloved above all.
